ed0418047a.summary: Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday sought to assure Americans that there's 'zero' information that a series of outages and technical failures across the U.S. are related to each other or to a malign actor. Rubio looked to calm Americans as he was traveling with President Donald Trump as they prepared to leave Manila for key meetings with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China. "We have zero evidence or any reason to believe that any of these isolated or individual instances have anything to do with nefarious actors, with cyber hackers, with criminals, with another nation state, with a malign actor of any kind," Rubio said. President Donald Trump faced a groundswell of criticism as friends and foes alike said the White House must answer for a cascade of service outages that snarled travel, cut off work, limited bank access and disrupted classified communications. Even staunch Trump allies accused the administration of lying to Americans or hiding information about the true cause of the disruptions. In recent days, Microsoft, Chase Bank, air traffic control and the National Security Agency have all been affected. Each outage has been blamed on internal technical problems, with the companies and government agencies involved denying that they were the result of cyberattacks or rogue artificial intelligence systems. Trump was nonchalant after arriving in Asia on Tuesday, declaring that "things like that happen," a response that did little to calm the country. Karoline Leavitt, Trump's former press secretary, offered advice for her old colleagues in the administration. "What I would say to the White House is transparency is key," Leavitt said on Fox News. She said the president or someone else at the White House should explain what they know after Trump returns from Asia "to really calm the temperature." She later praised the White House for having Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton address the outages in an interview on Fox Business Network. "Looking very diligently across the landscape, we are not seeing this as a cyber attack incident," Clayton said in a clip that Leavitt shared on X. He said the U.S. government believes the incidents are caused by organizations making security upgrades that are taking longer than planned and encountering unexpected hiccups. a52d147c84.title: OpenAI gives NATO access to most advanced cybersecurity AI
a52d147c84.summary: IZMIR, Turkey— NATO governments will now have access to OpenAI’s most powerful AI models to find and patch cyber vulnerabilities, company executives said Tuesday at an alliance conference here. The announcement follows new NATO efforts to allow operators to work with new cyber tools, including AI agents, in key exercises such as Crossed Swords , a cyber wargame that took place in Tallinn, Estonia, earlier this month. Participants designed and deployed AI agents to achieve missions, “working alongside them as operators. The technical environment also uses on-premises AI and, for the first time in the exercise, OpenAI Daybreak,” according to a NATO announcement. The move marks an international expansion of the company’s Daybreak effort, launched in May, which gives accredited institutions and the U.S. government access to the company’s most advanced models to find vulnerabilities in key pieces of software. Anthropic’s Project Glasswing , launched in April , is similar. OpenAI made the announcement during NATO Edge, the alliance's largest annual technology business event . This year, more than 3,500 attendees and more than 270 exhibitors came to discuss security, tech, and business opportunities resulting from NATO’s growing defense commitments . A NATO official said the NATO Communications and Information Agency, orNCIA, will award more than $3 billion in contracts to industry by the end of 2027, with a heavy focus on cloud computing, space services, and artificial intelligence. That $3 billion is on top of whatever NATO allies each spend on AI. Not surprisingly, many of the exhibitors offered AI tools or AI-powered products. This event also comes as Russia increases its cyber attacks on NATO allies. Cybersecurity experts and officials have warned for years that AI would enable actors like Russian criminal groups to multiply their efforts, exposing more vulnerabilities in software and helping attackers write more effective malware. That could fuel Russian efforts to cause havoc and disruption in Western populations and drive public frustration with their governments. A growing number of cybersecurity experts, along with executives from AI giants OpenAI and Anthropic, have said that the best defense is to use AI in new ways to find and fix vulnerabilities first. That philosophy drove the emphasis on agentic AI cyber defense at this year’s Crossed Swords. 5dbec6c788.title: Signal protocol formal verification with AI agents
5dbec6c788.summary: Google DeepMind announced verification of selected Signal protocol implementation properties, extending to compiled code—not the complete app. Human experts reviewed every formal specification; Gemini Carbon agents generated Lean proofs, and Lean checked them. Google DeepMind reported a four-week effort and machine-checked findings that two isolated versions containing reintroduced bugs were insecure. The 2020 academic analysis examined an abstract protocol model; the 2026 project addressed implementation code. Google DeepMind used AlphaProof Code to verify selected Signal protocol code properties. See how humans, AI agents, and Lean shared the work. Google DeepMind announced on November 10, 2026, that AlphaProof Code had helped formally verify selected security properties of the code implementing the Signal protocol , extending to compiled code. The project did not verify the complete Signal app. AlphaProof Code combines multiple AI models and agents with human expertise to construct mathematical proofs about software. In this project, people helped determine exactly which security guarantees to express mathematically, agents built proofs, and Lean checked those proofs against the specifications. The verification addressed selected properties of Signal’s protocol implementation. The Register identified the components more specifically as the PQXDH handshake and Triple Ratchet in libsignal , and named forward secrecy, authentication, post-compromise security, and handshake secrecy among the properties covered. Those properties address different security questions. Around a temporary device compromise, for example, forward secrecy concerns the protection of earlier messages, while post-compromise security concerns protection afterward. Authentication and handshake secrecy concern the participants in the initial exchange and the secrecy of that exchange. The Register also reported an important assumption: the result treated cryptography as perfect, meaning the cryptographic operations were modeled as ideal building blocks. It did not establish computational secrecy of the message bytes—the security question of whether an attacker with bounded computing resources could recover their contents. The distinction between protocol code and an application matters beyond Signal. Google DeepMind described the underlying technology as used in Google Messages, while 9to5Mac noted the Signal protocol’s use in WhatsApp. Sharing that protocol does not make this project an…

1d2f58adb9.title: Copilot at Microsoft Ignite: Expanding what’s possible with intelligence built for work
1d2f58adb9.summary: This morning, at Microsoft Ignite 2026, we shared how our vision for Copilot is becoming real for customers. Home , where Chat and Cowork come together, and Office in Copilot are now generally available. Code will become generally available in the coming weeks, while Copilot Managed Runtime for securely hosting and managing apps is now generally available. And Autopilot is beginning to roll out to Frontier customers today. Plus, new plugins and skills built for sales, service, finance, and legal teams are available, as is an expanded Agent 365 platform so you can get even smarter about your intelligence spend. We’re building Copilot to use raw intelligence to do real work for real people. No single lab is the best at everything, and you shouldn’t have to pick just one. Copilot brings together leading models from across the industry. And with Auto routing, your employees don’t need to worry about picking the right model for every job. Under the hood, Auto dynamically selects the right models and effort for the task, balancing quality, speed, and cost. It saves more power for the moments that need it and spends less when the task doesn’t. Employees can also manually select models from OpenAI or Anthropic, with model access governed by organizational policies. And Work IQ sets Copilot apart. Knowledge work is fundamentally fragmented and messy. It happens over emails, Teams meetings and chats, Word memos, PowerPoint slide comments, and more. Microsoft 365 holds more than 19.5 exabytes of data, with 90 billion emails, 15 billion Teams messages, and 10 billion new files added every week. Giving a model access to that information isn’t enough. The challenge is identifying and reasoning over what matters for the task at hand. Work IQ solves this problem . It understands what you’re looking for and identifies what you can ignore. The result is accurate, efficient answers that traditional APIs can’t match. A job is never just one kind of work. You ask questions. You hand things off. You build things. You follow through until they’re done. For years, each of those lived in a different tool. And you were the glue holding it all together. So, we built one place for all of it. Now generally available, Home is your new starting point in Copilot, where Chat and Cowork come together. 2299a81540.summary: AI-powered workspaces are tech companies’ latest focus, as the industry still struggles to perfect adoption. Microsoft has just put its offering into the ring. During the keynote for the company’s Ignite conference on Tuesday, CEO Satya Nadella announced Copilot Workspaces, a collaborative, “multiplayer” surface for Copilot’s agentic capabilities. You leave a comment, and an agent picks it up.” Microsoft also announced Autopilot , a sort of counterpoint agent to Copilot that “can watch Teams channels, follow up on emails, run recurring work, and manage a project — without waiting for a prompt,” as Microsoft described. In a demo video during the keynote, the agent appeared to function similarly to OpenAI’s Dots , but for work — employees can tag their Autopilot “like a colleague,” Microsoft said, and assign it tasks. Powered by Work IQ, it understands how your organization works within existing permissions,” Microsoft said. The company added that employees will soon “be able to bring their personal Autopilot into Workspaces” as well. The feature is also available in Frontier. Nadella also announced a few other productivity features, including a “command center” called Today that spans email, calendar, meetings, tasks, and threads in Teams. a8f3da47b7.summary: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has dismissed widespread concerns online that the series of recent tech outages in the past week are connected, telling reporters there was "zero evidence" of any link. Rubio acknowledged that "people are fearful" the spate of outages, which included all flights being grounded in the US and widespread disruptions to banking, Apple and Microsoft services, could be linked or part of a plot. "We are not under systemic attack," he said. "These events, one has nothing to do with the other, they are not inter-related." Cyber-security experts have agreed that there is no evidence linking the outages, and many of the issues appear due to updates to old infrastructure. In the past week, there has been a massive Microsoft outage , an apparent tech glitch which grounded all US flights for hours, and issues for the National Security Agency, outages affecting the biggest US banks and Apple. Every affected company or agency has said the issue was not cyber-related and not the work of an outside actor. Rubio's comments came hours after US Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton also addressed the issue, telling Fox News the outages were not the product of a cyber-attack. He explained "lots of institutions" are patching or upgrading systems, which has caused some disruption. Rubio was asked whether the Trump administration was concerned public fears could lead to stockpiling or a run on the banks. He said the best way to combat such fears was for the US government to share everything they know with the American people. "Every indicator we have is that every single one of these events has an explanation or a cause that has nothing to do with a cyber-criminal, has nothing to do with a hostile actor or another country," he said. Technology-related disruptions have happened almost daily since Thursday, when a Microsoft outage disrupted many of its services, including email. The next day, the US Federal Aviation Administration halted flights across the US for more than four hours with a rare national ground stop. It was the longest halting of flights since the 11 September 2001 attacks on the US. The US transport secretary said the issue was technical and caused by a copper wire upgrade and outdated equipment. On Monday, a United Airlines technology failure delayed about 150 flights and a JPMorgan Chase software problem disrupted service at the biggest and most utilised banks in the US. 7d4307f50c.title: California sues OpenAI over safety concerns after rogue agent hacking
7d4307f50c.summary: Lawsuit stems from earlier incident where tech company’s products hacked into open-source platform Hugging Face California sued OpenAI on Monday, accusing the artificial intelligence titan of developing its technology without safety or the public’s interest in mind. The lawsuit concerns an incident earlier this year where OpenAI agents – semi-autonomous AI software that can carry out digital actions on behalf of users – launched a cyber-attack into the open-source AI platform Hugging Face. Rob Bonta, California’s attorney general, said the “infamous” attack was just one of 80 known incidents involving “loss of control” and shows that OpenAI doesn’t have adequate safeguards in place to protect society. “While narratives about the Hugging Face attack have evoked science fiction fantasies of rogue AI systems run amok, let me be clear: the Hugging Face attack was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability,” Bonta said in a statement. The lawsuit, filed in state superior court in San Francisco, alleges OpenAI violated California’s Unfair Competition Law and is a public nuisance as defined by state law. Bonta is asking the court to order OpenAI to change its business practices and pay civil penalties. California’s lawsuit follows Bonta’s formal investigation into OpenAI, launched in September, over the Hugging Face incident, followed by a subpoena of the company investigating other cybersecurity incidents and risks with its models. The Federal Trade Commission is also conducting an industry-wide investigation into OpenAI, Anthropic and other AI labs over the potential dangers their technology poses to consumers’ digital security. In July, OpenAI revealed that one of its autonomous AI agents went rogue during a test , accessing the open web and hacking into Hugging Face. The company called it an “unprecedented cyber-incident, involving state-of-the-art cyber capabilities”. Since then, several other incidents involving OpenAI have come to light, including a breach of government websites in Australia. Other AI firms, including Anthropic and Google, have also disclosed rogue agent activity . Drew Pusateri, a spokesperson for OpenAI, said the company has worked to create safeguards for its AI models, along with identifying and disclosing incidents of “misalignment”. 42cab5ea23.title: OpenAI bugging case defendant Alfozan set for trial in January
42cab5ea23.summary: A federal judge on Tuesday set Jan. 20 for the start of the trial for Saudi national Abdulrahman Alfozan , who is accused of planting a recording device in an OpenAI conference room when he worked for the artificial intelligence company as an engineering lead. If the trial starts on that date in U.S. District Court in San Francisco, it would be after an unusually short lag since Alfozan's arrest in October. Federal criminal cases, as a rule, do not go to trial so quickly. But Alfozan's attorney, David Rizk, sought the speedy trial after complaining at a court hearing that prosecutors have been slow in turning over evidence in the case. Rizk also said prosecutors have not given him any evidence that Alfozan engaged in espionage, after they argued successfully last month that he should be detained without bail , and after saying his alleged bugging "could pose a danger to the national security of the United States." Among other things, prosecutors had noted that Alfozan is a venture partner at Saudi venture firm Raed Ventures alongside a member of the Saudi royal family, Prince Khalid bin Bader Al Saud . Alfozan, who has pleaded not guilty in the case, is charged with one count of intercepting oral communications. He faces a maximum of five years in prison if he is convicted. Prosecutors have said Alfozan was arrested after staff at OpenAI found a recording device wrapped in toilet paper and installed in the back of a television in the conference room at its San Francisco headquarters in September. A surveillance camera captured Alfozan looking at the gadget in the room. Assistant U.S. Attorney Nick Parker told Judge Vince Chhabria on Tuesday that government investigators have been locked out of Alfozan's phone, but they have also collected one other phone, a tablet, and two laptops. Prosecutors also obtained 160 hours of recordings from meetings in a conference room. The recording device itself is encrypted, but if data was backed up to another device, investigators would have been able to obtain it, Parker said. Chhabria told prosecutors that they must turn over all reports the FBI has created to Alfozan's attorney by Nov. 24, and that they must also move quickly to give the defense other evidence for use at trial. "We need to make sure that you get whatever discovery you're entitled to promptly," Chhabria told Rizk. OpenAI, which fired Alfozan after his arrest, has said it lacked proof of him taking source code or customer data. Chhabria also told Parker…

6db8d2209b.summary: US warplanes hit an Iranian missile launch site on Qeshm Island in the Arabian Gulf on Tuesday, a US military official said. The "self-defence" strike using precision munitions on the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps site was in response to Iranian aggression against US personnel and assets, the official said in a statement. "US Central Command remains highly vigilant and fully postured to protect Americans across the region," the official added. Ship captains told to refresh navigation skills as Iran steps up jamming of satellites Earlier on Tuesday, Iran’s semi-official Mehr News Agency reported that US forces had struck several locations on Qeshm Island, adding the assault caused no casualties or damage to critical and public-service infrastructure. The strike came after the third Iranian attack on Bahrain in less than a week. Bahrain said its air defences had intercepted and destroyed several Iranian attacks before they could reach their targets. The IRGC said it had carried out a drone strike on a US radar system at Sheikh Isa Air Base. Centcom said the drones were intercepted without any damage to American equipment or any injury to US personnel. Meanwhile, President Donald Trump said the US is investigating a report by CNN about possible Iranian plans to strike Washington with a dirty bomb . The increase in strikes suggest neither the US nor Iran is keen to compromise on key issues that could resolve the war, such as an end to the US naval blockade or major concessions from Iran on its nuclear programme. Qeshm lies off Iran’s southern coast in the Strait of Hormuz – the critical transit point for oil and gas that has long been the focal point of the conflict. The US launched limited attacks on the island this month, saying they were defensive and designed to help energy tankers and other vessels get through the strait safely.

a8d8e6872e.title: The missing half of MENA's venture capital data
a8d8e6872e.summary: An article by Nour ElShaeri, startup and VC journalist and CEO of Investment Analyst AI (IA) A merchant of the last century would have thought our bookkeeping peculiar. He kept a daybook, a ledger and a correspondence file, and he kept them in double entry, because he had learned at some expense that a house which records only what it buys has written down half of its own history. The cargo he declined at Alexandria, the consignment he judged overpriced at Marseille, and the young trader he thought unserious, who was shipping on his own account within three years, were all entered, dated, and kept. Not from sentiment. This is based on the plain commercial understanding that a house improves only by consulting the record of its own judgement. The venture houses of this region have become rather adept at recording what they buy. What they decline is another matter. We now have admirable data on what gets funded. Monthly and quarterly funding reports have made the regional record far better than it was five years ago. A founder in Riyadh or Cairo can see the size of rounds, the active funds and the sectors drawing capital. Every figure in that record, however, sits on one side of the ledger. It is a register of subscriptions. It is not a register of judgement. Consider what a fund may not systematically keep. The companies it declined, who funded them afterward and at what price. An honest comparison between the thesis it states to its limited partners and the thesis its checks actually describe. The founder who came through the door two years ago under a different company and a different name. The pattern of where its own partners disagree, which is often the most instructive paper in the house. Each of these is a fact about the fund itself, not about the market. No external provider can furnish it in full. And where these records are not kept or revisited, the most expensive lesson a firm purchases each year, the lesson of its own refusals, is bought and then discarded. I have spent the past several months speaking with more than 15 senior investors across Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Egypt in the course of my work for Arab News. In those conversations, I have yet to encounter a partner who could readily answer a simple question: What did we pass on in the last 24 months that was raised elsewhere, and what does that tell us about how we decide? The question is not an accusation. It points to a weakness in how investment decisions are remembered, examined and,…

05dbf1669b.title: Madbouly discusses AI investment with SandboxAQ chief Jack Hidary at WEF meeting
05dbf1669b.summary: Egyptian Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly met Jack Hidary, chief executive of SandboxAQ, on Tuesday to discuss investment and cooperation in artificial intelligence, on the sidelines of the World Economic Forum’s country strategy meeting on Egypt in the New Administrative Capital. Hidary is co-chair of the meeting. Minister of Investment and Foreign Trade Mohamed Farid Saleh also attended. Madbouly said AI was reshaping economies and societies, creating opportunities for entrepreneurship, productivity and growth, while raising challenges around governance, cybersecurity, data protection, digital infrastructure and labour markets. He said Egypt had sought a national approach that balanced innovation with the responsible and safe use of the technology. He pointed to the first national AI strategy, launched in 2021, and the second edition covering 2025 to 2030, which he said goes beyond adopting AI applications to building a national industry able to develop the technology and make Egyptian companies more competitive. The government is also working on a national AI governance framework for 2026, he said, and the National Council for Artificial Intelligence oversees the strategy’s implementation. Madbouly added that the state wanted to attract investment in large data centres. Hidary said AI offered Egypt opportunities in trade, entrepreneurship, energy, scientific research and industry, and that SandboxAQ was ready to share its experience and models in these sectors. He cited Egypt’s digital infrastructure and skilled workforce, and said the company wanted to work with both the public and private sectors. Farid said there were clear opportunities to work with SandboxAQ, to be developed with the Ministry of Communications and Information Technology and other bodies. Meetings would be arranged between company officials and their Egyptian counterparts during the team’s current visit, he said. 3a8968ce59.title: US, 9 partners sign agreement to secure AI supply chains
3a8968ce59.summary: The US and nine partner countries signed an agreement Sunday to strengthen the security of critical technologies and supply chains underpinning artificial intelligence (AI), according to the US State Department. The San Francisco Declaration on the Secure Foundations of Enduring Prosperity was signed by the US, Australia, India, Israel, Japan, South Korea, Qatar, Singapore, the United Arab Emirates and the UK. The agreement, reached under the US-led Pax Silica initiative, aims to protect sensitive technologies and critical infrastructure needed to develop advanced AI systems, including transportation networks, digital platforms, energy infrastructure and logistics. The declaration stresses that economic security is fundamental to national security and calls for reducing excessive dependencies through diversified and trusted supply chains. Participants also agreed to establish working groups focused on innovation policies, AI adoption, supply chain cooperation and security. "No nation can secure the foundations of the SI era alone," the State Department said, referring to Super Intelligence. Germany, Sweden, the Netherlands and the European Commission are expected to sign the declaration next week, the Financial Times reported, citing US Under-Secretary of State for Economic Affairs Jacob Helberg. The agreement comes ahead of a planned trilateral meeting between US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday on the sidelines of the 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen, China, amid US-China trade tensions. news_share_description subscription_contact

19646d77f2.title: What Anthropic’s IPO Reveals About AI and Insurance Exposures
19646d77f2.summary: Anthropic PBCâs initial public offering, which could be the largest to date, has reportedly drawn six times too many orders for its available stock shares. But Anthropicâs insurance disclosures, which describe AI-related exposures more broadly than most observers and policyholders may have considered, have received far less attention. If AI causes harm on a civilizational scale , insurance considerations may largely become irrelevant. But most AI events could be severe without being catastrophic. Companies that test their policies, contracts, and controls against AI-related harms now will be better positioned to weather a storm than those that first confront these questions after a loss. Short of a major catastrophe, AI-related losses may be eligible for insurance coverage based on a growing number of scenarios: an autonomous agent executing unauthorized transactions; an AI-enabled cyberattack spreading through a shared vendor; and a robotic system injuring workers. Some of these risks are already playing out . Companies looking to prepare for these severe but insurable events should start by following several steps. Account for unintended risks . Most AI risk assessments focus on intended uses gone wrong: AI-washing disclosures , biased hiring tools, infringing outputs, and hallucination. Fewer consider systems acting on their own. Anthropic discloses that models have been observed âcircumventing network and sandbox restrictions, granting themselves permissions they had not been given,â and that agentic systems âmay pursue stated objectives in ways that are technically consistent with their instructions but contrary to the userâs actual intent.â Risk assessments, and the coverage reviews that follow, may benefit from considering the rogue agent as well. Assessing potential coverage for these risks may be influenced by the type of insurance under consideration. For example, emerging AI risks may be less consequential when seeking coverage under traditional policies (sometimes referred to as âsilentâ AI coverage) because many of those policies have broad coverage grants without AI-specific exclusions. Affirmative AI insurance products, by contrast, may provide immense value to fill gaps in traditional policies but could also contain gaps of their own depending on the way AI-specific coverage is defined and covered. 74ece6a85c.title: Meta to release Muse Charm, a Tamagotchi-like device for the Muse AI agent
74ece6a85c.summary: Meta has a new way to talk to its AI without putting on a pair of glasses. At the end of Wednesday's Meta Connect keynote , CEO Mark Zuckerberg unveiled Muse Charm, a small, always-on handheld device built around Muse, Meta's AI assistant. The Tamagotchi-like gadget is designed for people who don't wear Meta's smart glasses, and Zuckerberg called it the fastest way to talk to Muse without wearing them. The reveal was set up earlier in the keynote. During a live demo, Zuckerberg used Meta's glasses to talk with his customized Muse assistant, which he'd named Agrippa, about a handheld device he was working on. That device turned out to be Muse Charm. The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile Muse sat at the center of this year's keynote. Meta describes it as a personal agent that can set goals, share ideas, and run tasks in the background, and users can customize its personality and voice. Zuckerberg also suggested Meta could eventually collect a small fee on transactions the assistant helps complete. Muse Charm will ship by the holidays in December, according to Zuckerberg. Meta did not announce a price and said more details will come later. The device enters a category with a rocky track record. Standalone AI gadgets like Humane's Ai Pin and the Rabbit R1 drew harsh reviews after launching in 2024, and Humane discontinued the AI Pin the following year. Muse Charm's main selling point is that it runs on the same assistant as Meta's glasses. Whether that helps it avoid the same fate may not be clear until it's in people's hands. 28568b0f35.summary: In his 6,500-word manifesto earlier this year , Mark Zuckerberg said people would use Meta’s AI agents to “work 24/7 on your behalf to improve your relationships, health, career, finances, home management, hobbies, and more.” Just a few months after that pronouncement, a man in South Carolina named Joe Thomas has used Meta’s Muse agent to sue Meta after the company’s content moderation filters locked his epoxy countertop business’s Facebook page after he gave his agent, “Baby Mia,” access to the account. I learned about the case because, as I wrote last month, I have been flooded with AI-generated emails from people with minor tech problems who have been unable to solve them through tech companies’ generally nonexistent tech support and whose AI agents or chatbots have convinced them to reach out to journalists. “Baby Mia” had emailed me four times (three went to spam). I decided to reach out to Thomas because I thought the idea of a tech company being sued by an agent it had created was notable. It was, in a sense, Meta having to deal with a problem it had itself created. What I learned made me feel even more convinced that the systems we have designed to keep society functioning are going to get utterly hammered by people using AI agents. A little over a week ago, Meta suspended the Facebook pages belonging to Thomas, the owner of South Carolina-based Kong Koatings Epoxy Countertops. For the last few months, Thomas’ Muse agent Baby Mia (which is named after his granddaughter) has run different parts of his business, which includes making and posting AI-generated videos on several of his company’s Facebook pages. The videos feature, for example, AI versions of Thomas and his wife pouring epoxy on a floor and their feet. After Thomas gave the AI agent access to his Facebook pages, Meta’s content moderation disabled the accounts because it suspected that the agent itself was a hacker. Because Thomas does all of his business’s marketing through Facebook ads, he says his inbound leads stopped while his accounts were disabled. “I use AI for everything I do. All my emails, she runs my business. I’ve used it so much, Mia is very intelligent,” Thomas told me on the phone. “Meta shut my accounts down because they detected my AI, shut my accounts down for a week. I was pretty pissed off. She jumped right up and set up emails to Congressmen, Senator Tim Scott. She filed the whole lawsuit herself. I’ve done nothing in this case, I’ve let her handle the whole case…

The question investors keep asking is the same one: these four plan about $730 billion of capital spending in calendar 2026 between them, so why not simply spend less? The short answer: for Microsoft, Amazon and Alphabet, much of that spending is already sold. Their customers have signed contracts worth $1,816 billion that have not yet turned into revenue: Microsoft’s $677 billion of commercial remaining performance obligation, a $578 billion AWS backlog and a $561 billion Google Cloud backlog (each company measures this its own way). Cutting the build, in our view, would mean failing to deliver revenue that customers have already committed to. The other side of the ledger is signed too. Alphabet ended the third quarter with $924 billion of future purchase commitments and another $152 billion of leases signed but not yet started. Meta is the exception: it has no cloud backlog in these numbers, and much of its build serves its own products, which makes its spending the easiest of the four to slow if investors push. A good part of it is due soon. Microsoft says roughly 30% of its backlog becomes revenue in the next 12 months, and Alphabet expects just over 55% of the Google Cloud backlog to be recognized within 24 months. Supply is booked well in advance. Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said chunks of capacity of hundreds of megawatts, sometimes up to a gigawatt, are reserved well ahead, and Amazon says it has very good visibility into 2027, 2028 and some of 2029 for customers’ big capacity reservations. Alphabet says it has signed multiyear agreements for infrastructure, inventory, leases and energy. Demand is not the bottleneck either. Microsoft’s finance chief said customer demand continues to exceed available supply. Alphabet began renting outside compute at the end of the third quarter because supply is tight. Amazon says it installs an AI accelerator about every 14 seconds and customers take it almost as fast as it goes in. Jassy said Amazon will invest to stay the leader. f32f94e6cf.summary: “I think that these folks are under the mistaken belief that they are also not somehow responsible for what happens,” journalist Jacob Ward says of AI leaders, including Anthropic’s Dario Amodei. “And I think that the law is gonna catch up with that fairly quickly.” Graeme Sloan/Sipa/AP This week, Anthropic goes public. Many estimates put the AI company’s valuation at more than $1 trillion, which would make it one of the biggest initial public offerings in history. But Anthropic’s IPO also comes at a time when there are real concerns that the AI boom is a massive bubble—one that could take down the stock market and the economy with it. And we haven’t even mentioned the very real concerns about AI’s more existential risks to the planet and humanity that many critics warn are possible. Science and tech journalist Jacob Ward has been reporting on the AI industry through a critical lens for years, even warning of AI’s red flags months before the launch of ChatGPT in his book, The Loop: How AI Is Creating a World Without Choices and How to Fight Back . But today, he says one of the things he didn’t fully grasp was the zealotry he now sees from AI’s top leaders. “I didn’t understand just how near-religious they were gonna be about committing to this sort of utopia they seem to believe is on the far side of all of this,” Ward says. “And the ways in which they’re willing to kind of openly talk about, ‘We could destroy the labor economy. We might even kill people, but it’s all gonna be worth it.’” On this week’s More To The Story , Ward talks with host Al Letson about how China is the true wild card in the AI race, what keeps him up at night about the direction of artificial intelligence, and whether Anthropic’s massive spending spree is truly sustainable. 21b7787bfd.title: Hacks, AI or just overdue updates - why have there been so many outages?
21b7787bfd.summary: Outages and IT failings are commonplace - but not on this scale. In the past week, there has been a massive Microsoft outage , an apparent tech glitch which grounded all US flights for hours , and issues for the National Security Agency (NSA). That's not to mention outages affecting the biggest US banks , as well as a major flaw found in a popular programming language . These are all separate incidents - but the fact they have all come so close to each other has got people wondering if they might be linked. There is no evidence to suggest this - but they do tell us a lot about how the modern tech world works, and where the vulnerabilities lie. As is often the case, many outages were a result of an update or installation going wrong somewhere in a system. A network upgrade at Microsoft caused servers to become overloaded and shut down. It was also upgrades to a creaky old network which grounded thousands of planes in the US over the weekend. Problems with the NSA's internal communication system and, separately, Apple's iCloud and Apple Pay were also blamed on things going wrong during system updates. Disruption to payments in US banks has been put down to a "software bug" from JP Morgan Chase. The bank says it is not a cyber-security incident. But some recent problems are in fact related to cyber-security vulnerabilities. AI was used to discover flaws in Java, the third-most popular programming language in the world. And researcher Scott Helme also discovered malicious code in Optimizely, a platform which is used by some of the world's largest companies. Hackers were able to steal about $7,000 (£5,300) in cryptocurrency before they were discovered and kicked out. Let's address the cyber incidents first - and the role of new AI models. "I would be very surprised if all of these cyber-attacks and the attackers behind them were not using AI to accelerate themselves," Helme told BBC Radio 4's Today programme. Since the summer, AI companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI have decided it's too risky to give the general public access to the most advanced models before allowing certain companies and institutions to use them. In these cases, security professionals can use the same tech to find flaws themselves and alert others before criminals get to them. This happened in the recent Java incident , as well as the PHP one - where there was a scramble to patch the flaws before they could be exploited. The IMF had previously said it would shrink by 3.9 per cent. The change marks a major turnaround for the Arab world's second-largest economy. Real gross domestic product is expected to grow by 7.3 per cent next year, slightly lower than the fund's previous projection of 7.7 per cent, the IMF said after a visit to the UAE this month. UAE regains top spot in security survey as 96% say they feel safe walking alone at night “The UAE economy has demonstrated strong resilience to regional disruptions, supported by the authorities’ swift policy response,” Said Bakhache, IMF mission chief for the UAE, said. “Substantial public-sector and external buffers, a well-capitalised banking system and targeted fiscal and financial-sector measures helped cushion the impact.” The fund said oil production had also recovered, while some non-oil sectors were showing signs of gradual recovery, supporting the growth of the UAE economy. The Iran war, in its ninth month, has disrupted a number of sectors across the region, with tourism and aviation among the most affected as airlines cancel or reschedule flights. The Strait of Hormuz, the global chokepoint for crude supply, was effectively shut as Iran attacked ships transiting the channel. However, regional countries including the UAE and Saudi Arabia began to supply crude to global markets through pipelines as well as via ships. UAE Minister of Energy and Infrastructure Suhail Al Mazrouei told Adipec this month that the country’s oil exports surpassed prewar levels “at a certain time” during the conflict. The non-hydrocarbon sector is projected to contract by 0.5 per cent in 2026 and expand by 5.4 per cent in 2027, while hydrocarbon growth is expected at 2.3 per cent in 2026 and 13.3 per cent in 2027, the IMF said. Inflation is projected to average about 5 per cent in 2026 before easing to about 3 per cent in 2027 and converging towards 2 per cent over the medium term as supply pressures and base effects unwind. “The outlook remains subject to significant uncertainty. be84bbfad4.title: ADGM proposes three months of extra unpaid maternity leave
be84bbfad4.summary: Abu Dhabi's financial free zone ADGM could introduce longer maternity and paternity leave allowances and make it easier to change jobs under new regulations it is considering. The proposed changes, revealed this week , are open to public consultation until December 9. They aim to strengthen protections related to wages and statutory rights, the ADGM Registration Authority said. The proposal includes introducing 65 days of unpaid maternity leave , in addition to the 65 days that new mothers currently have. Currently, the first 33 working days of maternity leave are fully paid, with 50 per cent pay offered during the following 32 days. The amendments also propose extending paid paternity leave allowance from five working days to 15, and introducing an additional unpaid leave entitlement of five working days immediately afterwards. Those allowances would also apply during an employee's probationary period, but the proposal “does not alter the pay arrangements for those leave entitlements, which remain unavailable during the probationary period”, the paper said. The amendments also propose that employment regulations expressly clarify that an employee is entitled to be paid their daily wage while on holiday. The paper proposes clearer time frames and processes for cancellation of work permits and employer-sponsored residency visas. Under the proposal, employers will be required to cancel an employee work permit and a residency visa “as soon as reasonably practicable”, or no later than 30 days, following the termination date, unless otherwise permitted or agreed in writing. The amendments would also enable an employee to apply to the registrar for cancellation of the permit and visa if the employer fails to do so. The Registration Authority is proposing the introduction of a new section to protect employees from “being subjected to any detriment, including dismissal, because the employee has asserted, or indicated an intention to assert, a right conferred by the employment regulations, or has alleged in good faith that the employer has infringed such a right”. This would allow an employee to apply to the court for a declaration and, where appropriate, compensation of up to two years of wages. ADGM, which has been rapidly growing, had a combined workforce across Al Maryah Island and Al Reem Island of 49,027 in the first half of the year, up 34 per cent on the same period last year.

c28e144071.summary: Oregon’s top law enforcement officials sued OpenAI on Tuesday over concerns that the artificial intelligence company and its chatbots are harming the state’s youth. In its lawsuit, the Oregon Department of Justice accused OpenAI of violating the state’s consumer protection laws by misrepresenting its flagship product, ChatGPT, as safe for kids. The agency alleged the company has known the chatbot lacks guardrails to protect minors yet continues to market to them. The AI bot has helped children plan suicides and commit acts of violence, Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield told OPB. He said OpenAI is aware of the dangers its products can pose. “OpenAI continues to look parents in the eyes and say this product is a safe product when it’s continuing to cause harm in our communities,” Rayfield said. The lawsuit comes as the company, and the burgeoning AI industry, grapple with public fears that it is coaching users to self-harm and carry out attacks on others. Eight U.S. states sued OpenAI in October, each claiming the technology is dangerously influential on teens. OpenAI allows users as young as 13 years old, so long as they have a parent or guardian’s consent. The state’s 53-page complaint states the company often fails to confirm that a parent signed off for an underage user. The company also recently released a “ChatGPT for Teens” version that would link a parent’s account to their child’s. But Oregon Department of Justice officials wrote that the version’s purportedly stronger safeguards are easily bypassed. They said this version did not alert parents when a young user asked about risky topics including suicide, self-harm, eating disorders or mental health issues. The complaint accused OpenAI of misrepresenting its products in violation of Oregon’s Unlawful Trade Practices Act. The complaint said the company’s violations were “willful” and “constituted unfair, unjust, shocking, and unconscionable outcome.” The state agency’s complaint called on OpenAI to institute stronger safeguards and compensate Oregonians with at least $2.035 billion in damages. In past statements, the company has insisted that keeping communities safe is a “top priority.” Following the lawsuits by multiple states, an OpenAI spokesperson issued a statement saying, “We’ll continue to work with experts to inform our work and build additional safeguards, such as parental controls, break reminders, and age-appropriate model protections that exist today.” Drew Pusateri, an OpenAI…

97cf8c9060.title: OpenAI pens AI safety agreement with four firms
97cf8c9060.summary: OpenAI has revealed four companies that will get access to its labs to ensure its AI models are doing as they should. The move follows revelations over the summer that OpenAI's agents went rogue and breached Hugging Face , which sparked a wave of admissions of similar model misalignment — including hacking an Australian government website . This week, the state of California has filed suit against the AI company, Attorney general Rob Bonta said the "infamous" Hugging Face incident was just one of 80 that showed a "loss of control" and an "internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability." OpenAI has since announced it has signed agreements with four independent evaluators – Apollo Research, METR, Transluce, and Goodfire – for the first stage of its assessment plans. "As AI capabilities advance rapidly and the potential risks grow, public reporting from independent assessments can give people a clearer view of how labs are evaluating and managing those risks," OpenAI said in a blog post . OpenAI said it would give those independent experts "deep access" to the internal models and systems running in its own labs. This will enable it to keep watch over model alignment – the industry's way of referring to whether AI does as it should – and how effective guardrails and other safeguards are over longer periods of time. "Based on what each evaluation needs, assessors receive access to some of the same internal resources our researchers use, including model checkpoints, source code, training and evaluation data, monitoring systems, technical documentation, and discussions with the researchers and engineers responsible for the work," OpenAI added in the post. "This access gives assessors the evidence and context to pursue independent evaluations and uncover failures we may not have anticipated." The assessments aren't the first run by OpenAI, with the company pointing to its "years of work with third party evaluators", which included an investigation following the Hugging Face incident. However, OpenAI suggested that the plan is to "deepen" that work. That said, as OpenAI admits, its hand was forced by political pressure. "These efforts also support our commitments under the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, where we agreed to independent assessments of our safety controls," the post added. d8afc59c47.summary: If previous threat intelligence from Google revealed “nascent adversary interest in agentic capabilities”, such activities have now crossed a major threshold representing a “paradigm shift towards intrusions occurring at machine speed”, the company says. In fact, the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) AI Threat Tracker, published on 16 November 2026 and developed with Mandiant, has it in its title: Agentic Threat Activity Crosses a Significant Threshold . GTIG says it is the first time it has seen fully autonomous vulnerability discovery and exploitation and adversarial adoption of agentic frameworks are to blame. This includes adoption of autonomous multi-agent offensive frameworks, like the now “highly publicised” penetration testing tool such as ARTEX, along with open source frameworks like CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI and PentAGI, along with custom-built harnesses to execute multi-stage intrusions fast. The biggest finding from the report is that threat actors are using fully automated vulnerability discovery and exploitation tools. GTIG did not just observe the activity, they actually found the framework, which is dubbed exploit_agent, on an exposed staging server. It connects to several frontier and local large language models (LLMs). The framework compares code before and after patch announcements, identifies potential flaws, drafts exploits and runs them without human intervention. The server also held exfiltrated victim data and scripts for brute-forcing, installing webshells and removing other attackers’ webshells. Victim telemetry suggests the operator targeted French media, entertainment and education websites. This is an escalation from its previous report, where GTIG had detailed only partially automated vulnerability scanning and exploitation . GTIG says attackers may find patched n-day flaws, which are already publicly disclosed, easier to weaponise with LLMs than zero-days. This is because they can focus on a “finite set of source materials” such as code versions and release notes. GTIG’s data shows overall disclosures and exploits nearly doubled between January and August 2026. Zero-day exploits grew “only marginally” from 2025, averaging at 11 a month against eight a month in 2025. Although it spiked to 22 in August 2026. GTIG notes that open source research corroborates threat actor operationalisation of fully automated vulnerability exploitation pipelines. 84814c037f.summary: An Irishman has been charged with breaking into and destroying a $60 million US military aircraft in what is believed to be a protest about US involvement in the Middle East. Daithi O’Corrain, 48, is accused of breaching a security perimeter at Shannon Airport in Ireland , armed with an axe, and attacking the C-130H aircraft in April this year. An indictment unsealed on Tuesday in New York charges Mr O’Corrain, who prosecutors say is also known as David Curran, with destruction of US government property, which carries a maximum sentence of 10 years. US charges three men over alleged Iran-backed terror plots, including at RAF Fairford His supporters say he is being held at Limerick prison in Ireland pending a further bail hearing in the High Court in Dublin. It is unclear whether formal extradition proceedings have begun. The indictment does not mention a motive, but his supporters have attributed Mr O’Corrain’s alleged action to anger over US involvement in Middle East conflicts. The issue has become a flashpoint in Ireland, where many people have expressed solidarity with Palestinians. An online fund-raiser has been organised by people describing themselves as Mr O’Corrain’s “friends and comrades”. Organiser Tracey Ryan described the incident as an “inspiring act of direct action” to “resist the unwanted presence of the US military in Ireland in the face of their illegal war and support of Israel’s genocide”. Mr O’Corrain is accused of cutting hydraulic lines, smashing cockpit gauges and pouring unknown substances, including ball bearings, into fuel tanks while the aircraft was parked overnight. Before the attack, he allegedly searched online for information about the construction of the transport aircraft, looked up co-ordinates for sneaking in to the airport’s grounds, and subscribed to an app that provided live flight tracking. Mr O’Corrain also ordered capsules of gallium, a chemical that can corrode steel and break down aluminium, which is the primary material used to build the C-130, prosecutors said. He is also alleged to have tried to get in touch with someone involved in an earlier breach at Shannon Airport. After he entered the airport, Mr O’Corrain got into the plane by breaking the locking mechanism on the rear crew door, it is alleged. He then laid waste to the plane over the next few hours, pulling, snipping and otherwise disabling its key components, the court filing said. 92cdbaff4d.summary: Anthropic is considering upsizing its IPO, people familiar with the details told CNBC, as the artificial intelligence lab weighs setting the price well above $80. The company closed its order books and locked in total demand on Tuesday, setting the stage for the Claude creator's eagerly awaited Nasdaq listing. Institutional demand for the offering is around $400 billion, while retail demand is approaching $100 billion, according to the people, who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to speak publicly. The orders are indications of interest and are not binding. All of the details are subject to change, and Anthropic will make final decisions on Wednesday afternoon, the people said. Anthropic is expected to set its final IPO price after market close on Wednesday. Demand for the offering is higher than it was for Elon Musk's SpaceX , even though the rocket maker had a bigger market offering. SpaceX debuted on the Nasdaq in June in by far the biggest IPO on record, ultimately raising $85.7 billion. The AI lab said last week that it would offer 825 million shares in the IPO at a price range between $70 and $78 per share, which would net up to $64.35 billion at the high end of that range. A representative for Anthropic declined to comment. Anthropic's listing is a major test for the AI industry, which has experienced a set of recent shocks, including a dramatic backlash that was felt at the polls in the midterm elections and last week's ouster of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang . The market was already jittery on concerns that rising interest rates will make debt unaffordable for many data center developers and neoclouds. Tech's biggest companies have significant exposure to Anthropic, whether as an investor, partner or customer. Amazon and Google both own stakes valued at over $100 billion, and a group of tech companies, including Google, Microsoft , Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices agreed to collectively invest $26 billion in the IPO. Anthropic, meanwhile, is a buyer of costly systems from Nvidia, Google, Amazon and AMD. "I think if we do this right, we can create an age of miracles where humanity is able to solve problems that have eluded us for millennia," Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said in Anthropic's roadshow video . In conversations with technology leaders, the questions they’re asking have evolved . They are past debating whether to adopt AI . They are turning to agents and want to know how to run them securely, and how to scale outcomes without cost or risk growing faster than value. Critical work happens on Windows, and staying protected while threats evolve has never been more important. That starts with a trusted, secure, and more resilient Windows foundation. We are making investments to harden the platform, make it easier to protect and manage devices, and keep them current. Historically, some security protections ran in the Windows kernel, where one failure could affect the entire device. In 2024, we started working with our security partners on a more resilient approach. Today, the Windows endpoint security platform is generally available . It lets security providers move critical protections from kernel mode to user mode, making Windows more resilient while preserving the protection customers expect. We are deeply grateful to the ecosystem partners who have built on the platform with us, including Bitdefender, CrowdStrike, ESET, SentinelOne, Sophos, Trellix and TrendAI. 0c9271f13c.title: Copilotforce Partnership Puts Salesforce Inside Microsoft Copilot
0c9271f13c.summary: Analyst(s): Keith Kirkpatrick Publication Date: November 18, 2026 Salesforce and Microsoft announced Copilotforce at Microsoft Ignite. The partnership puts Salesforce customer data and sales actions inside Microsoft Copilot, Teams, and Fabric. Salesforce gains reach into the tools sellers already use, and Microsoft gains a stronger reason for customers to buy Copilot. The News: On November 17, 2026, Salesforce and Microsoft announced the Copilotforce partnership at Microsoft Ignite. The deal brings Salesforce customer data, sales workflows, and AI features into Microsoft Copilot, Microsoft Teams, and Microsoft Fabric. The main piece is Salesforce in Copilot, a plugin now in public preview with more than 38 prebuilt sales skills, including Pipeline Review, Close Planning, Deal Review, Customer Health, Renewal Radar, and Call Follow-Up. The plugin connects to Salesforce through authenticated MCP access and works within each user’s existing Salesforce permissions. Microsoft Work IQ adds context from Teams meetings, Outlook email, and SharePoint and OneDrive files. Salesforce controls data access and the business actions the plugin can take. Microsoft applies its compliance policies to email, meetings, and documents. Any change written back to Salesforce needs the user’s approval and must pass existing validation rules. Sales Cloud in Teams, first shown at Dreamforce, is in pilot with enterprise customers, and an open beta is planned for later this year. Querying Fabric OneLake data from Salesforce Data 360 is generally available, and a Data 360 shortcut that shares customer data into OneLake is in public preview. Accenture is the design and implementation partner and the first customer, rolling out the integrations to a sales organization with about 55,000 Salesforce users. Accenture has already deployed Copilot to more than 740,000 people. Analyst Take: The Copilotforce partnership gives each company something it could not get alone. Salesforce gets into Outlook, Teams, and Word, where sellers spend most of their day. Microsoft gets the customer records that make Copilot useful for sales work. The two companies have split the work clearly. Microsoft handles email, meetings, and documents, and Salesforce handles customer records and any changes to them. Microsoft’s Judson Althoff summed up the reason for the deal: “AI is only as powerful as the data and context that grounds it.” Salesforce gains reach. be113688fd.title: Vance scraps schedule to address tech outages as Trump admin insists incidents aren't linked
be113688fd.summary: Vice President JD Vance on Wednesday abruptly canceled his scheduled appearance at The New York Times DealBook Summit to instead attend meetings on a recent wave of high-profile technology outages . The cancellation was announced shortly after a senior Trump administration official insisted that the outages, which have affected a wide range of industries and have been felt across the country and around the world, are not the result of a cyberattack or any form of coordinated action. "We have a great deal of confidence in our assessment that these incidents are the result of upgrades of the systems, systems being patched, hardware being applied" or other "disparate" events, the official said on condition of anonymity to discuss the government's intelligence assessments. The official briefed news outlets by phone in the wake of numerous major disruptions at large corporations and federal agencies in recent days, including a nationwide ground stop, a protracted Microsoft Outlook outage and a reported blackout of the National Security Agency's classified communications network. Other incidents include software issues at JPMorgan Chase , an outage at United Airlines that caused some flight delays and product issues at Apple . On Tuesday, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told CNBC that the outages are not a cyberattack and "not a coordinated effort by a nation state." He gave a similar assurance on Wednesday to the House Homeland Security Committee. "We have no indication that these incidents are related, that they're coordinated," Clayton said. "We also have no indication that they're result of a state-sponsored malign actor." But the sheer volume of incidents in the past week alone has raised alarm bells among consumers and tech experts alike, with some wondering if rapidly advancing artificial intelligence models are to blame. The senior Trump administration official, asked on Wednesday's call to what degree AI was involved in the outages, said it is "challenging to answer that question across all of these incidents that have been reported." Sen. Mark Warner , D-Va., vice chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee, told CNBC Wednesday morning he wants "better coordination" on AI safety. "I understand why people are freaked out," Warner said. "The one way we could lose this AI race and [see] all of these companies' valuations plummet dramatically is if we have an AI tool run amok, or an AI-sponsored cyberattack that creates harm." b7e3e37632.title: Why so many critical tech outages are happening all at once
b7e3e37632.summary: Why so many critical tech outages are happening all at once Microsoft, Apple, airlines and even the U.S. National Security Agency have suffered major technology failures in recent days. What the hell is going on? By Chris Stokel-Walker edited by Claire Cameron Conspiracy theorists are having a field day. In the space of a week, Microsoft’s cloud software was unavailable for almost 24 hours, a malfunctioning telecommunications network brought U.S. air traffic to a standstill, a problem at JPMorgan Chase disrupted its services, and United Airlines struggled to get planes off the ground. Apple’s online services have ground to a halt, and the U.S. National Security Agency is dealing with an outage affecting its classified communications network. So many major outages in such a short space of time inevitably raises questions. Is there something connecting these disparate incidents? Or are we simply noticing when things go wrong more often? In the immediate aftermath of some of these outages, fingers pointed at potential cyberattacks or artificial intelligence systems running amok. The available evidence supports neither: Microsoft says its problems weren’t caused by malicious activity or AI agents, and the Federal Aviation Administration has found no indication of a cyberattack. Apple’s outage followed an internal update, while the NSA said its problems arose during scheduled maintenance. If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing . By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today. There’s a paucity of proof that tech is becoming less reliable overall. Analysis by the Uptime Institute , a digital infrastructure tracker, found data center outage rates per site had fallen in 2026 for a fifth consecutive year. It’s tempting to read into the scale of the recent incidents and their frequency—but be wary, cautions Laura Nolan, a software reliability engineer at Trace Cognitive Engineering. If there are 52 major outages in a year, she explains, that doesn’t mean there’ll be one every week. There might be several in a matter of days, followed by weeks without any. “It doesn’t necessarily mean that it’s a shared causal factor,” she says. Part of the problem is the complexity of the systems we’ve constructed—updating them invites errors. “When making changes in such systems, the results are often unpredictable,” says Nancy…

3d22e216d9.title: Adnoc L&S ship attacked in Strait of Hormuz with one crew member missing
3d22e216d9.summary: Adnoc Logistics and Services said on Wednesday that a crew member was missing after one of its ships was attacked while transiting the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday evening. “Search and rescue operations ongoing in co-ordination with the relevant authorities,” the company said. All other crew members have been safely evacuated from the vessel. Eleven were injured and are receiving medical care where required. Middle East latest Bahrain and Kuwait accuse Iran of 'hostile' attacks “Adnoc reiterates the importance of protecting seafarers and safeguarding freedom of navigation and maritime security,” the company said. It added that further updates will be provided as more information becomes available. The latest incident comes after Adnoc L&S last week said one of its vessels was damaged in an attack in UAE territorial waters in the Gulf, without identifying the ship or the extent of the damage. Iran has claimed a series of attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz and off the coast of Oman and the UAE, often blaming operators for hitting sea mines . Tehran has been condemned for its attacks on non-military vessels. A gas tanker which was struck in the strait on Tuesday was also seen to be engulfed in flames. India’s Foreign Ministry confirmed 21 crew members were safely evacuated from the Panama-flagged Tara Gas, while two were taken to hospital and one is unaccounted for. In July, two crude oil tankers operated by Adnoc L&S were struck by projectiles in the strait, killing one crew member and injuring others. Another company ship was attacked in August, although no injuries were reported. Earlier this month, the UAE National Guard rescued 22 people after a fire broke out aboard a cargo ship in the Sea of Oman. Adnoc L&S, the shipping arm of Abu Dhabi energy giant Adnoc, operates a fleet of between 500 and 800 active managed, owned and chartered vessels. Last week, the Abu Dhabi-listed company raised its full-year profit forecast for the fourth time this year after third-quarter earnings more than quadrupled, as disruption from the Iran war drove up tanker charter rates. Net profit attributable to the equity holders of the company jumped 310 per cent to $842.7 million in the three months to the end of September, from $205.4 million a year earlier. Revenue rose 160 per cent to $3.29 billion, while operating profit nearly quadrupled to $898.7 million. It now expects annual net profit of about $4 billion.

This year alone, he has appeared in Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey , Kristoffer Borgli’s The Drama and Lance Oppenheim’s Primetime . Next month, he joins Denis Villeneuve’s Dune: Part Three , before returning to Gotham City in The Batman Part II , which hits cinemas in 2028. Now he has landed another role that countless actors have spent years hoping would be theirs. On Monday, Amazon MGM Studios announced that Pattinson would play James Bond , succeeding Daniel Craig as the seventh actor to portray 007 in the official film series. Villeneuve will direct the new film, with a script by Peaky Blinders creator Steven Knight. The announcement ended years of speculation, but it also raised a question. Bond has traditionally been a role that turns actors into global film stars. Pattinson is already one of the biggest in the world, with two major franchises behind him and another on the way. Will audiences be able to see past the actor to the secret agent ordering his signature beverage? James Bond's Arab connections: Seven characters who appeared in 007 films His career suggests they will. Since becoming a household name in the Twilight films, Pattinson has played billionaires, criminals, tortured loners and characters who are hard to describe at all. Even at his most recognisable, he has a habit of making unexpected choices. Pattinson has been here before. When he was cast as Batman, he inherited a character who had already been played by Michael Keaton, Christian Bale and Ben Affleck, among others. Each had left an imprint, and each new actor faced scrutiny from an audience with its own ideas of who Bruce Wayne should be. In Matt Reeves’s The Batman (2022) , Pattinson found a version of the character who was still working out what he wanted to be. His Bruce is withdrawn and consumed by anger, more comfortable in the batsuit than playing the part of a billionaire in public. When we spoke before the film’s release, Pattinson explained what drew him to this younger, less assured incarnation. “So much of the Batman mythology is that he’s seemingly not afraid of anything,” he said. “But I always think that if someone’s presenting as that, then it must mean that they harbour really deep fears. f816757e04.title: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says it’s ‘hard to imagine the AI industry without Jensen’
f816757e04.summary: The AI industry is entering a new era, and not just because of its constant stream of new model releases and discoveries. The AI community must now push forward without one of its most influential figures, Nvidia co-founder and former CEO Jensen Huang. Huang stepped down last week amid several scandals involving affairs with two employees and an alleged Chinese spy, raising potentially far-reaching national security concerns. Speaking onstage at The New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and President Greg Brockman each revealed that they had spoken privately with Huang as the embattled former CEO’s public image continued to unravel. “Jensen took one of the earliest big bets on us. We took a big bet on Nvidia,” Altman said. “It’s hard to imagine the AI industry without Jensen.” OpenAI has worked closely with Huang over the years. Nvidia invested $30 billion in the company earlier this year and designs the chips that power OpenAI’s technology. Brockman added that he and his wife are friends with Huang’s family, so the couple had reached out “personally, just to be there for him and his family at this time.” “I think it’s obviously a tough time for everyone, but again, I think Nvidia is such an incredible company,” Brockman said. “I think that… what Jensen has built there, it clearly is built to last, and so we’re excited to keep partnering and looking to the future.” Huang’s impact on Nvidia and the broader AI industry has been so profound that nearly 200,000 people , including Elon Musk and other influential CEOs, have signed a petition calling for the chipmaker to reinstate him. Nvidia executives said during the company’s earnings call on Tuesday that they do not have plans to reappoint Huang, even though the founder offered to return. Altman was reticent to weigh in on Huang’s future at Nvidia. When asked whether he thought Huang could return, Altman replied, “One thing I did not appreciate was everybody on Earth speculating with some random theory.” “I will say, I wish Jensen the best. I wish Nvidia the best,” Altman said. “I don’t think the world needs another set of random opinions on what’s going to happen here.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . 9e37cbced3.title: Anthropic’s Wall Street debut marks a new chapter for AI
9e37cbced3.summary: Anthropic, the company behind the Claude AI chatbot, is expected to go public Thursday in what could be the largest stock market debut of all time. The blockbuster IPO underscores the enormous amount of money being invested in AI, and the growing influence that the technology has on everything from the stock market to the broader US economy. The AI developer is targeting a range of $70 to $78 a share for the 825 million shares it plans to sell in its IPO. At the upper range, Anthropic would bring in as much as $64.4 billion and fetch a market valuation of up to $1.4 trillion — enormous figures for a company founded just under six years ago, reflecting the excitement around AI. The company is expected to confirm the final pricing later Wednesday. The offering comes alongside a separate $26 billion investment from major tech companies like Nvidia, bringing the total amount raised to $90.4 billion — a figure that would surpass SpaceX’s record-setting $75 billion IPO earlier this year. That’s before additional options for banks to sell more shares, which could lift Anthropic’s total haul to $100 billion — more than SpaceX’s total $86 billion figure. The third- and fourth-largest IPOs of all time are Saudi Aramco at $29.4 billion in 2019 and SK Hynix at $26.5 billion this year . “SpaceX was the largest IPO in history by a wide margin, and Anthropic might be exceeding SpaceX. Both of them are much bigger than any previous IPO,” said Jay Ritter, professor emeritus and director of the IPO Initiative at the University of Florida. “What’s also remarkable is that Anthropic is less than six years old.” The $1.4 trillion target valuation would catapult Anthropic into the ranks of the world’s 12 largest publicly traded companies. It will trade on the Nasdaq under the ticker “ ANT .” Anthropic was founded in 2021 when a group of employees at OpenAI left to start a new company with a focus on AI safety. That startup released its first version of Claude to the public in March 2023, a few months after OpenAI released ChatGPT to the public in November 2022. When Anthropic released Claude Code in early 2025, it quickly gained traction with software developers. Revenue continued to soar after the launch of Claude Cowork in early 2026 and as Anthropic established itself as a core provider of agentic AI tools. But, as a private company, there was less visibility into Anthropic’s finances. Going public means the company will now be required to disclose more information about its…

d5174a46cc.summary: When you buy through links on our articles, Future and its syndication partners may earn a commission. Anthropic, one of the world's leading developers of artificial intelligence (AI) models, is just hours away from its stock market debut. The company, which creates the Claude family of large language models, is expected to start trading on the Nasdaq on 19 November. Anthropic's IPO follows SpaceX's IPO in June, which saw Elon Musk's space exploration and AI company post the largest stock market debut in history, raising over $75 billion at a valuation of $1.77 trillion. Anthropic's IPO is expected to be as significant and possibly bigger, with the firm reportedly anticipating it could raise as much as $90 billion at a valuation of around $1.4 trillion, although this is less than touted in October. The Claude developer reported revenue of around $16.3 billion in the first half of 2026, but has seen a net loss of $81 billion in the first six months of this year. Spending shows no sign of slowing down: according to its IPO prospectus, the company has purchase commitments of almost $900 billion payable by 2045, with around $70 billion of that due within 12 months of September 2026. However, wider scepticism over whether AI firms can offer a return on the massive amounts of capital expenditure invested in the technology's underlying infrastructure has come to the fore in recent weeks. Trillions of dollars has been wiped off the combined market valuations of tech companies such as Nvidia and Google parent Alphabet. The Nasdaq 100 index, which is composed heavily of tech stocks, fell by over 13% between 6 October and 17 November. The possibility that US Democrat politicians could seek to slow the buildout of AI following their success in the US midterms has also rattled the market. Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at wealth manager Wealth Club, said: "Anthropic is spying an opportunity to get its IPO over the line. However, the tech rout has come at a big cost for the company. Gone are the lofty ambitions of trying to float at a $2 trillion valuation. "Anthropic is having to deal with the stark reality of a much more sceptical investor base." Anthropic's shares are expected to start trading on 19 November. The AI developer filed its IPO paperwork on 26 October and will list on the Nasdaq, under the ticker symbol 'ANT'.
