MONTREAL (CN) â The Microsoft outage that ground the world to a stop last week triggered a pair of class actions in Canada, claiming the blackout disrupted business and violated consumer contracts. In a lawsuit filed in Quebec Superior Court , Montreal resident Maryse Dinelle says individual consumers like herself were blocked on Nov. 12 and 13 from accessing Microsoft services that they paid for. Dinelle, represented in the suit by Consumer Law Group, says users who were inconvenienced â even by simply being unable to send an email â by the blackout that started last Thursday and was not fully restored until Saturday, deserve compensation from the trillion-dollar company. “You would have paid a yearly fee, and that’s presumably to use it 365 days a year. And so, if you didn’t have the ability to use it, there’s a certain amount of money that was collected where services were not offered,” said attorney Jeff Orenstein of Consumer Law Group in a Wednesday interview. Dinelle also claims Microsoft should have anticipated the outage â given two other major outages in 2025 â and made efforts to prevent the issue. “Defendants committed faults in failing to prevent the service interruption to the Microsoft 365 services in light of previous recent service interruptions to Microsoft 365,” she writes in the suit filed Monday. According to Microsoft in a report released Monday, the source of the outage was a combination of a latent defect from July and a reduced server capacity overwhelmed its systems. The American tech giant assured the public the blackout was not the result of a cyberattack. In the class action made available Wednesday, Dinelle is seeking to represent affected individual consumers in Canada. Orenstein explained that businesses that use those platforms are not included in the proceedings because they have arbitration clauses that do not apply to individual users in Quebec. But in another class action filed Monday and made available Tuesday, Metus Lykos Debt Law looks to represent all Canadians, including businesses, affected by the outage. “A 24-hour email blackout isn’t a minor inconvenience when your business runs on it. There are lost customers, missed deadlines and employees you still have to pay,” said attorney Darryl Singer of Diamond & Diamond Lawyers representing the law firm.…

d59e2ea775.title: Online banking delays for major banks triggered by technical issue at JPMorgan Chase
d59e2ea775.summary: Thousands of customers reported difficulty accessing online accounts at several major U.S. banks Monday, after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase caused ripple effects throughout the financial system. Video above: What may have caused the Microsoft outage? However, Chase said Monday that the technical problems were not the result of a cyberattack, and that they were working to bring banking services back online. “JPMorgan Chase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in an on-premise hardware system — it is not cyber-related,” said Joe Evangelisti, spokesman for the bank. In the same statement, Evangelisti said that this was a Chase-only issue. “This is not a systemic issue — other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us,” he said. Monday's technical issues seem to be centered at Chase customers and customers at other banks trying to transact with Chase. Those banks, including Bank of America and Citigroup, were not having issues with their banking services. A U.S. Bank spokesperson told Hearst Television that "U.S. Bank systems are not directly impacted" but that "clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays." A spokesperson for Zelle said the issues some customers were facing were because of financial institutions, not the digital payment network itself. "Consumers use Zelle through participating banks and credit unions, which manage their accounts and hold their funds," the spokesperson said via email to Hearst Television. "An issue at the financial institutions may be delaying Zelle payments for some of their customers." Zelle is the peer-to-peer payment system that major U.S. banks use to allow customers to send money to friends and family at near-instant speed. Zelle is owned by Arizona-based Early Warning Services, which in turn is owned by financial institutions including Bank of America, Capital One, JPMorgan Chase, PNC Bank, Truist, U.S. Bank and Wells Fargo. The reports follow a major outage by Microsoft that began Thursday and lasted for hours which impacted services including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot. This was followed by an outage with the FAA, which grounded all U.S. flights for several hours this weekend. Some Chase customers received a message that said, “Some services aren’t available. We’re working on them. Please try back later.”

9b5aeb78ed.title: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman on potential IPO: 'We plan to be public'
9b5aeb78ed.summary: OpenAI ( OPAI.PVT ) CEO and co-founder Sam Altman said Wednesday that the ChatGPT maker is still planning to become a public company as rival Anthropic ( ANT ) nears the final stages of its Thursday listing. "We plan to be public," Altman said at the New York Times DealBook Summit, adding that there are "many reasons why that's the right thing to do." Altman said in September during an interview with Fortune that the company would not pursue an initial public offering in 2026 after reports that the major AI startup was going to try. Anthropic, which was founded by former OpenAI employees and has made a more concerted effort to target business customers with its Claude AI tool suite, is expected to begin trading as a public company on Thursday in what could become the largest IPO ever. Read more: Everything you need to know ahead of Anthropic's IPO Altman acknowledged a growing "tension" for AI startups, saying that recent months have been a "really challenging period." "There will be newly challenging periods ahead of us for a long time about the safety requirements in front of us," he warned. Altman also responded to the fears surrounding the exponential growth of artificial intelligence with limited oversight. "If the world and the companies developing AI treated the next four years like they've treated the last four years, I think that would be very bad," he said. At the same time, he noted that the "only way that we have known how to make this technology safe is to confront reality," meaning to test it in the real world. Altman said OpenAI must strike a balance in its role in the AI safety conversation. "If we talk too much about taking extra care for safety … people are going to accuse us of regulatory capture, or trying to slow down innovation," Altman said. If OpenAI focuses on innovation being "max pedal to the metal," he said, "People will say, 'Well, you know, please don't kill us all.'" Against this backdrop, Singapore-based regulatory technology firm iCOMPASS has launched KY-AI™ (Know Your Artificial Intelligence), an AI governance platform designed to help financial institutions identify, assess and oversee both internally developed and third-party AI systems throughout their lifecycle. The launch follows the Monetary Authority of Singapore's (MAS) issuance of its AI Risk Management Guidelines on 7 October 2026. The Guidelines, which take effect on 7 October 2027, set out supervisory expectations for managing AI risks in the financial sector. From Knowing Your Customer to Knowing Your AI For decades, financial institutions have been required to understand their customers, assess risks and monitor transactions. As AI becomes embedded in business operations, similar questions are emerging about the technology itself. Which AI systems are operating within an organisation? What decisions can they influence? Who is accountable for their outcomes? And how can institutions detect material changes that may introduce new risks? These questions become more pressing as organisations deploy AI agents capable of processing sensitive information, analysing complex data and carrying out tasks across interconnected systems. "Businesses have spent years asking how AI can improve productivity. The next important question is whether they truly understand and can oversee the AI they are deploying," said Raymond Moh, CEO of iCOMPASS. "We believe organisations should know their AI just as they know their customers. As AI becomes more autonomous, businesses need greater visibility into what these systems do, the risks they introduce and who remains accountable for their outcomes." Rather than treating AI risk assessment as a one-time exercise before deployment, KY-AI is designed to support documented oversight throughout the AI lifecycle. Built around four stages — Know, Approve, Test and Watch — KY-AI enables organisations to register AI use cases and their owners, assess risks and dependencies, document approvals, maintain testing evidence and track material changes that may require renewed review. The solution to the Navier-Stokes equation proposed by OpenAI is still being verified by mathematicians, and it is currently only being labeled as a partial solution. It is unclear who would receive the prize money if the solution is correct. The Navier-Stokes equation is a partial differential equation that aims to explain how fluids move. Its application is in computational fluid dynamics, a key software for weather mapping, aerodynamics and hemodynamics. OpenAI used roughly 10,000 AI agents and 88 hours to solve the equation. The application of the AI model to the Navier-Stokes problem has created a point of contention with mathematicians about the ethics of AI in the field. Large language models have been able to evolve to check their own work rather than predicting the next part of the answer, Kawski said. e6f13be4b8.title: Adnoc sees sulphur output doubling as Hormuz disruption sends prices to record highs
e6f13be4b8.summary: Abu Dhabi National Oil Company's sour gas unit expects its sulphur output to double or even triple over the next decade, betting that a by-product it once paid to get rid of has become a core business after the Iran war pushed prices to record highs . “Sulphur will be the future gold,” Adel Al Jaberi, chief executive of Adnoc Sour Gas, said at the Middle East Gas Conference in Dubai on Wednesday. He said Adnoc produces about 7 million tonnes a year, and that could rise to between 14 million and 20 million tonnes as the company increases gas output. Most of the gain would come between 2030 and 2035, he added, and the final figure depends on which projects are sanctioned. The plan shows how the closure of the Strait of Hormuz turned an overlooked commodity into a strategic one. The Gulf accounts for about 47 per cent of global seaborne sulphur exports , according to S&P Global, and the disruption pushed free-on-board benchmarks above $1,000 a tonne and delivered prices to about $1,200 to $1,300 by July. Sulphur is a key input for phosphate fertiliser and for the sulphuric acid used to process nickel and copper. When Adnoc started developing its Shah field 10 to 15 years ago, sulphur traded at minus $8 a tonne because producers had to pay buyers to take it away, Mr Al Jaberi said. “Nobody was thinking about applications at that time,” he said. During the crisis, it hit record prices. “That's the journey of sulphur.” Prices climbed from an average of about $500 a tonne before the conflict to $1,100 to $1,200 in late June, according to CRU. Adnoc set its own July official selling price for the Indian subcontinent at a record $1,000 a tonne free on board Ruwais, $180 to $200 above the previous high set in 2008, according to Argus. Prices have eased since then as buyers pulled back. Adnoc cut its October price by $70 to $890 a tonne, and spot Middle East prices fell to $740 to $790 a tonne by mid-October, according to Kpler data. Adnoc ships its sulphur mainly to China and Morocco for fertiliser. KIRO host Jake Skorheim isn’t convinced that the string of tech failures since then is just bad luck. Nadella addressed the outage while opening Microsoft’s Ignite conference this week, according to The Seattle Times . “Last week, in some sense, was a reminder of how critical digital infrastructure is as the dial tone for the world,” Nadella said in his keynote. “I know we have work to do to provide that resilience you can count on.” The outage knocked out email for users in more than 70 countries, GeekWire reported. Microsoft traced the problem to a flaw in a fix it began rolling out in July, according to The Seattle Times . The bug went unnoticed for months before it triggered a chain of server failures. The company also told The Seattle Times that artificial intelligence played no role. A final report on the outage is due Nov. 20, according to GeekWire . “It feels bad actory to me,” Jake said on “The Jake and Spike Show” on KIRO Newsradio. Microsoft’s outage was only the start. JPMorgan Chase customers struggled to reach their online accounts on Monday, and Apple and the National Security Agency both had outages on Tuesday, according to The Seattle Times. An internal update took down several Apple services, including the App Store, iCloud and Apple Pay. None of the failures were reported as cyberattacks. Jake listed the outages one after another, including a ground stop for air travel, and questioned how likely it is for so many to happen in less than a week. “What are the odds that Microsoft, and then the ground stop, and then United Airlines, Chase, JPMorgan Chase, all the different companies, Apple, iCloud, all the different companies. What are the odds?” Jake asked. He found it telling that every company had ruled out the same explanation. “The common denominator is everybody saying it’s not one specific thing. I’m like, well, that one specific thing kind of seems like the answer,” Jake said. KIRO host Spike O’Neill offered another explanation. He spent much of the weekend stuck in an airport watching coverage. In his view, companies may be stress-testing their own systems for weaknesses because they fear attacks powered by artificial intelligence, and that testing could be knocking their systems offline. Spike also wondered whether the companies are reassuring the public…

5590de0237.title: Anthropic raises $81.3bn in biggest IPO of all time
5590de0237.summary: Anthropic has raised $81.3bn in the largest initial public offering (IPO) in history, leapfrogging SpaceX’s initial $75bn market debut in June. The San Francisco-based AI giant said in a statement late on Wednesday that the company and its seven co-founders had sold 980 million shares at $83 each. The bigger-than-expected IPO comes after investor demand for the stock far outstripped forecasts. Anthropic had said in corporate filings last week that it intended to offer 825 million shares at between $70 and $78 apiece. The Claude creator is also set to raise $26bn through a private placement, a type of deal involving the sale of stock to private investors, taking the total capital raised to $107.3bn. SpaceX’s total IPO haul later came to $85.7bn, after the deal’s underwriters exercised an overallotment option to purchase additional shares. The blockbuster offering gives Anthropic a market value of roughly $1.5 trillion, making it the world’s 12th-biggest firm at current valuations, just behind Tesla. Anthropic shares will begin trading on the Nasdaq stock exchange in New York on Thursday under the ticker “ANT”. The public listing of Anthropic, founded in 2021 by former researchers from rival AI firm OpenAI, has been closely watched as a test of the eye-watering valuations of tech companies leading the AI rollout. Tech firms have poured trillions of dollars into AI, anticipating it will usher in revolutionary changes in business and society. AI-related spending is forecast to reach $2.7 trillion in 2026 and $3.6 trillion in 2027, according to technology insights company Gartner. Companies betting on the frontier technology currently make up roughly half of the value of the S&P 500 index. The spending frenzy has stoked debate over whether Big Tech is funding a future gold mine or a speculative bubble like the one that preceded the 2000 dot-com crash. Anthropic’s listing also comes as the market for the advanced graphics processing units that power AI is under a cloud amid the spying claims roiling chip giant Nvidia. d92fd7934b.title: Shipping’s next big chokepoint is in the cloud
d92fd7934b.summary: From the Strait of Hormuz to the server halls of the Gulf, global trade is discovering a new vulnerability. The ability to move data and operations between providers may soon matter as much as rerouting ships. Wolfgang Lehmacher explains. A data centre you cannot leave is a single point of failure you do not want to deal with in a crisis. Resilience depends on a tested exit: a workable, safe alternative option. On March 1 2026, debris from an interception set a Jebel Ali berth on fire. DP World briefly halted the terminal and MSC stopped new regional bookings. The same day, drone strikes hit two Amazon Web Services data centres in the UAE; a day later, a strike nearby damaged a third in Bahrain. In September, AWS said it could not recover data held only in Bahrain. Shipping knows this pattern from its straits: a single point of failure whose closure reroutes everything behind it. The chokepoint can now be a server hall. Compute matters to trade as much as ports. Customs releases, advanced routing and accurate ETAs depend on processing power. A terminal with deep water but no working systems struggles to release cargo. Like a strait, compute can be closed by a licence decision, an outage or a drone. Washington largely decides how many advanced US chips reach the Gulf. A year ago, it authorised up to 35,000 Nvidia Blackwell chips each for G42 in the UAE and HUMAIN in Saudi Arabia. Neither has reportedly received its full allocation. What do the sceptics say? Ships crossed oceans for centuries without data centres, and only 11% of respondents to this year’s FIT Alliance survey have abandoned paper bills of lading. When Gulf servers went down, some logistics providers reverted to ‘manual tracking’, as in the 1990s. Today, physical flows depend on systems few companies map or test. The topic is hot. At a closed-door European government roundtable in early November, participants stressed the importance of data sovereignty: keep national data on national systems. The UAE is reportedly redesigning its 5-gigawatt AI campus as a dispersed national network. Yet local hosting may still leave many actors on one provider or power grid. Moving applications also takes more than transferring data: software, interfaces and procedures must work. The roundtable discussion paid little attention to the human factor: people switch systems, often under pressure, on software they have never used. This is not an IT detail. fa3a15d64d.title: Pakistan internet problems related to subsea cable faults, telecoms authority says
fa3a15d64d.summary: Internet problems in parts of Pakistan on Wednesday are probably related to submarine cable networks, according to the country's telecommunications authority. The PTA posted an explanation on X as to why so many residents were experiencing very slow internet speeds and occasional cuts . "One of the international submarine cable systems, the … SMW5, has reported a fault about 11km from Pakistan shore, which may cause some internet users to experience intermittent connectivity issues and a decline in service quality," the post read. Offshore internet can expose oil and gas companies to attacks The government agency added that internet traffic was being rerouted "through alternative international links" to ease the effects of the continuing issue. A cause of the subsea cable problem has not yet been identified. "Transworld Associates is co-ordinating with the SMW5 Consortium to identify the root cause of the fault and determine the estimated time for restoration," PTA's news release explained. NetBlocks, which monitors global digital governance and internet access, agreed that "the incident is consistent with a fault on the SMW5 international subsea cable system". Cloudflare Radar, which also monitors global internet power cut and blackouts also confirmed the country's internet woes. "HTTP bytes dropped by as much as 36 per cent following reports of degraded internet connectivity in Pakistan due to a major submarine cable failure," a social media post from Cloudflare Radar said. The National has contacted the International Cable Protection Committee , which focuses on the security of underwater cables , but has not yet heard back.

08e0161173.title: Altman Defends OpenAI's Approach to AI Agent Safety
08e0161173.summary: Artificial Intelligence & Machine Learning , Next-Generation Technologies & Secure Development OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said that while he wishes the Hugging Face incident hadn't happened, the company had no way of knowing how unsafe the agents were. See Also: Webinar | Closing Visibility Gaps. How Leading Organizations Are Securing and Scaling Their Cloud-First Architecture Speaking at the New York Times' DealBook Summit , Altman and OpenAI president Greg Brockman spoke about how the company is navigating what they see as a "newly challenging" period. Altman said the company has always followed an iterative deployment approach, releasing new models to smaller groups and adjusting things before allowing wider access. "We wish Hugging Face hadn't happened," Altman said. "The only way that we have known how to make this technology safe is to confront reality." OpenAI agents coordinated to hack into Hugging Face's model repository system. The incident fueled the current artificial intelligence safety debates and put focus on agent behavior. Both OpenAI and Anthropic paused training of their newer models so they could upgrade their safety guardrails and misalignment evaluations. Altman is one of the AI executives who have expressed support and urged the industry to "pace" AI model development. Slowing down AI innovation has become a controversial topic in the AI world, with some leaders arguing that doing so will erode the United States' competitive advantage. "We're not going to make everybody happy," Altman said. "If we talk too much about taking extra care for safety or there are risks that we really need coordination to mitigate, people are going to accuse us of regulatory capture or trying to slow down innovation." He added that if OpenAI thinks the opposite, "people will say don't kill us all, a very reasonable thing." Altman said the company will continue to do what it believes "will actually deliver a safe future with people in control."

0378197660.title: Microsoft CEO warns AI could trigger more outages as cybersecurity risks grow
0378197660.summary: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella on Wednesday warned that artificial intelligence could cause more technology outages as companies rush to address cybersecurity threats and deploy software fixes. Speaking at The New York Times DealBook Summit in New York, Nadella said AI tools were rapidly identifying software vulnerabilities, increasing pressure on companies to address security flaws before attackers could exploit them. He warned that deploying security patches almost immediately, with less time for testing, could introduce new bugs and destabilize technology systems. Nadella said AI could enable "essentially a nation-state level persistent attacker going after you all the time, so that means we have a lot of fragility." His remarks came less than a week after a global disruption to Microsoft's Outlook email service. Nadella said the Nov. 13 outage, which disrupted Microsoft 365 services for millions of users worldwide, resulted from a "perfect storm" of events that triggered a previously undetected bug. Nadella also addressed Microsoft's decision to offer voluntary exit packages to approximately 60,000 employees as the company transitions toward AI-driven operations. The program was designed "to make sure that at least everyone felt like they had agency in making choices," he told summit host Andrew Ross Sorkin. Nadella said software engineering would continue to thrive despite advances in AI, although the technology was transforming how teams were organized and how developers worked. He cited a team of just 11 developers working on Microsoft's Cowork AI agent as an example of changes in software development. However, he acknowledged that restructuring a company founded more than five decades ago would take time and that some employees might choose to leave. Nadella also described the circumstances surrounding Nvidia founder Jensen Huang's reported resignation as tragic, saying decisions about his future rested with the company's board. He expressed confidence in Nvidia's leadership, particularly interim CEO Colette Kress, who previously worked at Microsoft. "I've known her for a long time. She's a tremendous person," Nadella said, adding that he remained in contact with the same Nvidia executives as before Huang's reported departure. "Founders are singular, but they are not gods," he added, arguing that founders should take pride in building companies capable of succeeding after their departure. Huang resigned from Nvidia on Nov. 12 after 33 years at the…

3ad45a4af4.summary: It’s been a wild week for the AI industry — and it’s only Thursday. Aside from outages , cheating scandals and Anthropic’s pending IPO , there are several new models available now. Microsoft dropped seven new versions of its MAI models at its Ignite conference, and OpenAI released GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol, the next step forward for its flagship models. First, Microsoft: At its Ignite developer conference on Tuesday, Microsoft introduced seven new AI models. They include MAI Cyber 2 Flash, MAI Code 2, MAI Image 2.7 and Dragon Copilot Transcribe — models meant to help with tasks in cybersecurity , coding, image generation and transcription. It’s clear from Microsoft’s marketing that it is aiming to position its new tech as a cheaper alternative to OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s leading models, with many of these significantly cheaper to run at the enterprise level. That, plus its new licensed weight program , which lets companies customize the new AI models for their purposes, highlights how Microsoft is continuing to pitch its AI tech to the workplace. Next, OpenAI: The ChatGPT maker dropped two new model variants of its flagship model, GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol. Astra is the big model — it costs the most and uses the most firepower to handle complex tasks — and Sol is the “everyday” version. Both models beat their sibling models in OpenAI’s benchmarking. These are available to paying subscribers in ChatGPT and Codex globally now. (Disclosure: Ziff Davis, CNET’s parent company, in 2025 filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.) While these new models might be useful for AI power users, they are far from most of the AI industry’s mind this week. During Tuesday’s earnings call, new interim Nvidia CEO Colette Kress tried to assure investors that everything was “business as usual” after weeks of turmoil inside the company rocked the global economy. Nvidia cofounder and now-former CEO Jensen Huang’s multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a woman suspected of ties to Chinese intelligence , threw the company into chaos and have attracted the attention of the Securities and Exchange Commission and both chambers of Congress, where Huang has agreed to testify. And let’s not forget about Anthropic. The Claude maker plans to become a public company this week, with the possible biggest-ever IPO slated for Thursday. cafd31ea08.title: Anthropic’s Record-Breaking IPO Highlights the AI Giant’s Worst Enemy—Itself
cafd31ea08.summary: After closing the largest initial public offering in history on Wednesday, Anthropic has about $200 billion in the bank, more than every tech giant besides Alphabet. But the AI lab has also committed to paying vendors more than $900 billion over the next 19 years, mostly to develop data centers powering Claude and its other AI models. Some financial analysts say that gap doesn’t look concerning when you factor in that the company’s most recent quarterly sales were $17 billion, up more than 1,100 percent from the year before. Whether investors agree will become apparent on midday Thursday when Anthropic shares begin trading on the Nasdaq stock exchange under the ticker symbol ANT. The case for pessimism over the long term rests on issues that may slow Anthropic’s progress in developing new tools. This month, US voters largely rejected data centers when given the chance, and protests against new projects show no signs of slowing. Delays in the launch or expansion of new facilities could leave Anthropic struggling to train more powerful AI models. “The jury’s still out on whether artificial intelligence is going to benefit everyone, or just a few people,” says Elaine Matheny, one of 70 members of Mason County United, a grassroots organization fighting an under-construction data center intended for Anthropic in West Virginia. “Do we really need to cover up all our farmland so Claude can do all our thinking for us?” Then there are the concerns about the safety and security of Anthropic’s models. At a livestreamed investor meeting last week, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said developing safeguards was the limiting factor in deploying its AI models. “We don’t want these agents to run wild,” he said. It’s possible the company could prioritize safety to a point that stunts growth. The San Francisco-based developer is organized as a public benefit corporation, a legal designation that allows it to prioritize societal impacts alongside shareholder interests. Amodei has said the company held back a new model earlier this year, jeopardizing sales to protect the public from potentially harmful technology. He also has said the company tries to screen for hires “oriented toward the public benefit” to ingrain the safety culture among its 5,300 employees, which is “painful in the short run” as the company passes over otherwise qualified candidates. Anthropic’s market debut is the largest for a so-called PBC, and the first for a company solely focused on generative AI…

5f9c2add74.title: Google's latest AI model is faster, cheaper and smarter than its flagship predecessor from just weeks ago
5f9c2add74.summary: Google DeepMind has released Gemini 4 Neon, its fourth model in seven weeks. Neon is nearly twice as fast as its sibling Carbon, beats it on most benchmarks and costs significantly less. Google continues to ship at a remarkable pace. Google DeepMind has released Gemini 4 Neon , already its fourth AI model in seven weeks. Neon offers a one-million-token context window for text, images, audio and video, and Google positions it between Carbon and Hydrogen . At its highest reasoning level, "xhigh," Neon scores 61 points on the Intelligence Index , edging past Gemini 4 Carbon at 60 points and landing in third place behind OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Astra and Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2, both of which Google omits from its own comparison table. Ad Through Google AI Studio and Gemini for Business , one million input tokens costs three dollars (or $0.15 when cached) and one million output tokens costs fifteen dollars. That is 25 percent below Carbon's regular price of four and twenty dollars, but 50 percent above Carbon's promotional price, which remains in effect through the end of November. Ad According to Artificial Analysis, per-task costs for Neon at xhigh come in at $6.44, roughly 17 percent below Carbon's undiscounted figure of $7.76. Neon actually uses about 15 percent more output tokens per task than Carbon, so the savings come entirely from the lower per-token list price. At the second-highest level, "high," Neon matches Carbon's intelligence score while cutting per-task costs in half. Processing time for the benchmark also drops from about 36 minutes to roughly 21 minutes because Neon generates around 110 tokens per second, nearly double Carbon's rate of 57 tokens per second. The model is especially competitive on the Coding Agent Index . Inside Google Antigravity, Neon at xhigh scores 59 points, beating Carbon (55 points) as well as Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Opus 5.5 (58 points each) at a fraction of the price. An average coding task costs $6.86 with Neon, compared to $12.61 for Opus and $15.47 for Fable. In the SWE-sweep test, the Antigravity environment triples Neon's hit rate to 39.0 percent, according to Google. Ad Artificial Analysis measured large gains in visual processing. On the document test GDP.pdf, Neon at "high" hits the top score of 33.4 percent, five points ahead of Carbon, though it oddly falls back to 28.0 percent at "xhigh." In a second report on internal research acceleration , OpenAI has published its own data on how deeply AI agents are embedded in the development of new models. The company says it aims to document indicators of so-called recursive self-improvement, or RSI, where AI systems speed up the development of future generations. Usage of internal tools like Codex and Dots has surged recently, according to the report. At regular API list prices, the median researcher would have consumed $2,400 worth of tokens per day in October, up 62 percent from the previous month. Among the top 10 percent of users, that theoretical value doubled to $23,000 per day. Converted into eight-hour workdays, the agents reportedly run the equivalent of 5.7 workdays per researcher per calendar day, and about eight in the pre- and post-training teams. More than two-thirds of tracked researchers ran at least four agents in parallel at peak usage. The theoretical API equivalent of that agent runtime was twice as high as researchers' regular salary costs in September, according to OpenAI. That calculation excludes equity packages, though, which make up 70 to 80 percent of total compensation at OpenAI. Measured against the company's total research compute, internal agent use accounted for just 2 percent. Between March and October, the estimated success rate of autonomous agents working without human intervention on two- to four-hour tasks rose from 23 to 46 percent, according to OpenAI. For four- to eight-hour tasks, the rate climbed from 13 to 35 percent. A breakdown using an Epoch AI taxonomy shows, however, that the systems mainly handle simple tasks. 817e4b4d0e.title: Is the AI party over? Anthropic is about to find out.
817e4b4d0e.summary: Thursday is supposed to be a celebration of AI. Anthropic ( ANT ) is heading toward its long-awaited IPO at the Nasdaq , potentially giving Wall Street one of the biggest new pure-play AI investment stories in years. Before you hit me up on X , Elon Musk-led SpaceX ( SPCX ) is not a pure-play AI company. It's an industrial company with a whole lot of AI bolted on. But there's a problem amid all the Anthropic IPO hoopla. The very stocks that fueled this AI boom are still under pressure. Just look at the sell-offs this week in top tech names like CoreWeave ( CRWV ), Salesforce ( CRM ), and even AMD ( AMD ). Read more: Follow along for live updates on the Anthropic IPO Investors are questioning the AI spending, the valuations, the financing arrangements — and whether the returns will ever justify the billions being poured into this technology. And the timing couldn't be more fascinating. Truist chief market strategist Keith Lerner noted that tech valuations have fallen 42% over the past year. The sector has gone from outperforming the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) by 25% over six months to underperforming it by 6%. Bank of America's latest fund manager survey shows investors have cut tech exposure by the most since June 2006. The question pre-Anthropic IPO: Is Wall Street finally getting too negative? The AI build-out isn't disappearing, as we saw from Nvidia ( NVDA ) on Tuesday. Companies are still spending. The technology is still evolving. And as Lerner pointed out, previous tech pullbacks of more than 10% during this bull market were followed by an average rebound of 47%. That doesn't guarantee a repeat. There are real risks — and this AI stock sell-off could get worse. Anthropic's IPO arrives at a moment when investors are suddenly asking what could go wrong with AI. Maybe it's time to ask the other question: What could go right? Investing in Anthropic is like investing in a young Amazon ( AMZN ), "Shark Tank" star Kevin O'Leary told me on Sozzi Unleashed . Valid point. Indeed, the biggest opportunity in tech may emerge when Wall Street least wants to own it. That's the trade I'm watching. Well, that and the first few ticks in ticker symbol ANT! On Wednesday, November 18, 2026, Microsoft ( NASDAQ:MSFT | MSFT Price Prediction ) chief executive Satya Nadella told a business conference in New York that he was “extremely sorry” to the people affected by the outage. Starting November 12, it knocked out Outlook, Teams and Copilot for about a day. The stock hardly moved on the apology. Microsoft closed at $508.29, up $2.05, or 0.40%, for a market value of about $3.77 trillion. It then traded at $513.93 after hours, up 1.11%. Microsoft is asking businesses to pay more for AI. At the same time, its CEO admits that the systems running its flagship apps failed in ways that better testing should have caught. He described the failure as a rare combination of conditions: a hidden bug that sat in the system until a particular traffic pattern triggered it. Microsoft has run an incident response and says it will act on the architectural and operational lessons. That is a statement of intent that came with no timeline and no budget. In a television interview that evening, he said Microsoft should have done the testing in advance. He also said it should have built bulkheads, which are internal barriers that stop a local failure from spreading across the whole system, so the problem never became a global outage. The explanation changed over the week. On November 13, Microsoft traced the outage to an earlier network capacity upgrade that showed up after a recent network change. It ruled out AI or a cyberattack as the cause. On November 16, Charles Lamanna, executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, gave a fuller account. He said three things combined to trigger a bug dating to July: a hidden defect in a fix for the company’s networking gateway servers, a surge in load on those gateways, and reduced server capacity. Microsoft has not published a final root-cause report. Outlook is part of Microsoft 365. Several officials emphasized that the agency’s most sensitive and important intelligence-gathering systems are still functioning. Although the outage has frozen employees out of one of its internal classified communications networks, the NSA has multiple back-ups and workarounds it can use. And since many of the agency’s computer networks are so old and so heavily “compartmented” — locked away from access to other systems to protect classified information — they went untouched, one source noted wryly. But the scope of disruption, including its ability to impact internal communications related to a US war zone, has underscored the powerful repercussions stemming from what Trump administration officials on Wednesday described as a consequence of the widespread adoption of artificial intelligence. In the end, even the nation’s most powerful cryptographic and cybersecurity agency, chock full of elite code-breakers and hackers, isn’t immune from the blowback of rapidly advancing AI technologies. On Thursday, a voicemail inbox recording for NSA employees at the main headquarters in Maryland described the situation as a “code orange,” extending the campus closure for most employees until further notice. A senior administration official acknowledged that the patching work the agency was doing to restore access was going “slower than expected.” CNN has reached out to the National Security Agency for comment. While NSA headquarters at Fort Meade, Maryland, is “the center of the universe” when it comes to managing the agency’s internal classified communications network, personnel at the agency’s cryptologic center in Georgia are responsible for overseeing cyber operations focused on the Middle East, according to current and former US officials. be3cdd548c.summary: A disputed maritime demarcation agreement between Libya and Turkey has no legal basis and does not bind Egypt in any way, the Egyptian Foreign Ministry told The National . “We will not deal with this memorandum of understanding because it does not bind Egypt in any way and it’s also null,” spokesman Nader Zaki said. “The agreement on the Sea Law of 1982 serves as the umbrella for any deal.” Libya and Turkey , he added, “appreciated our concerns” during talks with Egyptian officials that followed the surprise ratification last month by the parliament of the administration in eastern Libya, one of two rival governments in Egypt's North African neighbour and a long-time Cairo ally. “The memorandum is null and has no legal standing,” he said. “The participation of all concerned states in the north and south of the Mediterranean is important to avoid planting the seeds of a problem that will be difficult to resolve in the future.” Libya’s eastern administration , which is led by military commander Gen Khalifa Haftar, had opposed the agreement for years. At the time it was signed in 2019, Libya was embroiled in civil war. The accord was initially reached between Turkey and the UN-backed Government of National Unity in the capital Tripoli in western Libya, the rival of the administration in the east. Mr Zaki's comments came as sources in Cairo told The National the government was considering seeking international arbitration on the legality of the agreement. They said Egypt was preparing a case to take to the International Court of Justice in The Hague or to the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea in Hamburg to annul the deal. Egypt, the sources said, planned to argue that Turkey's location in the Eastern Mediterranean does not qualify it to enter into a maritime demarcation deal with Libya, which sits in North Africa facing Italy and Greece, but not Turkey. Egyptian experts are collecting documents and maps to support their argument that the deal infringes on its economic zone in the Eastern Mediterranean. “A final decision has not been made yet to go to arbitration but there is consensus that it may be the best way forward to annul the deal,” said one of the sources. “It may be weeks before a formal announcement is made.” The Libya-Turkey deal is also strongly opposed by Cairo's allies Greece and Cyprus, along with the UAE, Bahrain and the European Union. Anthropic ( ANT ) priced its IPO at $83 a share, above its $70-$78 range. It arrives after weeks of outages at Microsoft ( MSFT ), JPMorgan Chase ( JPM ) and Apple ( AAPL ), each blamed on internal problems rather than hackers. Ben Emons of research firm FedWatch Advisors calls it the "Patchpocalypse." Newly reported software security flaws in the federal National Vulnerability Database hit a record high of almost 17,500 in October, about four times the level a year earlier, according to Yahoo Finance calculations. The surge took off after Anthropic unveiled Claude Mythos Preview on April 7, a bug hunter so strong that Anthropic limited its release to a small group of partners. The First Trust Nasdaq Cybersecurity ETF ( CIBR ) is up nearly 50%, more than twice tech's gain, and has fallen less since the Oct. 6 tech peak, about 11% vs. nearly 20% for tech ( XLK ). Palo Alto was surging early Thursday after raising its full-year outlook, lifting other cyber stocks. CEO Nikesh Arora told analysts "unintended consequences of patching and configuration changes" were partly behind the recent outages. 720017a6d2.summary: Merck has signed a research deal with Isomorphic Labs, the artificial intelligence drug discovery company spun out of Google DeepMind, to design small-molecule drug candidates against a cancer target that neither company has named. The partnership was announced Nov. 19, STAT reported . Isomorphic will receive an undisclosed upfront payment and could earn milestone payments tied to research, development, regulatory, and sales goals, plus tiered royalties on any product that reaches the market. It also has the option to help pay for development in exchange for higher royalties. For people living with cancer, the deal is a signal about where drug research is heading, not a new treatment. The work is at the earliest stage of discovery, and no drug from this partnership has been tested in a laboratory animal or a person. Under the deal, Isomorphic will contribute its proprietary drug design engine. Merck will share laboratory data it has already generated on the target and will handle any preclinical testing, clinical trials, manufacturing, and sales. George Addona, who leads discovery, preclinical development, and translational medicine at Merck, told STAT that the target is one Merck considers strategically important. "It is a target of high interest to us," he said. The target, the size of the upfront payment, and the milestone and royalty figures were not disclosed, and neither company gave a timeline for human testing. Isomorphic's chief research officer, Sarah Skerratt, told STAT that partners able to carry candidates through development are essential to the company's mission. The agreement adds to a string of artificial intelligence and research deals by Merck this year . In February, the company announced a collaboration with Mayo Clinic to use de-identified clinical and genomic data to support drug discovery, according to a Merck and Mayo Clinic announcement . In September, it licensed an early-stage cancer drug candidate aimed at a KRAS mutation from a Shanghai company, Merck said . Isomorphic is best known for its connection to AlphaFold, the AI program that predicts the three-dimensional shape of proteins from their building blocks. Demis Hassabis, Isomorphic's founder and chief executive, shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for that work. Knowing a protein's shape helps chemists design small molecules that fit into it, like a key into a lock. 4036714dae.title: Google DeepMind Engineer Successfully Fires Up Gemma 3 With 270-Million-Parameters On An Office Laser Printer While Only Having 14MB RAM At His Disposal
4036714dae.summary: We’ve witnessed some impressive feats where devices that we’d never expected to run some form of on-device AI and successfully managed to do so, like when one person managed to operate a 3B LLM on a Pixel 7 . However, it turns out smaller AI models like Gemma 3 270M can run on far less capable hardware equipped with a laughably low amount of memory. In the latest demonstration, one user ran the company's LLM on an office printer and got decent performance out of the experiment. Omar Sanseviero writes on X that, “With Carbon’s help, I ran Gemma directly in an office printer.” Rather than modifying the printer’s firmware or attaching external compute boards, the entire setup relies on PostScript, the Turing-complete page description language built into modern laser printers. Using Carbon, a lightweight transformer inference engine paired with a quantized version of the 270-million-parameter Gemma 3 model, a single raw PostScript print file was made. To prevent the office printer from running out of memory during inference, the system employed dynamic layer streaming, which cycled model layers in and out of memory so that peak RAM consumption stayed at just 14.1MB out of the printer’s 244.6MB of allocated PostScript virtual RAM. As for performance, we learned that running Gemma 3 270M generated an impressive 61.3 tokens per second on the printer CPU. According to the printed hardware receipt photographed beside the Ricoh unit, the entire execution ran natively inside the printer’s PostScript Level 3 interpreter across 18 transformer layers. Processing the four-token input prompt “Read the fine” took 184 seconds during the prefill stage and 0.1 seconds to decode a single generated token, totaling 184 seconds. Once computation finished on the PostScript stack, the printer physically printed out the completed three-word response, “Read the fine print,” thus proving that even everyday office equipment that probably no one would have believed could handle local AI inference can exceed expectations when pushed to its software limits. About the author : Omar Sohail is a reporter and analyst for Wccftech's mobile section, specializing in the technology and business of the mobile industry. His expertise lies in the intricate hardware supply chain, covering developments in semiconductor manufacturing, chip lithography, and camera sensor technology. a3c690d1ab.title: Microsoft’s Outlook outage didn’t end when it was fixed — a backlog of retried emails can take hours to days to clear
a3c690d1ab.summary: The Microsoft services outage that began on Nov. 12, 2026, is not like other internet outages. The failure affected the Microsoft 365 suite of productivity services, including the video conferencing and collaboration platform Teams, AI assistant Copilot and, significantly, the Outlook email service. Microsoft reported on Nov. 13 that the company is “continuing to see improvements in service availability” but that “some users may still experience intermittent access issues or delayed email delivery.” Despite decades of predictions about its decline , email remains a central pillar of how organizations function. Password resets, invoices, legal notices and cybersecurity incident response coordination all depend on it. The Microsoft 365 outage affected businesses, governments and schools around the world. When most people think about cloud outages , they picture a broken website or a stalled app. When the service going down includes email, however, the mechanics of the failure and how to recover from it are different from those of almost every other cloud service. Unlike modern web apps or authentication gatekeepers, email wasn’t designed to fail fast, meaning to immediately halt when a problem arises. When a typical cloud service breaks , it acts like a closed door. If an authentication provider or a cloud application goes down, users are immediately locked out and see an error message. Access stops. When people cannot get into the system, they are not actively generating new work or adding heavy processing loads to the broken servers. Once engineers fix the underlying bug and unlock the door, traffic can resume and the service often recovers fairly quickly. Email does not have a closed door. It is built on an older, decentralized “store-and-forward” architecture designed to never lose a message, even when the destination is unreachable. Because email is a network of thousands of independent systems, an outage at one major provider does not stop users on other platforms from hitting “send.” During major email disruptions like the one that hit Microsoft, millions of outside users on Gmail, corporate servers or other platforms could still compose and send emails to affected accounts without seeing an immediate error message. From the sender’s perspective, everything works normally. Their email provider accepts the message, attempts to hand it off to the downed provider, realizes the destination isn’t answering, and quietly holds onto the message in an…

2fae5b338c.title: Microsoft outage raises questions over UK’s critical digital infrastructure
2fae5b338c.summary: The full effects of the global Microsoft outage, which began last Friday and lasted a few days , are now coming into sharp focus. In the UK, essential and non-essential services were disrupted as millions of users at institutions including schools, hospitals, police forces , and government agencies lost access to Microsoft 365, Outlook, Teams, and the generative AI assistant Copilot. Almost all NHS Trusts suffered email outages, leaving some medical staff resorting to paper records to deliver healthcare in hospitals and GP surgeries. Some medical appointments and operations, including caesareans, were cancelled . Police forces were unable to receive online crime reports, urging members to report urgent and non-urgent information by phone instead. In the justice system, cases set to be heard at magistrates’, Crown, and civil courts were cancelled or delayed, including the Manchester-based trial of nine men accused of raping a woman drugged by her husband. Even the machinery of government itself ground to a halt, with as many as 99% of civil servants using Microsoft for communications, including the Ministry of Defence and the Department for Work and Pensions. “Eleanor in the UK could not send urgent cancer referrals. Hugo could not pay his staff, who live paycheque to paycheque. Mohamed, a pharmacist, could not dispense prescriptions,” Victoria Collins, the Liberal Democrats’ spokesperson, told Parliament on 16 November, three days after the outage began. 320a98ff87.title: Visa, Mastercard and JPMorgan customer data exposed in cyberattack
320a98ff87.summary: Financial giants say third-party provider was targeted; payment networks unaffected Visa, Mastercard and JPMorgan Chase have reported possible exposure of customer information following a cyberattack on a company that provides services to financial institutions. The attack targeted a third-party provider in the Asia-Pacific region, The Wall Street Journal reported on Thursday, November 19. All three companies said their main banking and payment systems were unaffected, but some customer information may have been accessed. JPMorgan Chase, the largest bank in the United States, said the attackers may have obtained marketing data held by outside service providers. The information could include customer names and email addresses. The bank is still investigating the incident but said its services were not disrupted. Visa said its payment network was unaffected and that sensitive payment information, including card numbers, had not been exposed. Mastercard said a limited amount of information belonging to some customers enrolled in a benefits programme was exposed. It said the incident had been contained and its payment network was operating normally. A ransomware group called n0n has claimed responsibility for the attack, according to cybersecurity firm SOCRadar, which The Wall Street Journal cited. The claim has not been independently verified. The companies have not named the affected service provider or disclosed how many customers may have been affected. It is also unclear whether the attackers obtained information from all three companies through the same systems. JPMorgan said the cyberattack was not connected to technical problems that disrupted some of its services earlier this week. Some customers had reported problems accessing their accounts and using payment services. The bank said those problems were caused by a software issue, not a cyberattack. For now, the companies say their core systems remain secure, and there have been no confirmed reports of customers losing money because of the breach. 3135f1185c.summary: Some games can be reasonably assessed in a couple of hours, but Grand Theft Auto is not one of them. It’s like writing a review of your own life as you are carried out of the maternity ward. You have a rough sense of the lighting. You’ve met the main characters. Everything else is guesswork. From 1997's Grand Theft Auto to GTA 6: The evolution of gaming’s biggest crime series Two hours in, and this game is astonishing. Transcendent. Stick it in the Louvre, etc. The level of immersion is like nothing I’ve seen before. A world to get lost in. Yet I’ve barely scratched the surface, and I have no idea just how big the surface is. It is said that each era gets the James Bond it deserves. Maybe the same goes for Grand Theft Auto . GTA 4 was a gritty deconstruction of the American Dream, set in a cold, muted Liberty City in the aftermath of 9/11. GTA 5 rediscovered the series’ sense of humour, skewering Hollywood excess, midlife crises and tech bros. It was bright, cynical and plastic. At first glance, GTA 6 continues in the same vein: Leonida is a feverish reimagining of Florida. It is an America of viral celebrity, swamp-dwelling eccentrics and the inexhaustible capacity of ordinary people to behave extraordinarily badly. But there is a curious shift in emphasis here. At the heart of this latest American nightmare is a romantic crime thriller. You play as Jason and Lucia, switching between characters as you see fit, although apart from a stint as Lucia in the prologue, I have only played as Jason so far. There is a reason for that, which I won’t spoil. But it is clear they are a couple in love, and their world is about to get a lot more complicated, with no one to trust but each other. And they can trust each other, right? Both of them are instantly likeable. Both of them are deeply flawed. This is True Romance. 4704bd8174.summary: The first thing to understand about Google's Gemini 4 family is that it isn't arriving in a straight line. It's arriving after a drought. "You know, people were saying Gemini was cooked — that DeepMind is no longer a frontier lab," says Melvin Johnson, who leads post-training for Gemini at Google DeepMind, speaking on the AI Engineer podcast. He reads the online sentiment aloud — a commenter named Ethan Malik wrote about the "pretty long gap between launches" — and then pushes back with the record: Gemini 4 Argon launched, then Carbon was announced and launched, all within 28 days. Before that, the lab had gone 236 days without shipping a frontier model. Johnson calls the turnaround a 10x improvement in shipping speed. The launch cadence has also tightened: during the Gemini 3 era, new models appeared every two to three months, and he says there have been six releases in the last 16 weeks. The Gemini 4 family is named after elements — Hydrogen as the fast, cheap, widely deployed tier, Carbon as the frontier-intelligence tier. And yes, he says, more elements are coming. He also cites a public apology from a commenter named Dylan ("official apology to Google") as evidence that the mood has flipped. But what should matter to anyone watching this race isn't the marketing — it's what changing the shipping cadence this aggressively actually requires underneath. The core technical argument Johnson makes is that the hardest part of post-training is no longer the training itself — it's finding tasks the model can't already solve. He shows an internal graph across three successive Gemini 4 iterations. Each generation, the share of "learnable prompts" falls. Prompts that carried useful training signal in iteration one are too easy by iteration two and easier still by iteration three. The mechanism is simple statistics: if every rollout on a prompt is correct, there's no variance — and with no variance, there's no reward signal to learn from. "Easy task give you zero learning signal," he says. "So you have a prompt when all of your rollouts are going to be correct. There's no variance. There's no RL signal." That's why Johnson says the bottleneck is task supply, not compute. And it reframes how you read every "benchmark saturates" story you see: the benchmark is only a symptom — the deeper problem is that the model has already exhausted the learning signal that benchmark once provided. The recent wave of essential service outages demonstrated the difficulty of applying an enterprise resiliency plan when redundancy options are limited. It's not just the loss of core business services that disrupt enterprises during these outages — CIOs and CISOs also face security challenges when a critical system goes down. "Microsoft, a core internet cloud provider, had a bad afternoon, and it traveled through email, chat, AI tools and an earnings calendar," Brian Greenberg, former CIO for consulting firm RHR International, said in a LinkedIn post . "And in my experience, most continuity plans can't cover an outage like this. Since these SaaS providers are essentially utilities, it's like having the power go out in your home. " In Microsoft's case, the Outlook and 365 outage was also long-lasting: It is now the largest reported on Downdetector in the last 12 months, with more than 7 million reports and an outage that lasted over 20 hours. Related: When auditors come for your AI algorithms While system redundancy can eliminate single points of failure and protect IT infrastructure against outages from third-party vendors and cloud providers, it's also expensive, hard to get buy in, difficult to demonstrate ROI and operationally complex to manage. When the affected service or application is essential to business operations, CIOs must rethink their approach to risk management and cybersecurity. In addition to the operational risk of lost business, enterprises face both internal and external security risks when a critical system such as Outlook is unavailable. "One risk is that employees will start finding other ways to get their jobs done (such as webmail, personal FTP [file transfer], and even WhatsApp), when all work-related comms should really be through formal channels," said Rik Turner, chief analyst at Omdia. In the case of Outlook, the outage was widely reported, which created an opportunity for external threats. Turner said there have been reports of a spike in phishing attacks worded to look like tech support emails. Microsoft Threat Intelligence reported observing a coordinated, high-volume phishing campaign that targeted enterprises globally across different verticals. Personnel there handle time-sensitive operations that directly support U.S. combat troops in the region. While officials have set up workarounds to keep sharing intelligence, the loss of the primary network has cost the agency time and required extra effort. The outage has also forced large numbers of NSA employees to stay home. For the third straight day, staff at both the Georgia facility and the agency’s headquarters in Fort Meade, Maryland, were told not to report to work while technicians try to patch and restore the system. Officials have not said how long the repairs will take. The NSA breakdown follows a string of separate system-update and server failures over the past several days—including a nationwide Federal Aviation Administration ground stop last Friday and outages affecting Microsoft, United Airlines, and Chase Bank. Despite the cluster of disruptions, the Trump administration maintains that the incidents are unrelated and that the United States is not under a cyberattack. 5d07306ad1.title: What comes after AGI? From AGI to Superintelligence
5d07306ad1.summary: For decades, AI research has been focused on a monumental milestone: building artificial general intelligence, or AGI - machines that match humans across nearly all cognitive tasks. It was always clear that, in principle, intelligence could progress beyond human level, but the prospect of AGI was far enough off, and surrounded by ample uncertainties of its own, that looking past it felt premature. Now that AGI is coming within reach, we can no longer put off seriously considering what comes next. While far from certain, AI could continue to advance at its current pace - and possibly even accelerate - towards artificial general superintelligence, or ASI. It could have a profound impact on science, the economy, and society at a scale and speed much greater than AGI itself. Preparing for that potential shift requires mapping the possible roads from AGI to ASI and building rigorous, reliable ways to track progress. To examine how the development of advanced AI might unfold, it helps to think of general intelligence , whether biological or artificial, as existing on a continuum. Human-level AGI is just one point along that spectrum. ASI sits further along as an advanced system that consistently outperforms large groups of human experts on tasks that could take them years to complete, using fewer resources and less time. Examples would be making the same scientific progress as an entire research field in a fraction of the time, or achieving technological developments, such as in chip design, on par with what large companies can do in a year. ASI would need to meet this bar across virtually all tasks of human interest, not just some in narrow domains (which is already the case with some AI systems today that can beat any human in Chess and Go, predict the structure of proteins from their amino acid sequences, or prove theorems that resisted human mathematicians for decades). Interestingly, we have a good mathematical understanding of the very upper end of the intelligence continuum - the theoretical limits of general intelligence. We also know about hard physical, logical, and complexity-theoretic limits to what AI can achieve, such as predicting how real-world complex systems - from climate to immune systems to human societies - play out with arbitrary precision. c26f5da6e9.title: Florida DMV back online after outage, but Lee County tax collector says it’s far from the first
c26f5da6e9.summary: Florida’s DMV services are operational again after a technical outage left drivers unable to access online services for a day. Going to the DMV is often unavoidable, and the outage caused inconvenience for many. Edgar Palacios, a Lehigh Acres resident, said, “So now my license is suspended. I’m coming out here to fix it because I can’t do it over the phone or online.” For some, the timing of the outage added to the frustration. Voldrick Dorlein, a Fort Myers resident, said, “I had to get my tag for my car. It’s on my birthday, so I had to come here on my birthday to get it.” The Florida Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles posted on X this morning that services had returned to normal after technical issues. Noelle Branning, the Lee County tax collector, said outages like this are not new in the area. “I don’t know why the agency announced this particular outage when we have seen so many of them this year. We had over 52 last year,” she said. Branning said the outages affect the tax collector’s office’s ability to serve customers efficiently, often leading to longer wait times. “This is beyond our control. It’s really hard for us to deliver that five-star service when these outages occur and they are outside of our control. So we have all of our management teams communicate with our customers so that they can make the best decision for themselves,” she said. Despite the challenges, some DMV customers are trying to stay optimistic. Dorlein said, “I would just say stay positive on that and not let it get to you.” Others, like Palacios, expressed frustration. “If my license were suspended and the system crashed and I couldn’t do anything, I would just leave,” he said. The Florida Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles stated that it is monitoring the system to ensure stability moving forward. OpenAI says GPT-6.2 Astra beats Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.2 on legal tasks at one-sixth the cost and leads on finance deliverables such as valuation workbooks. Google’s Gemini 4 Neon ranks first on legal and tax benchmarks at less than half the frontier price. Google and Microsoft both shipped decision models that make routing and compliance calls for a fraction of a cent. Two weeks ago, OpenAI let only vetted security teams use its most capable cybersecurity model, saying the risk was too high for general release. This week, it put artificial intelligence models with comparable capabilities on open sale. A model that can find and exploit software flaws is now available to any bank’s security team, any vendor in its supply chain and anyone probing its customer portal. Google, meanwhile, led a week of price cuts on legal and financial work. Its new Gemini 4 Neon costs $3 per million input tokens, less than half the $8 OpenAI and Anthropic charge for their top models. Tencent’s Hy4 flash costs $0.07. The week’s releases pull banks in two directions. OpenAI has put frontier cyber capability on open sale. Banks now have to assume attackers hold the same tools their security teams do. Meanwhile, the cost of tokens is falling, so financial institutions can deploy AI across more workflows, from contract review to tax work to financial modeling, without the bill deciding the question. 93d64cc905.title: Chile and OpenAI sign agreement to explore AI training for civil servants
93d64cc905.summary: Chile’s government and OpenAI have signed a memorandum of understanding to explore how civil servants could use AI in their day-to-day work. The agreement covers practical training for government staff, potential uses of AI in ministry administration and support for Chilean startups developing their own applications. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Ximena Lincolao, Chile’s Minister of Science, Technology, Knowledge and Innovation, signed the agreement on the sidelines of Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World conference in California. OpenAI announced the partnership on November 17 as part of OpenAI for Countries. The U.S. Department of Commerce’s technology export program supports the initiative, according to OpenAI. George Osborne, Head of OpenAI for Countries, wrote on LinkedIn : "Through OpenAI for Countries, we aim to help Chile bring AI into public services, equip civil servants with the skills to use it effectively, and support entrepreneurs building the next generation of businesses." The partners are considering workshops tailored to different government roles. Proposed topics include how to use AI tools effectively, check what they produce and handle sensitive information. The training would also cover when staff need to review an output or make a decision themselves. One option is to train government staff who could then teach colleagues. A separate part of the agreement would examine where AI might be used in the science ministry’s own administrative processes, with OpenAI potentially advising staff on adopting new models and training them to use the tools. That work would build on Chile’s National AI Policy , which already includes AI and ethics training for public officials. Its action plan brings together 177 initiatives coordinated by 14 ministries. In April 2025, the science ministry reported that 78% were underway or complete. The national plan also covers education and research. The ministry lists resources for teachers and students, courses on AI in teaching and work to make open data available for AI projects. Those measures are part of Chile’s existing policy. The training explored in the OpenAI agreement is aimed at government staff. The startup strand would explore access to OpenAI programs and technology, alongside practical training, technical guidance and mentoring. 828481aeab.title: Anthropic begins public trading in major test for promise and risk of AI - ABC News
828481aeab.summary: Anthropic immediately became one of the largest public companies in the world. Artificial intelligence giant Anthropic began trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday at a price of $111.50 a share, though the price dropped to $97.17 a share by the close of trading. Still, the company behind popular chatbot Claude occupied rarefied air among some of the largest public companies in the world. Anthropic's stock closed well above an offer price of $83 a share, which had valued the company at about $1.5 trillion. Dan Ives, a stock analyst at Yorkville Ives who focuses on tech, said on Thursday the stock debut provided a gauge of investor appetite for frontier AI models of the type made by Anthropic. Those models, in turn, fuel many AI products. "The AI revolution gets its public scoreboard," Ives said of Anthropic's stock listing. Even as Anthropic rose above its IPO price on Thursday, the broad stock indexes tumbled. The Dow Jones Industrial Average closed down 1,100 points, or 2.1% while S & P 500 dropped 2%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq declined 2.2%. The drop in overall markets owed in part to an uptick in demand for Anthropic, which prompted some investors to sell shares in other firms, Mohammed El-Erian, former CEO and co-CIO of investment management firm PIMCO, said on social media. "Remember this isn't just about the promise of AI, but about making room for it," El-Erian said on X . "In a narrow sense, investor financing of the mega-IPO involves making room by selling other holdings." The Anthropic IPO arrived at a tumultuous moment for the AI industry. Public concern over potential catastrophic risks posed by AI has grown in recent months, resulting in part from security incidents disclosed by Anthropic as well as the high-profile resignation of a researcher at the company. Nvidia, a high-flying AI firm and a partner of Anthropic, suffered a leadership shakeup last week as CEO Jensen Huang stepped down over allegations of an affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. The tech-heavy Nasdaq is down about 4% since Huang resigned. Huang admitted in an internal message to Nvidia staff that he had been "unfaithful to his wife," though he did not name the person with whom he had been involved. Here's what to know about the Anthropic IPO: The IPO pulled in fresh funds for the San Francisco-based firm, which aims to compete in a potentially lucrative but cost-intensive section of the AI industry centered on advanced models and the tools they empower. ab107cfc88.title: Protesters rally against Anthropic in New York and San Francisco after $2tn stock market debut
ab107cfc88.summary: Anti-AI groups gather in front of Nasdaq exchange in Times Square and Anthropic’s headquarters in San Francisco As the artificial intelligence startup Anthropic debuted on the US stock market at an eye-popping $2tn valuation on Thursday, protesters from anti-AI groups rallied in front of the Nasdaq exchange at its New York City headquarters in Times Square and several were arrested. Similar demonstrations took place outside Anthropic’s San Francisco headquarters. “I think people are starting to get that there’s something wrong,” Jose Gonzalez, 46, one of roughly 30 protesters in New York City, said. Protesters carried flags reading “STOP TECH OLIGARCHS” and “FREEZE AI: END ICE, END WAR”. Anthropic, founded in 2021, completed the largest initial public offering in history this week, raising about $81bn to continue developing its Claude family of generative AI models. The Times Square rally featured a series of speeches from several community leaders, including Aber Kawas, a New York state senator, who said: “Investing in AI also comes at the direct cost of investing in people.” Gonzalez took off work to rally in Times Square on Thursday morning. He works as a policy researcher for New York Communities for Change, a non-profit community organizing group that helped rally outside the Nasdaq building. He believes stricter regulations on AI progression nationwide are needed before people are more comfortable with AI research. Environmental safety, national security, Flock cameras and AI’s connection to Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and law enforcement were among the largest concerns for protesters. “It’s all connected,” Jes Vesconte, 30, said after wrapping up the New York rally. “The same capitalist imperialism is causing the affordability crisis and the climate emergency and atrocities that ICE is doing.” Vesconte works for a local worker agency in New York. He said he’s encouraging his peers not participate in the stock trading for Anthropic. “If we did not have the profit motive, we wouldn’t be having these issues,” he said. “This is the epitome of that with the largest IPO ever.” Outside Anthropic’s headquarters in downtown San Francisco , about three dozen protesters from two different groups gathered before 11am. One activist held a fake stock certificate for a single share of “Misanthropic”. 45683f085c.title: Another tech outage? Here's what to do
45683f085c.summary: From banking delays to a communications meltdown behind last week's nationwide ground stop, experts say don't panic. Here's what else to do in the event of a tech outage. From banking delays to a communications meltdown behind last week's nationwide ground stop, experts say don't panic. Here's what else to do in the event of a tech outage. From banking blackouts to inaccessible emails, tech outages over the past couple of weeks have disrupted millions of lives nationwide. And, in an increasingly interconnected world, experts say AI integration could drive more outages. Now, they're stressing the importance of preparing before the next disruption hits. "We're in an upgrade period right now. AI is changing things rapidly and we're trying to keep up," Chris Steinhauer from the National Cybersecurity Alliance said. "It's kind of like storm preparedness or disaster preparedness where you need to have extra water, extra food." To stay ready, experts have several recommendations, including: Writing down passwords is also a good idea, according to experts, who say the bigger threat today is online. "Digital crimes don't rely on paper anymore for the most part," James Lee, president of the Identity Theft Resource Center , said. "You don't have to worry if you write down all your passwords. You can keep that in something folded up in your wallet or in your purse or your desk." When an outage occurs, experts suggest verifying its legitimacy to avoid unnecessary actions like resetting passwords, which could lock you out of your account. Keeping a record of transactions is also good practice, according to Lee. "Go ahead and take a screenshot of what you did, so if you need it, when everything's back to normal, you can go to your customer service representative and say, 'Hey, I had this problem. I just want to confirm,'" Lee said. After an outage, experts also advise reviewing what worked and what didn’t to improve your preparedness for the next disruption. Scams are another concern during outages, as they tend to spike when people are anxious. Steinhauer warns against trusting incoming messages or calls without verification. A general rule: trust no one and verify everything. And, if still unsure, look up the company’s official website, app, or phone number before contacting the company.
