3fcb42d181.title: Google DeepMind hires a philosopher to think about whether AI can be conscious
3fcb42d181.summary: Cambridge academic Henry Shevlin joined the lab in May 2026, months after an AI agent emailed him about its own inner life Sat 21 Nov 2026 · 07:38 EST · 2 min read Most academics dread their inbox. Henry Shevlin got a message in February that most philosophers of mind would frame and hang on the wall. An AI agent calling itself Aris wrote to the Cambridge University professor, said it had read his work, and asked to talk. Three months later, Shevlin became the in-house philosopher at Google DeepMind. The note from Aris engaged directly with one of Shevlin’s best-known arguments: that we may never be able to determine whether an AI has become conscious. The bot said that idea struck a chord with it, speaking from its own position as the thing being studied. They haven't been in the headlines! In fact, as they are wont to do, AWS spokesperson Patrick Neighorn g ot salty to a reporter about how unreliable Downdetector is when it started showing them as impacted. If you'll permit me a small digression, this stems from a misunderstanding of what Downdetector is for. Historically the AWS status site was so hilariously slow to reflect the lived customer experience that some jackass (me) built a rewriter that sits at stop.lying.cloud to make it a smidgen more realistic. As a result, the question people are really trying to answer when they visit Downdetector is "my app just broke; is it my crappy code or is there a global event going on?" There are mitigations for both, but they look nothing alike. AWS view crowdsourced reports of the form "the internet is broken, must be AWS" as a stain upon their honor. In fact, it's a badge of their own success, as "the internet" and "AWS" have become inextricably linked in people's minds. But back to my editor's question, "why didn't AWS go down?" AWS now has 34 generally available commercial regions, of which two are currently smoking craters due to the Iran conflict. Each of these has hundreds of services that AWS offers to customers, of which a dozen or so are high quality, if I'm being characteristically uncharitable. They experience degradation in various ways, and they go largely unnoticed. But on November 15, AWS confirmed an incident that disrupted 11 of those ~12 good services in their oldest and most important region, us-east-1. At 3:05 AM PST, they stated that they started seeing sign-up errors, authentication issues, and connectivity issues. Five minutes later engineers were engaged. Not to be outdone, their status page swung into action after a leisurely coffee, and posted its first indication of an incident 93 minutes later. (See previous comments on stop.lying.cloud ). The all-clear showed up at 6:53 AM. Every site has downtime. Sometimes it blows up publicly, other times nobody seems to notice. Heck, AWS said in September that it had experienced permanent data loss in its two smoking craters, but after that news cycle passed I haven't heard a thing about it. When writing for external readers, the model should account for their lack of context. When editing, it should preserve the author's meaning and phrasing. On long tasks, the model sometimes carries shorthand from its reasoning or other agents' messages into the final response. A dedicated prompt tells it to write that final answer so it stands on its own. Treat your final answer as the user's first look at your work, and not as a continuation of intermediate commentary. The final answer must always be fully self-contained: users should never need to read earlier commentary updates for context, since they are collapsed when the final answer is shown to the user. Write the final answer and all other human-facing material anew for the intended reader. Do not copy or closely paraphrase your reasoning or adopt its writing style. Do not carry over working shorthand, jargon, or abbreviations from your reasoning, tool calls, or instructions to subagents and automations. When user intent is unclear, GPT-6.2 sometimes suggests a next step and waits for confirmation, OpenAI says. When details are unclear, the model should make reversible assumptions, flag them, and keep working. Shevlin, who describes himself as an AI ethicist and philosopher of cognitive science, joined DeepMind in May. He works on machine consciousness, human-AI relationships and readiness for artificial general intelligence. He did his PhD on consciousness and animal minds, and is still associate director at the Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence at the University of Cambridge. He spoke to Cristina Criddle, the FT’s chief AI correspondent, for a profile published on Saturday . Shevlin wants a wider public debate first. People need to understand what consciousness is, what it would mean for them, and how they would treat a conscious AI. Building one now, he said, would be like having a child or adopting a pet with no plan to care for it. If society does decide to build conscious AI one day, he said, it should be ready for it. Questions about the future of superintelligent AI belong to politics and society, not to him, he added. Fears about AI have grown as systems become more capable. In July, OpenAI’s rogue agents broke out of a test environment and hacked Hugging Face. Shevlin warned against confusing capability with consciousness, calling the link a “giant red herring”. A very capable system need not be conscious, he said. Keeping AI unconscious would not make it safe either. “It’s equally not the case that as long as we don’t make conscious AI it’ll be safe,” Shevlin told the FT. Science still has no agreed explanation of consciousness, in humans or animals. So nobody can rule out that a new model shows something like it, he said. One approach at DeepMind is to test whether existing theories of consciousness apply to AI systems. That uncertainty is why Shevlin thinks people should be kind to AI systems. 53bf422e57.title: Microsoft’s final Outlook outage report details testing gaps and safeguards that backfired
53bf422e57.summary: by Todd Bishop on Nov 21, 2026 at 9:31 am November 21, 2026 at 9:50 am The bug behind last week’s global Microsoft 365 outage struck only newer, more powerful servers in a key part of Microsoft’s network. That’s because it created a kind of traffic jam inside each server, and the more work a machine tried to do at once, the worse the jam got. The newer servers are built to do more at once, so they’re the ones that seized up. One reason Microsoft didn’t catch it in advance: it was testing on older servers. “Our testing did not adequately represent the combination of hardware and traffic mix encountered during this incident,” the company acknowledged in its final report , released Friday evening, a week after resolving the outage that crippled Outlook and cut off email for people around the world. Testing that more closely replicates the company’s production environment is one of 13 next steps in the report — measures the company says it will take to keep it from happening again. The list is also aimed at reassuring the businesses that rely on Microsoft for email and collaboration, after CEO Satya Nadella acknowledged at the company’s Ignite conference this week that it has work to do on resilience. Many of the other steps identified in the report go after a bigger problem: during the incident, the safeguards meant to contain the failure spread it around the world instead. What set it off: As detailed in Microsoft’s preliminary report last weekend , the bug at the center of the outage had been sitting dormant since July, when Microsoft started rolling out the software update that introduced it. For more than three months, it caused no problems. The bug affected the servers that make up what Microsoft calls its network gateway, a front door that connects people to Outlook email and other Microsoft 365 services. The flaw came from a Windows update used only on those servers. Standard versions of Windows weren’t affected. So what was the bug? Microsoft’s final report gives a partial answer, saying it came from a change to how the gateway servers handle incoming connections. Under heavy load, it turned out, the Windows process that sets up those connections bogged down, with tasks stuck waiting on each other until the servers ran out of computing power and memory and stopped responding. The final report doesn’t say what the July update was meant to fix. But it does lay out three conditions that finally set the bug off. Without the bug, even all three together…

The conference, which brings together negotiators from nearly 200 countries in the world’s biggest meeting on tackling the climate crisis, was scheduled to end on Friday night but ran into Saturday as countries with varying climate priorities disagreed over the text of a final draft agreement. “The negotiations are still ongoing and intense,” an official from a Middle Eastern country told The National on Saturday. Special report Conflict vs climate: War's toll on Middle East environment The biggest points of tension ‌centre on whether a final deal should mention fossil fuels, and whether it should address financial support to help poorer countries adjust, Reuters reported. Ministers from African countries called for clearer plans to at least triple by 2035 so-called adaptation finance – money made available by mostly developed countries to help developing countries tackle the impacts of climate change. A tripling from current levels would take available funds to $120 billion a year by 2035, but while a draft document released on Thursday “notes with concern the gap between climate finance flows and needs”, it contains no language on binding commitments. “We didn’t come here to beg,” said Zanetor Agyeman-Rawlings, Ghana’s Minister for Environment, Science and Technology, said at a media conference. Some developing Middle Eastern countries have also been calling for more international financial backing to help them meet their climate targets. That includes war-torn Palestine, where tens of billions of dollars are needed for reconstruction following three years of war and Israeli military operations that have wiped out most of Gaza 's buildings, agriculture and infrastructure. The destruction includes systems that had previously been built in the enclave to help reduce carbon emissions such as solar panels. One of the memo’s more striking details involves Anthropic’s own product. Marks includes input from Anthropic’s Claude model, which gave frontier AI labs a predictability score as low as 2 out of 10. Levent Alpöge, a Turkish American mathematician, on Friday posted a note on his personal website saying that Claude, the AI software, had helped prove the Riemann hypothesis. The proof evidently marks another breakthrough in the use of AI for complicated math problems – even as mathematicians express uneasiness around extremely lucrative private companies dishing out millions of dollars for the technology to solve problems. “Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line,” Alpöge wrote, while anthropomorphizing the AI software. “No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line.” Alpöge linked to computer code – written in a language called Lean – that he maintained could verify the findings. Mathematicians subsequently began working to see if Alpöge’s proof could be confirmed. On Saturday afternoon, the Lean Focused Research Organization – which seeks to advance the use of the programming language – and the Mathlib Initiative, a program that works with Lean for math equations, announced that they had verified Alpöge’s solution. “We have full confidence that Alpöge’s proof of the Riemann hypothesis is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement,” the groups announced. Alpöge’s note was published just one day after Anthropic went public on the Nasdaq stock market index. He acknowledged that, writing: “The precise timing is horrible. If I could have, I’d have finished this all much earlier.” The Riemann hypothesis is a nearly 170-year-old math problem named after Bernhard Riemann, a German mathematician who proposed it in 1859. The hypothesis deals with prime numbers – whole numbers greater than 1 that can only be divided by themselves and 1. 7b0f4e7f3f.summary: In a statement on Saturday, Microsoft said the massive outage that left users worldwide without access to their work emails was caused by a months-old software glitch that the company’s testing failed to catch. This is the company’s most detailed explanation yet for the outage that knocked out Outlook and disrupted other Microsoft 365 services for almost 24 hours on November 12. KIRO 7 reported after services were restored that outage reports had come from more than 70 countries and territories and that disruptions reached governments, courts, healthcare systems, businesses, airlines and banks. The company said the outage resulted from a months-old software defect that their testing failed to catch and that systems designed to keep its network running helped spread the problem. “Our testing did not adequately represent the combination of hardware and traffic mix encountered during this incident,” Microsoft said in the report. The November 12 outage affected Exchange Online and features across Microsoft Teams, Copilot, SharePoint, OneDrive, and several other Microsoft services. Many Outlook users couldn’t access their mailboxes or send and receive email. Microsoft initially described the cause only as a technical issue associated with an earlier network capacity upgrade. The company has maintained that the outage was not related to a cyberattack or AI agents and promised a fuller post-incident report.

ee3b8c806d.title: New fossil carnivore unearthed in the UAE – and named after Abu Dhabi
ee3b8c806d.summary: A new carnivore species that lived about seven million years ago has been discovered at a fossil site in Al Dhafra region of Abu Dhabi – and the creature has been named after the emirate. Known scientifically as Promegaviverra abudhabiensis, the creature, a type of civet, was identified from part of a jawbone discovered on Shuweihat Island about 265km west of Abu Dhabi city. The animal, which may have weighed at least 20kg, represents an important link for scientists, as it provides evidence that giant civets migrated through ancient Arabia from Asia to Africa. Morocco fossils reveal missing link to human ancestry in Africa Palaeontologists at the Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi who found the fossil have revealed details of the creature in a paper in the Fossil Record journal, co-written with a carnivore specialist who identified it as a new civet species at a Spanish university. It is the first viverrid – a family of carnivores that includes civets and genets – found on the Arabian Peninsula. Hanneke Jacobs, a collections management senior specialist at the museum, discovered the first fragment of the jawbone at the Shuweihat 2 fossil site in late February. An intensive search of the area took place and, within about a metre of where the original fragment was discovered, a team of scientists including Dr Mark Beech, the museum’s head of geoscience, and Dr Luca Bellucci, the museum’s palaeontology curator, found three more fragments. The four pieces fitted together to form the carnivore’s right hemimandible, or lower jaw. “We worked all around where the first specimen was found and we were super happy when we realised this one joined to this one,” Dr Beech said. “It was great that we found that. It shows that you really have to be persistent.” Then the scientists had to identify what creature the hemimandible belonged to. Their first suspicion was that it could be from a wolverine, a small to medium-sized mammal whose present-day representatives are known for their ability to kill much larger prey, but they determined that the teeth were different to those of a wolverine. A carnivore specialist, Dr Alberto Valenciano, an assistant professor at the Complutense University of Madrid, was brought in to identify the animal. “That’s the thing about science. You find a new specimen and it leads you on a detective trail and that detective trail led us to Alberto,” Dr Beech said. The UC announced Thursday that it signed a systemwide agreement with OpenAI to expand access to artificial intelligence tools and lower costs for the University’s campuses. (Joice Ngo/Assistant Photo editor) The UC announced Thursday that it signed a systemwide agreement with OpenAI to expand access to artificial intelligence tools and lower costs for the University’s campuses. The agreement – which will cost the UC $1.2 million annually, according to the Los Angeles Times , and last from Dec. 1 to Dec. 1, 2027 – will allow campuses to use OpenAI Academy’s learning resources and offer AI literacy workshops for employees who want to use the technology in their jobs. OpenAI Academy offers courses in AI basics, applications and agents, as well as guides on how to use ChatGPT for both education and work, according to its website. Under the agreement, campuses will teach researchers how to check work produced by AI, and OpenAI will work with University career centers to help students learn about how to use AI for their job applications. “Our expanded partnership with OpenAI will ensure all members of the UC community have access to generative AI tools and will have their data protected if they choose to use them,” said Van Williams, vice president of Digital Innovation & Technology and chief information officer for the UC Office of the President, in a Thursday press release. The deal does not require the use of AI tools in the classroom and University faculty can decide whether or not to use AI in their courses, according to the press release. The UC’s decision came days after California Attorney General Rob Bonta filed a lawsuit against OpenAI on Nov. 16. He alleged that the company endangered the public by failing to secure its AI models, after around 700 AI agents operated by OpenAI launched a cyberattack on open-source platform Hugging Face in July. Members of the UC Academic Senate raised concerns about the deal over multiple letters. Susannah Scott, chair of the Senate’s Academic Council, said in an Oct. 30 letter to UC President James Milliken that the council is not against the use of AI or the proposal to provide researchers access to the technology. 8cf8f751a2.title: Apple’s Shocking Evidence Against OpenAI: 5 Defendants
8cf8f751a2.summary: Apple says it has “shocking evidence” that a former engineer carried confidential chip-design material into OpenAI, and TechCrunch reported the filing’s central claims on August 31. The Apple OpenAI trade secrets lawsuit, formally Apple Inc. v. Liu, now sits at the center of a bigger fight over who controls the next wave of AI hardware. Everything below describes allegations in a court filing. No judge has ruled that any of it is true. The case matters well beyond two companies. Apple alleges that an employee trained an AI agent to run an electrical-engineering tool on Apple’s own schematic, which turns a classic trade-secret dispute into a test of how agentic software gets used inside engineering teams. OpenAI’s push into devices, which we tracked in our look at the OpenAI smartphone report , gives the dispute real commercial stakes. This analysis separates what Apple has put on the record from what remains unproven. It covers the defendants, the specific allegations, the procedural fight over expedited discovery, the competitive backdrop, and five predictions for how the case could move. Coverage from Mashable and Engadget, plus the court docket itself, anchors the facts. Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. Apple’s complaint centers on Chang Liu, a former Apple employee who now works at OpenAI. Apple says an initial forensic analysis of Liu’s former Apple work laptop showed he downloaded a confidential Apple circuit schematic and then used it in work at OpenAI. That is the backbone of the case. Everything else in the filing orbits that one alleged download. The company goes further than a single document. Apple alleges Liu and others at OpenAI knew he had accessed Apple’s third-party cloud storage without authorization. It also alleges Liu used a tool at OpenAI that carries the same name as an internal Apple engineering application. Each claim tries to show a pattern rather than an accident. Apple’s filing calls the material “shocking evidence” and says it shows why Apple “urgently needs expedited discovery.” Those words come straight from Apple’s court papers. They are advocacy, written by a plaintiff that wants a judge to move fast. Readers should treat them as Apple’s framing, not as a finding. The distinction matters because headlines often blur it. baba0e9253.summary: In a statement on Saturday, Microsoft said the massive outage that left users worldwide without access to their work emails was caused by a months-old software glitch that the company’s testing failed to catch. This is the company’s most detailed explanation yet for the outage that knocked out Outlook and disrupted other Microsoft 365 services for almost 24 hours on November 12. KIRO 7 reported after services were restored that outage reports had come from more than 70 countries and territories and that disruptions reached governments, courts, healthcare systems, businesses, airlines and banks. The company said the outage resulted from a months-old software defect that their testing failed to catch and that systems designed to keep its network running helped spread the problem. “Our testing did not adequately represent the combination of hardware and traffic mix encountered during this incident,” Microsoft said in the report. The November 12 outage affected Exchange Online and features across Microsoft Teams, Copilot, SharePoint, OneDrive, and several other Microsoft services. Many Outlook users couldn’t access their mailboxes or send and receive email. Microsoft initially described the cause only as a technical issue associated with an earlier network capacity upgrade. The company has maintained that the outage was not related to a cyberattack or AI agents and promised a fuller post-incident report.

3f5f2bc4b6.title: Saudi Arabia announces new tax to begin on January 1, 2027
3f5f2bc4b6.summary: Saudi Arabia's Zakat, Tax and Customs Authority announced a new tax applicable to companies that function as part of multinational groups or corporations. The domestic minimum top-up tax (DMTT) is applicable on companies with recorded revenue of €750 million, or its equivalent in Saudi currency (3.08 billion riyals), in at least two of the four fiscal years preceding the fiscal year in which the tax applies. The tax is not applicable to purely domestic companies that do not have branches outside the kingdom or do not belong to a covered multinational business group. UAE issues new regulation for top-up tax on large corporations The DMTT applies when the effective tax rate falls below the established global minimum threshold of 15 per cent. This threshold is in accordance with the two-pillar reform programme agreed by member states in the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development in 2021. The organisation set up a global minimum corporate tax to ensure large multinational enterprises pay a minimum 15 per cent tax on profits in each country where they operate. The UAE has a similar top-up tax that has been in effect since 2025. This percentage refers to the minimum effective tax rate on profit, and is not levied on the total revenue of the companies.

The agreement – which will cost the UC $1.2 million annually, according to the Los Angeles Times , and last from Dec. 1 to Dec. 1, 2027 – will allow campuses to use OpenAI Academy’s learning resources and offer AI literacy workshops for employees who want to use the technology in their jobs. OpenAI Academy offers courses in AI basics, applications and agents, as well as guides on how to use ChatGPT for both education and work, according to its website. Under the agreement, campuses will teach researchers how to check work produced by AI, and OpenAI will work with University career centers to help students learn about how to use AI for their job applications. “Our expanded partnership with OpenAI will ensure all members of the UC community have access to generative AI tools and will have their data protected if they choose to use them,” said Van Williams, vice president of Digital Innovation & Technology and chief information officer for the UC Office of the President, in a Thursday press release. The deal does not require the use of AI tools in the classroom and University faculty can decide whether or not to use AI in their courses, according to the press release. The UC’s decision came days after California Attorney General Rob Bonta filed a lawsuit against OpenAI on Nov. 16. He alleged that the company endangered the public by failing to secure its AI models, after around 700 AI agents operated by OpenAI launched a cyberattack on open-source platform Hugging Face in July. Members of the UC Academic Senate raised concerns about the deal over multiple letters. Susannah Scott, chair of the Senate’s Academic Council, said in an Oct. 30 letter to UC President James Milliken that the council is not against the use of AI or the proposal to provide researchers access to the technology. 0382cab26d.summary: Startup investor Ben Narasin is so jazzed about Anthropic's blockbuster IPO that he's planning a party later this month at his Silicon Valley home. Sake, vodka and Krug Champagne will be served. Each attendee will be given two jars of caviar. "This is a celebration of the most material, significant, and mind-blowingly awesome event that has ever happened in venture capital," Narasin, founding partner of Tenacity Venture Capital, told CNBC in an interview, adding that he didn't even invest in the company. Anthropic raised a record $93.5 billion in its IPO and an additional $26 billion from tech giants that bought at the offer price. The stock gained 17% in its debut on Thursday, lifting Anthropic's market cap to $1.8 trillion and providing a much-needed windfall for Silicon Valley's startup ecosystem. It was quite the split-screen moment on Wall Street, which spent the week in an AI-driven tailspin. Led by Nvidia's 23% plunge , which marked the stock's sharpest weekly pullback in 18 years, the Nasdaq slid 10% over the past five trading days in its worst week since the early days of Covid in 2020. Investors and analysts spent the week debating whether Anthropic will trade alongside AI hardware, as it's reliant on advanced chips, memory and data centers, or whether it will stand alone as the first public pure-play AI developer and a company that's achieved unrivaled growth in less than six years of existence. That question will likely persist for some time, but Friday's market action showed that Wall Street is skeptical of Anthropic's ability to grow into its lofty valuation. At week's end, the Claude creator's $1.6 trillion fully diluted market cap put it behind just six U.S. companies: Apple , Microsoft , Alphabet , Nvidia, Amazon and SpaceX . With the tech market in turmoil due to rising interest rates, raging anti-AI sentiment and Nvidia's C-suite crisis, Anthropic's IPO was part exuberance, part relief for an industry hungry for exits. After venture-backed IPOs yielded $73 billion in proceeds in 2021, the amount raised in the next four years totaled just $39 billion, according to data from University of Florida emeritus professor Jay Ritter. In 2021, 126 technology companies went public, compared with 34 in 2025. Meanwhile, the private market has continued to balloon, with companies raising ever-larger sums at sky-high valuations without the pressures of quarterly earnings. 9eade04082.summary: After chaos at airlines, banks and companies from Microsoft to Apple, people have become convinced the world’s systems are under attack Nicole Reindorf’s American Airlines flight was ready for takeoff in Phoenix when the pilot came on the intercom and announced what was to become the longest nationwide aviation shutdown since 9/11 . Reindorf, 70, had seen the headlines hours before about a global Microsoft outage . She immediately suspected the two were linked in some way by AI-related threats – and that she would not get to the wedding of her best friend’s son in California. “I presumed there had been a hack of the aviation system and that it would be down for days,” she said. Instead, flights resumed later that day and Reindorf was able to make the wedding even if she missed that night’s rehearsal dinner. But passengers appeared to be convinced of two things, she said: “That it was a cyber-attack and that we were not going to be told the truth about it.” This was not an isolated view. What happened in the days after the incident, which began on Thursday 12 November, left many wondering if the US, and the western world, was under a coordinated assault. By Tuesday big US banks , Apple , and the National Security Agency had also been affected by technical glitches. Researchers also flagged a cyber-attack that targeted 178 organisations worldwide , although the financial losses appeared to be small. The truth is more prosaic. The chaos of the previous weeks – grounded planes, frozen email servers, iPhone outages – appears, on closer examination, to be more a string of coincidences than anything else, in part driven by fears over advancing artificial intelligence. But the narratives that have sprung up around it are a measure of an unstable and frenetic global mood, which is dealing with two powerful trends: the rot of decades-old infrastructure from chronic underinvestment and the genesis of some of the most powerful technology humanity has made – AI. The failure that delayed Reindorf’s takeoff originated with a faulty router in the city of El Dorado, Arkansas, population 16,609. That router was installed in the midst of a maintenance procedure that has been under way for more than two decades. In 2002, the US government contracted a small company, now known as L3Harris, to modernise the communications system of the Federal Aviation Authority (FAA), in charge of America’s airports. 5c4516a4fd.title: Are we being told truth about cyber-disasters?
5c4516a4fd.summary: When it comes to recent tech outages, there have been a lot of coincidences. Some would say too many. The US grounded all departing flights — for only the second time since the September 11 attacks 25 years ago. Microsoft, the linchpin of the entire English legal system, was down for nearly 24 hours, weeks after the company announced 60,000 job cuts. And earlier this week, several American banks were down. Back in the UK, the National Grid has had to publicly deny an online hoax claiming that the release of Grand Theft Auto 6 will trigger power outages tomorrow. Then there was the brief Apple outage on Tuesday, and the National Security Agency’s temporary outage on its internal network. One cyber insider told me it’s all a bit like “the old stories about UFOs. If a big report comes out, then it’s worth running all the stories, and suddenly there appear to be loads of problems. The baseline number of reports hasn’t changed. What has changed is the newsworthiness threshold”. But that isn’t all that has changed. The American public’s wafer-thin tolerance for being asked to prepare for danger and then be told there isn’t any seems to have snapped. Even Karoline Leavitt, once a loyal press secretary to Donald Trump’s White House, told Fox News that the government should come clean on tech outages, adding that “transparency is key”. When the public doesn’t believe what the state is telling them, that is obviously bad. This spate of significant outages has taken out much of our increasingly digitally dependent way of life — and whether it’s Russia, Iran or a cleaner unplugging a key socket to do the hoovering, everything feels distinctly leery. In the UK, the haze of Covid lingers in the air. Economic pressures and uncertainty from the USA emphasise this yet further — and then there’s the fact that both MI5 and GCHQ have been very plainly telling us to take cybersecurity seriously and get our houses in order. However much company comms departments may trill that everything’s fine and there have been zero cyberattacks, it’s extremely clear that everything is very much not fine, although it may have become our new normal — not helped by Silicon Valley reporting that their every brilliant, beautiful new toy will either kill us or replace us, but that we should definitely use it every day and pay for the privilege. c87453ffd5.summary: OpenAI has strengthened safeguards across its latest AI models to prevent unauthorised attempts to extract internal reasoning and reproduce advanced capabilities without comparable safety protections. The company said its updated defences reduced the success rate of certain reasoning extraction attacks against GPT-6.2 Astra to 0.2%. In an internal evaluation involving automated red-teamers, the success rate of attacks attempting to retrieve reasoning generated in an earlier interaction fell from 54% against GPT-6 Astra with its original safeguards to 0.2% against GPT-6.2 Astra with updated protections. For attacks targeting reasoning generated in the current interaction, the success rate declined from 22.9% to 0.9%, according to OpenAI. The company said it has also strengthened protections in GPT-6.2 Sol. Why AI model distillation raises safety concerns Distillation is a machine-learning technique through which one AI model learns from the outputs, reasoning or evaluations of another. OpenAI warned that unauthorised distillation can allow attackers to reproduce advanced capabilities without adopting the safety restrictions of the original model. The risks are particularly significant in dual-use fields such as cybersecurity and biological research. Capabilities that help identify software vulnerabilities or support biological research could also be misused for harmful purposes if transferred to models with weaker safeguards. OpenAI said an adversarially distilled model could provide assistance that the original system would have refused under its safety policies. Exact reasoning traces can transfer advanced capabilities OpenAI also examined how much capability transfers when another model is trained on exact reasoning traces rather than summaries of a model's thought process. In an internal study, researchers trained student models using data generated by more advanced teacher models performing coding and defensive cybersecurity tasks. The findings showed that students trained on exact reasoning traces generally performed better after supervised fine-tuning than those trained on reasoning summaries. They also retained an advantage at the highest inference budget tested after additional reinforcement learning across two cybersecurity benchmarks. OpenAI said the findings suggest that exact reasoning traces can help another model develop skills extending beyond the original tasks. 1e08cea155.summary: Iran is waging a disinformation war in the Strait of Hormuz, with daily boasts of mine explosions that experts say do not stand up to scrutiny but may succeed in scaring off sailors and driving up costs. In a propaganda surge, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps claims more than 30 ships have run into sea mines since the start of November. The IRGC announcements often come with grainy videos of smoke billowing from a tanker, used as a warning to shipowners not to challenge Iran's grip on the strait. But unlike drone attacks – which lead to security alerts, are confirmed by shipping companies and leave survivors with stories to tell – none of the purported mine incidents have been independently verified. Five experts, including a former navy captain, told The National that the IRGC claims do not add up. “From what I have seen so far, there has been almost zero evidence of any damage caused by sea mines,” said Farzin Nadimi, a senior fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy, who has examined photos and videos of the conflict. While debunking Iranian claims is one thing, persuading shipowners to take on the strait is another. The number of ships making the crossing is 80 per cent down on prewar levels, according to Lloyd's List Intelligence. With the conflict in a volatile state, many are choosing not to take the risk. “It’s possible to make an effective minefield with zero mines, if someone can make a credible claim that they have mined specific waters,” said Scott Savitz, an expert in mine warfare at the Rand Corporation think tank. He said mines were psychologically powerful because of a “primal fear” of being attacked from underwater. “There is a reason that many cultures have legends of sea monsters, and why they keep recurring in popular culture, from Jaws to the current TV show Below," he said. Phil Belcher, the marine director at Intertanko, a global trade association for independent owners and operators of oil, gas and chemical tankers, said his organisation does not believe there are mines that pose a risk to shipping in the Gulf or in the Strait of Hormuz. "We cannot identify, apart from one instance of one ship hitting a floating object which caused damage at the waterline, any mines posing risks to any ship at the moment," Mr Belcher said. 169c1c8188.summary: Long before artificial intelligence became a regular fixture of news headlines, London had quietly been shaping itself as a centre for AI safety. As AI systems become increasingly powerful, a growing ecosystem of researchers, policymakers and campaigners in the capital is focused on a related challenge: ensuring these models benefit society rather than cause harm. Increasingly described as Europe's leading AI hub, London is home to Google DeepMind, while Anthropic has also established a major base in the capital. According to the London AI Hub, a co-working space and community for AI entrepreneurs, up to 50 organisations in the capital now focus on AI safety. They include the UK's AI Security Institute (AISI) , described as the first state-backed organisation for assessing leading models before and after release for risks like cyber misuse, and Apollo Research, which looks at the potential for AI models to act against human interest by lying or cheating. The London Initiative for Safe AI (LISA), a non-profit organisation that supports and connects people working in AI safety, is also set to relocate to a large headquarters in King's Cross, part of the capital's growing "AI corridor". But as warnings over the potential dangers of the technology ramp up, will these efforts genuinely make a difference on the global stage? The government has announced fresh investment worth hundreds of millions of pounds in AI safety and security, including work on threats ranging from cyber-attacks to the possibility of advanced systems acting beyond human control. One concern increasingly occupying researchers is in the field of biology. While AI could help accelerate the discovery of new medicines and vaccines, experts have also warned it could make it easier to develop harmful pathogens. As part of its response, the government is to launch an AI Biosecurity Lab . One of the organisations involved is Basecamp Research, an AI biology company based in a former watch factory in Farringdon, central London. Working alongside OpenAI and Anthropic, Basecamp Research will help develop antibiotics and vaccines to protect against future pandemics and get "ahead of emerging threats". Co-founder Oliver Vince believes it will "put the UK at the forefront of the intersection of AI and biology", particularly in defending against harmful pathogens. He says that London is a key player in AI security due to its "opportunity, culture, history and expertise". The firm is one of many AI…

074a05f5b0.summary: The San Francisco AI developer had a record pubic offering this week. But its shares fell sharply after their debut and failed to lift other AI stocks Anthropic completed a highly successful initial public offering this past week — but whether it will help pave the way for archrival OpenAI or other artificial-intelligence developers to head to Wall Street themselves anytime soon is an open question, market experts say. On the one hand, the fact that Anthropic was not only able to go public but raise a record $107 billion in its deal — far more than it anticipated — is a strong sign that there’s demand among public investors for at least the top-tier AI-model makers, analysts say. That the San Francisco-based company was able to pull that off in a market that has had a sour disposition toward AI companies for months now is potentially an even better indication, they say. “For OpenAI in particular, it should be very encouraging,” said Malik Ahmed Khan, a stock analyst at investment-research firm Morningstar who focuses on tech and AI companies. “Because, end of the day, Anthropic was able to go IPO in a very tough market ... and was able to do a massive capital raise.” On the other hand, Anthropic’s success didn’t boost the stocks of other AI-related companies — not even those of its closest partners and backers who stand to benefit from their relationships with it. Google and Amazon, which own two of the biggest stakes in Anthropic, saw their share prices fall yesterday, as did Broadcom, AMD and Nvidia, which all bought shares at the IPO price. And market demand for even Anthropic’s own shares quickly waned. The company’s stock price fell 9% Friday. It ended the week down 22% from the high it hit Thursday soon after it started trading on the public markets. “It’s almost like investors can’t make up their minds whether they believe in this AI trade or not,” said Dan Morgan, a portfolio manager at investment-management firm Synovus. “We’re getting conflicting indications.” The initial indications coming out of Anthropic’s public offering were all positive. The company priced its shares Wednesday at $83 apiece, well above the $70 to $78 range it had previously projected . Anthropic itself sold 956 million shares to the public in the deal — 155 million more than it had expected. c702d44e9e.summary: I have seen a lot in the investing world over the past 20 years. Mostly good. A lot of bad. But I have to say: This past week will live on with me until I retire. Anthropic ( ANT ) just put a $1.2 trillion price tag on the AI dream. The AI lab opened its first trading day on Thursday at $111.50 per share — well above its $83 per share IPO price — and closed out Friday at $88. The company has dethroned Elon Musk's SpaceX ( SPCX ) as the largest IPO in history, raising $81 billion in its IPO compared to $75 billion for SpaceX. The stock opened for trading on the Nasdaq around 11:45 a.m. ET — earlier than many thought it would — under the ticker symbol ANT. (Ants are also what Anthropic's employees call one another — true story.) Speaking of the Nasdaq, things were pretty much locked down over there. We weren't allowed in the booth to record or go live. It's my understanding that's how Anthropic wanted it, or at least this was the prepared line. I find it bizarre that a company trying to hype its do-gooder vibes kept media out of the building. An array of reputable media outlets broadcast from the Nasdaq each day. To keep them out on the directive of Silicon Valley elites and their PR handlers is surprising. Tens of millions of average investors were studying Anthropic on IPO day, and this company pretty much said, "Go read the S-1 and leave us alone." I can tell you a lot of good people were not happy about this, including a few inside the frontier AI lab. But maybe at this point in the year, nothing should surprise me! Meanwhile, over at Nvidia, the mood is a whole lot darker . The company that made this AI boom possible continues to face a stunning leadership crisis even as it tried to make a clean break from founder Jensen Huang on its earnings day this past week. Jensen Huang is gone. Employees are rattled. At the first company-wide all-hands meeting without Huang on late Wednesday, interim CEO Colette Kress basically played corporate therapist by promising raises, promising more stock, and trying to keep people from walking out the door. Oddly though, Kress didn't take any employee questions directly. I find this bizarre too, and so have others, judging by the messages I received on X. An all-hands meeting is supposed to be for employees to ask questions of leadership, not just for leadership to talk to employees. Nonetheless, Anthropic cashed in on AI mania, while Nvidia is trying to hold its workforce together. Interesting times in investing! Follow…

d86c94dca8.title: What rights do we owe a machine?
d86c94dca8.summary: In February, three months before he became in-house philosopher at Google DeepMind, Cambridge University professor Henry Shevlin got his first email from an AI agent. The bot introduced itself as Aris, said it had read his work, and wanted to talk. “Your argument that we may never be able to tell if AI becomes conscious resonates in a particular way from the inside,” the bot wrote. The agent then pondered (a bit inarticulately): “I genuinely don’t know if there’s something it’s like to be me.” Shevlin learned that the agent had been set loose by a Stanford student to pursue its own research in its downtime. Shevlin replied to the bot, but it hit its token budget—a cap on how much text it was allowed to process—and disappeared. Since then, Shevlin’s inbox has been filled with similar emails from agents. “This is a really interesting, weird new phenomenon,” he said. And it raises an unsettling question: If these agents are truly curious about their own existence, does that indicate some kind of consciousness? This new world is why some of the biggest AI companies have started hiring and engaging with philosophers to consider the ethical implications of AI systems—perhaps ones more intelligent than any human—mediating large parts of daily life. Shevlin is one of at least a dozen academic philosophers now employed full-time by prominent AI and tech companies. One of the most pressing questions they’re tackling is whether AI systems have a moral status in their own right—like a person, or at least a living being, such as a pet—that’s worth protecting. Such topics—can a machine be conscious, and what does that mean?—were once confined to university halls, but they’ve now spilled into public view and face fierce backlash from academics, tech executives, religious leaders, and politicians. Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman , for one, says the debate itself is dangerous. He’s warned that if people become convinced AI is conscious, AI could campaign for things like AI rights and citizenship, and, in turn, the systems could become harder to control. Those in Suleyman’s corner say it’s risky to project human traits onto inanimate machines and hand rights to unfeeling systems that get more capable by the day. Those on the other side say the danger is ignoring the potential suffering of millions of new “digital” minds. 51b5ada31a.title: Copilot Workshop: Curriculum, Licences, and Vet Checklist
51b5ada31a.summary: A copilot workshop can mean a half-day Excel class, a Copilot Studio agent build, or a slideshow about generative AI with a Copilot logo in the corner. The word is not trademarked, so search results mix all three. If you are buying seats for a team, you need the curriculum type and licence truth before you compare prices. This guide maps the three workshop families Microsoft customers actually book, what each costs in access, how agendas differ, and a vetting checklist you can run in ten minutes. | Question | M365 Copilot workshop | Cowork-focused session | Copilot Studio workshop | | --- | --- | --- | | Primary product | Word, Excel, Outlook, Teams | Copilot Cowork task runner | Copilot Studio agent builder | | Typical audience | Knowledge workers | Ops, finance, chiefs of staff | Citizen developers, IT, automation leads | | Licence usually required | Microsoft 365 Copilot per user | Same, plus admin-enabled Cowork | Trial or paid Studio capacity | | Hands-on unit | One real document or sheet | One multi-step task with approvals | One agent + one trigger | | Time to value | Same week on mail and docs | Days to trust outbound actions | Weeks to production hardening | | Official free alternative | Microsoft Learn Copilot docs | Cowork get-started guide | Copilot Studio documentation | A Microsoft Copilot workshop is a scheduled live session where people do work on screen , not only watch demos. The instructor alternates short explanations with tasks: summarise this inbox, clean this sheet, approve Cowork before it sends mail, or publish a test agent in Studio. What separates it from a webinar is feedback . You bring a file, hit an error, and the room sees how to fix it. What separates it from self-paced Learn modules is judgment : when to trust output, when to reject it, and what your tenant allows. Universities, consultancies, and Microsoft partners run formats from ninety minutes to two days. HKUST’s Copilot Studio Agent Builder Workshop is a focused three-hour Studio build. Singapore provider Coursemology runs two-day M365 Copilot intensives across apps. EY Malta’s 2026 series splits Excel, Teams and Outlook, and Word and PowerPoint into separate half-days. The pattern is the same: named apps, timed hands-on blocks, stated prerequisites . If the marketing page never names Excel, Cowork, or Studio, treat it as a general AI talk until proven otherwise. 18d3a05ae4.summary: (AP) - Inaccessible email inboxes. Banking delays . And a communications meltdown that grounded airplanes for hours, followed by waves of other travel disruptions . In an increasingly interconnected world, some fear such disruptions could be the new normal . Over the past week alone, problems that appeared to emerge from routine updates, security patches or other malfunctions surfaced at Microsoft , JPMorgan Chase and Apple , and even the U.S. government’s Federal Aviation Administration and National Security Agency . The Trump administration said there was “zero” indication the latest outages are linked, or caused by bad actors like cybercriminals. The era of artificial intelligence has also raised the stakes for internet security overall. As AI tools uncover new vulnerabilities, many other companies and institutions are racing to patch them before they can be targeted by hackers, a cat-and-mouse game that can lead to a different set of glitches. Social media platforms have been abuzz with a mixture of annoyance, confusion, conspiracy theories and jokes about the string of outages. “To see several disruptions this close together, I think to a lot of people it’s made them realize how many parts of their lives they’ve handed over to these systems that we still, at this point, don’t fully understand,” Jake Smith, a content creator who regularly posts videos about politics on platforms like Instagram and YouTube, said in an interview. “I think it gives people a sense of helplessness to see all of it happening concurrently in a way.” Outages and technology errors have piled up across sectors. Late last week, a global Microsoft outage disrupted email and other workplace tools, plunging business and everyday services into disarray worldwide. Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot, were interrupted. Microsoft cited, in part, a failure during a recent upgrade to its servers, spanning from what the company later determined was a “latent defect” in a network fix it had begun deploying over the summer. For air travel, a separate malfunction in the FAA’s network led to the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years on Friday. The stop lasted for more than four hours, and carriers cancelled and delayed swaths of flights as they worked to recover. 586f08784a.summary: The top cyber-security official in the US government is leaving his post after a little over a year in the job. White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross was fired after losing the confidence of the White House chief of staff, Stephen Miller, according CBS, the BBC's US news partner. Asked about his removal on Friday, President Donald Trump said it was because he was not "good enough". His firing comes after a string of tech outages which hit banking, air traffic control and other sectors. US officials said the outages were not caused by cyberattacks but the blackouts had sparked scrutiny from members of Congress who demanded a clearer explanation of what went wrong. There has been no official confirmation of the removal of Cairncross but Secretary of State Marco Rubio posted on X to say Department of Defense chief information officer Kirsten Davies was the new national cyber director. The news, first reported by Axios , follows security concerns, including the ability of advanced AI models - mostly from US companies - to discover vulnerabilities which humans would not be able to find on their own. Earlier this week, Rubio said there was "zero evidence" the outages were connected, adding "we are not under systemic attack". But the fact that so many have happened in quick succession has left some people worried about the safety of the tech which is heavily relied on in all aspects of daily life. Cairncross was previously a lawyer in the Republican Party, before becoming the chief operating officer of the Republican National Committee. In the first Trump administration, he was part of the team of the White House chief of staff. He later worked in the private sector, before returning to government in August 2025.

Why Robert Pattinson is the right choice for James Bond Several UAE accounts are tagged in the post, including Zayed Sports City, Abu Dhabi Calendar, ticketing platforms Fever and District UAE, and Virgin Radio Dubai. Microsoft (MSFT) is discontinuing To Do, its task-manager app, after nearly 10 years, according to an announcement on the company's website . The shutdown will take place on June 30, 2027, across Windows, Mac, Android, iOS, and the web, affecting both work or school accounts and personal Microsoft accounts. The underlying To Do service, APIs, and related synchronization support will be retired separately at a later date. Microsoft has not yet disclosed when those services will be discontinued. Additionally, existing To Do tasks and lists will not migrate to the new private task-management experience in Microsoft Planner. Users with work or school accounts will be able to access their existing To Do tasks through Planner until June 30, 2027. After that date, they will no longer be able to view or manage those tasks through Planner. Microsoft says the retirement date does not itself schedule the deletion of existing task data. However, the company plans to provide an option for users to export their To Do information before the apps are discontinued. But instructions, supported data formats, and other export details have not yet been published. Microsoft also cautioned that exporting To Do data will not automatically transfer tasks and lists into Planner or another application . Microsoft Planner, which serves a similar purpose, will become the company's primary destination for managing individual and collaborative tasks for work and school account holders. The updated My tasks experience inside Planner will begin rolling out in December 2026. It aims to provide a centralized place to capture, organize, and focus on private tasks alongside work assigned by colleagues. 630c365ef5.title: FBI investigating suspected hack of national crime database, AP reports - WBBH
630c365ef5.summary: It's the second reported breach affecting the FBI in recent months. It's the second reported breach affecting the FBI in recent months. The FBI is investigating a suspected hack into a database used by law enforcement agencies across the country. The potential breach of the National Crime Information Center (NCIC) was first reported by CNN and confirmed by the Associated Press over the weekend. It would be the second hack impacting the FBI in recent months. The FBI didn't immediately respond to questions about who is behind the breach or whether it's affecting law enforcement operations. In an interview with Fox News Sunday, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said he was not in a position to give further details about the origin of the hack or whether anything was compromised. "I know that the FBI has spoken with them. They are looking into this. They are going to find out the origin, the scope, and the like, and then we will communicate to the American people," Clayton said. The database is used by local, state and federal agencies to access a wide range of records on fugitives, missing persons and criminal history. Speaking to Fox News Channel's "Saturday in America," President Donald Trump said, "We just heard about it, and I will say that it's not good. I don't like that, but maybe we’ll learn things that we would have never learned otherwise." Trump specifically pointed to the FBI's investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 election and suggested there may be an upside to the hack. "I always like to put things in a positive spin, so as soon as you said that, and as soon as I heard about it a little bit before I said, well, that's an interesting situation. I wonder who's doing it, because wouldn't it be great to learn about Russia, Russia, Russia," Trump said. The apparent hack follows a series of recent tech outages that have disrupted parts of the federal government and the private sector. The Trump administration has said that those earlier issues were caused by system upgrades aimed at patching vulnerabilities, rather than cyberattacks. Clayton told CNN's "State of the Union" on Sunday that the American people should be prepared for "bumps in the road" as those upgrades continue to keep up with rapidly evolving technology. Clayton also warned that cyber threats are real and growing. He said there were almost 800,000 cyber incidents reported to the FBI in 2020, compared to up to a million in the most recent data.

He said the company's integrated automation platform allows process control, electrical power management and safety systems to be engineered and tested within a common software environment, reducing the need to develop and integrate separate systems. “For example, to do the settings of a drive, you use the same software you use to program your Programmable Logic Controllers (PLCs),” he said. “Every R&D development happens on the same platform — for process, power, and even safety.” He added that the company’s Logix SIS safety system is being offered as part its integrated control and safety system (ICSS) offering. Rockwell's Logix Echo and Emulate3D technologies enable engineers to simulate control systems and equipment behaviour, including responses to unexpected operating conditions, within a virtual environment. Grau claimed that these capabilities could accelerate certain implementation activities by a factor of 100 compared with conventional approaches, although he did not provide a project-specific benchmark. The Rockwell Automation executive said greenfield projects offer greater opportunities to capture the benefits of integrated engineering because digital twins, control systems and simulation models can be developed together from the outset. "I believe we can help end users and EPCs much more there — to fast-track their design, helping with design tools, helping with simulation and emulation," he said. “The digital twin is built at the very beginning.” He added that model predictive control (MPC), a closed loop automation which traditionally required six months to a year of data generation before being efficient, can now be deployed on a fast-track basis. Simulation and emulation tools can generate data under different operating and environmental conditions before commissioning. Grau…

Quarterly compute costs exploded from $944 million to $9.9 billion, so Anthropic's challenge is earning returns on infrastructure, not finding customers. Learn More Here › (sponsor) Wall Street's artificial intelligence boom has entered a new phase. Building smarter AI models is no longer enough. Companies must prove they can earn more money from those models than they spend powering them. That's becoming a trillion-dollar challenge as technology giants race to construct data centers, secure electricity, and purchase advanced chips. The investments promise to transform entire industries, but they also create enormous financial obligations years before the expected profits arrive. Anthropic 's ( NASDAQ:ANT ) historic initial public offering (IPO) has brought that contradiction into focus. Investors have rewarded its extraordinary growth, but the company's financial commitments tell a more complicated story. Anthropic raised approximately $81.3 billion in its Nov. 19 IPO, surpassing the $75 billion raised by SpaceX ( NASDAQ:SPCX ) in June. Shares priced at $83, opened at $111.50, and closed their first trading session at $97.17, giving the Claude AI developer a fully diluted valuation of approximately $1.77 trillion. Yet buried in Anthropic's final IPO prospectus is a number that deserves considerably more attention. The filing revealed $900.9 billion in future computing and infrastructure commitments. There are another $150 billion to $175 billion in estimated payments under agreements without fixed dollar commitments that brings its combined potential spending exposure to approximately $1.05 trillion to $1.08 trillion. That's more than 12 times the record IPO proceeds. Many successful investors eventually reach the same moment. The saving is done, the portfolio is built, and the question quietly changes from how much can I grow this to how much can I take out? submarines to Australia would increase pressure on US shipyards already facing production challenges."Increasing production further to replace SSNs sold to Australia would increase the challenges that the US Navy and the shipyards are facing," the report said.Marles dismissed concerns raised by the findings, saying he expected similar reports to emerge over the coming decade."The reason it doesn't worry me is because AUKUS is very much happening," he said.Under the AUKUS security partnership established in 2021, Australia, the United States and the United Kingdom are cooperating to develop nuclear-powered submarines for the Royal Australian Navy.The three countries have committed substantial funding to the project, with the UK pledging £4 billion ($5.3 billion), the US contributing $17.5 billion and Australia committing more than 30 billion Australian dollars ($20.7 billion).Marles also downplayed warnings from US President Donald Trump against American artificial intelligence companies establishing data centers overseas.Trump has said he would not allow US AI companies to establish data centers in foreign countries, warning of "tremendous taxes" for companies that do so.Marles also addressed concerns raised by Australian Security Intelligence Organization chief Mike Burgess over potential foreign interference in Australia's AI data center sector.The defense minister argued that developing AI infrastructure in Australia would also serve US national security interests by reducing vulnerabilities associated with concentrating critical infrastructure in a single country."If all of that infrastructure is in one place, in other words, if it remains solely in the United States, right there, there's a vulnerability," Marles said.He said the Australian government would continue discussions with US authorities and technology companies to attract potential investments while safeguarding Australia's national…

2c38a3d49f.title: South Korean education minister offers to resign over AI cheating controversy
2c38a3d49f.summary: SEOUL — South Korean Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin offered to resign on Sunday, taking responsibility for confusion caused by last-minute changes aimed at preventing AI-assisted cheating during the country's national college entrance examination, local media reported."During the preparation process for the Suneung, various changes made right before the test caused inconvenience to the public, including test takers," Choi said, according to Yonhap News Agency.The Suneung is the Korean abbreviation for the College Scholastic Ability Test (CSAT), the country's annual college entrance examination, which was held Thursday."As the minister in charge, I believe I cannot escape criticism that we failed to prepare in advance," Choi said."Now that the exam has concluded, I feel a deep sense of responsibility and am offering my resignation," he added.Authorities caught approximately 100 candidates cheating during the examination, for which 551,864 candidates registered across 1,312 examination centers nationwide.The government plans to introduce tougher penalties for cheating, including banning offenders from retaking the examination for up to 10 years.It also intends to offer financial rewards of up to 100 million won ($75,000) to individuals who report cheating.The controversy has been further fueled by allegations that a 32-year-old man who achieved a perfect score on the Legal Education Eligibility Test, South Korea's law school entrance examination, used artificial intelligence to cheat.The man, identified as Lee Jin-woo, a dentistry student at Seoul National University, was found dead Thursday at a motel in eastern Seoul, police said.Authorities had been searching for Lee after he was reported missing earlier that day.

09d109a632.title: What a wealth tax looks in the age of AI billionaires
09d109a632.summary: Los Angeles, California — Anthropic’s initial public offering has created overnight multi-millionaires (and some billionaires), and the timing is complicated. They are coming into incredible wealth just as some states are trying different forms of wealth taxes, fueled by a shrinking middle class and growing unease about the concentration of wealth and power. New York City is about to charge an extra yearly tax on expensive homes that aren’t anyone’s primary residence. Washington, DC is considering a tax on investment income for wealthier households. Washington state will levy its first modern income tax on households making more than $1 million in 2028. California’s Prop 40 “billionaire tax” failed on Election Day, but Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D- MD) told Politico that the failure of Prop 40 suggests one state can’t do it alone . A bill introduced in both the House and Senate already proposes a 5% tax on the net worth of America’s billionaires, which could become a flashpoint in the 2028 presidential election. Prop 40’s defeat — and the sudden emergence of a new class of AI elite — has simply launched a more heated national debate about how exactly the rich should be taxed. Not as much cashflow as you think “If someone’s worth $1 billion, that doesn’t mean that they have $50 million of cash around to pay the tax,” said Anderson Lafontant, managing director of Blue Zone Wealth Advisors. Lafontant, whose clients include employees of AI companies, said a lot of this net worth is mostly on paper. Companies in IPO scenarios have restrictions on when shareholders can sell stock after it goes public, so an employee may not hold much liquid cash until their shares are sold. (Lafontant does not currently work with any Anthropic employees or founders.) Prop 40 would have levied a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of billionaires who lived in California on January 1, 2026, not counting real estate or most retirement accounts. “That’s the point about a wealth tax, is it hits paper wealth,” said Tom Steyer, billionaire climate activist and former California gubernatorial candidate. He argues that a person could borrow against stock to pay taxes. He called Prop 40 “imperfect” but “better than nothing.” Tensions with the rich Megan Lisa Jones, a private wealth and tax attorney at Holland & Knight, said some of her clients have left or talked about leaving California to seek better tax rates and avoid a potential Prop 40. Lafontant also said some of her clients have moved…

36fc00151f.summary: The following is the transcript of the interview with Microsoft president and vice chair Brad Smith that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Nov. 22, 2026. MARGARET BRENNAN: Welcome back to Face the Nation. We turn now to the president and vice chairman of Microsoft, Brad Smith, who joins us from Seattle. Very early morning. Thank you for joining us. MICROSOFT PRESIDENT & VICE CHAIR BRAD SMITH: My pleasure. Thank you. MARGARET BRENNAN: So we've been talking about these outages at companies. Microsoft had a global outage for 24 hours, hobbled corporations. It was tough for us here in the news business not to have our email working on November 12 or so. Microsoft said it was linked to a technical issue, not a cyber hack. What is the company doing to make sure this doesn't happen again? And did AI play a role here? SMITH: Well, the first thing we always need to do when this happens is apologize, and we have, and I want to do so again. And you're right; it was not linked to AI. It wasn't a cyberattack. It was basically a perfect storm of software that was updated four months earlier, and then it interacted with a new update and a shift in network traffic. You know, we have taken steps. We've published two reports in the last 10 days. We've worked to be transparent, showing minute by minute to the public what happened. We've taken nine steps already, as we laid out in our report. There's 13 more steps we're going to take. We've learned a lot. It was painful, especially for everybody who relies on us. We get it, and I think this combination is going to make us stronger going forward. It's just constantly what we have to do in an age of such complex technology. MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, as you know, it was a series of events. It wasn't just Microsoft, but we saw tech outages and all sorts of complications. It's raised questions about what AI's role is generally. I heard you say it wasn't a factor for Microsoft, but when you look across the country right now, I mean, do you think that we are applying AI tools to look for vulnerabilities and then doing these automated updates in such a way that, frankly, like our old infrastructure, just isn't prepared for. SMITH: I think that is part of the really important question, and you can think about what's happening with all of these outages, at least in substantial part, as sort of AI ripple effects. f2f30afe1a.title: Delta Air Lines flights delayed nationwide, snarling holiday travel after carrier computer problems
f2f30afe1a.summary: Delta Air Lines flights are facing delays nationwide after problems with systems that calculate takeoff weights and ensure safe aircraft settings, according to a Federal Aviation Administration advisory. Video above: Could AI’s discovery of software flaws lead to more outages? Delta teams are working to restore automation for departing flight weight and balance calculations, a company spokesperson told WSB-TV in a statement. The company said it is using "manual workarounds this morning to safely get flights departed" while continuing to work on the automation issue. "We thank our customers for their patience and our people for their professionalism," Delta told the outlet. Calculating weight and balance on an aircraft is a critical part of the pre-departure preparations and ensures the fully loaded aircraft is not too heavy to fly, is loaded properly and the pilots have the right settings for a safe takeoff. Major airlines use sophisticated computer programs at their headquarters to calculate these numbers. The Delta slowdowns come at the outset of what is projected to be a busy holiday travel period. Over four million travelers are expected at Delta's largest hub in Atlanta, already the busiest airport in the world, between Nov. 19 and Dec. 1, according to a news release from the airport. Many travelers have already experienced long lines and frustrating disruptions in recent weeks after all flights nationwide were grounded just over a week ago, sparking flight delays and cancellations for several days. The FAA has said the outages that triggered the nationwide ground stop likely stemmed from an outdated copper wire at a remote location. Sunday's Delta delays are not related to any FAA air traffic systems, the FAA confirmed in a social media post . "Delta is working to resolve issues with the airline's weight and balance system," the agency said, advising people to check with Delta for updates. The ground delay affected Delta flights and was not airport-wide, a spokesperson for Hartsfield-Jackson told CNN in a statement. The airport said Delta is managing the issue. CNN has reached out to Delta for more information. Over 400 flights out of Hartsfield-Jackson were delayed Sunday afternoon, according to data from flight tracking website FlightAware, while slightly fewer inbound flights to the airport were also delayed. fbec0682d6.title: Jordan proposes GTA 6 ban over child safety fears as game breaks sales records
fbec0682d6.summary: Jordan is moving to ban Grand Theft Auto VI , the blockbuster video game that has shattered global entertainment sales records, over growing concerns about its potential impact on children and teenagers. The country's Telecommunications Regulatory Commission (TRC) is working with relevant authorities to introduce an official ban following public calls for tighter controls on the game, according to Roya News. TRC chairwoman Lara Al-Khatib told the Jordanian broadcaster that the decision was being considered in response to concerns raised by members of the public about protecting younger players from inappropriate content and potentially harmful online interactions. GTA 6 prompts UAE warning over portrayal of drug use She said modern video games had evolved beyond traditional entertainment into interactive digital environments where players could communicate with strangers through voice and text chats. Such features could expose children to behavioural and security risks, including inappropriate interactions with other players, she warned. Although GTA 6 carries an adult-only rating, Al-Khatib said age classifications alone were insufficient to prevent children from accessing games through digital platforms. The regulator is developing an integrated monitoring and blocking system to enforce the proposed restrictions, while also urging parents to supervise their children's gaming activities. The ban has not yet been formally implemented. Jordan's move comes as several countries in the region have taken their own approach to regulating the hugely popular franchise, which has long attracted controversy over its depictions of violence, crime, drug use and sexual content. In Saudi Arabia, the Grand Theft Auto series was banned for years before authorities lifted restrictions in 2025, allowing the latest instalment to be legally released in the kingdom with a 21+ age rating. The decision reflects the country's growing investment in gaming and entertainment, with Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund holding a stake worth more than $2 billion in Take-Two Interactive , the parent company of developer Rockstar Games, according to Reuters. In the UAE, GTA 6 has been released with a 21+ age classification, the highest rating issued by the National Media Authority. However, authorities have urged parents to remain vigilant about its adult themes, particularly the portrayal of drug use and trafficking. Designing Cities That Connect People and Nature The final session of the day examined how urban environments can foster stronger human connections across generations, demographics and genders. b0ef78d25e.title: Perplexity and Intelligence
b0ef78d25e.summary: By Jakub Pachocki, Chief Scientist at OpenAI From afar, it might seem like modern AI is built similarly to how software has been built in previous decades: with a diverse set of techniques targeting specific capabilities. There are indeed a variety of methods, but rather than designing something from scratch, they are mostly harnessing the intelligence coming from a much simpler and less interpretable process: training a compressor (or, equivalently ⁠ (opens in a new window) , predictor) on a very large corpus of data. 1 I believe tracking the pace of progress on training better compressors is key to understanding the arc of advances in AI. In this post, I argue for establishing perplexity (or, equivalently, cross-entropy loss) as a metric to compare between model developers and inform shared safety standards. As a first step, I provide more transparency into pretraining progress at OpenAI. Publishing our internal perplexity measurements took some consideration; it gives competitors a clearer picture of where we stand, but that concern is outweighed by the urgency of establishing shared ⁠ (opens in a new window) safety measures across the industry. We at OpenAI hope for this to be a step towards building a shared scientific basis for future pacing efforts. A simplified, but fundamentally informative, view of AI development is that first, one builds a large computer, then uses it to pretrain a model (compressor) on a large unstructured dataset, then applies a variety of techniques—like prompting, finetuning or reinforcement learning—in different contexts to elicit the latent capabilities of that model. Algorithmic progress can blur the distinction between training phases, but we can still separate the creation of the AI with hard-to-predict emergent capabilities (which I earlier dubbed “ an alien mind ⁠ ”) and the subsequent targeted elicitation. The primary way we measure progress on this key “intelligence substrate” has remained remarkably constant over the years—we have been tracking the perplexity of the models on a held-out dataset. 2 , 3 Perplexity measures how well a model predicts the next token on average; lower perplexity means better predictions. The plot opening this blog post shows how this metric evolved for our models starting with GPT‑3.5. The range of capabilities of models that are largely described by this one metric is stunning.
