5419d2d50f.title: OpenAI’s chief scientist sees major AI pretraining breakthroughs as soon as 2027
5419d2d50f.summary: Jakub Pachocki argues perplexity should be the shared yardstick for pretraining, and calls for limits on scaling until monitoring catches up Sun 22 Nov 2026 · 12:29 EST · 3 min read OpenAI ’s top researcher thinks the next big leap in AI training could arrive sooner than many expect. Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki said rapid progress in deep learning research could deliver major pretraining breakthroughs as early as 2027. Pachocki laid out his thinking in a post titled “ Perplexity and Intelligence,” published on November 22, 2026. The core argument: the AI industry should use perplexity as a common metric for judging pretraining across different labs. Technically, Pachocki framed the metric as cross-entropy loss per token. A token is a small chunk of text, often a word or part of one. Cross-entropy loss tracks how far a model’s guesses land from the actual answer, so lower numbers mean better predictions. His case for standardizing on it is straightforward. Labs currently tout their models using a patchwork of benchmarks, each with its own quirks. A shared pretraining metric would let outsiders compare apples to apples, rather than apples to a press release. The most eye-catching detail in the post is a specific figure. Pachocki pointed out that models reaching a log-perplexity of approximately 0.76 have previously been linked to significant breakthroughs in solving complex math problems. According to the research summary, this observation came from internal work at OpenAI. Researchers there noticed a relationship between perplexity thresholds and sudden gains in what models could actually do. Pachocki used that pattern to hint at what could come next. If similar thresholds exist for other capabilities, the deep learning field could see comparable advances as soon as 2027. He framed this as a possibility, not a guarantee. Daily. Free. 0592135739.summary: (AP) - Inaccessible email inboxes. Banking delays . And a communications meltdown that grounded airplanes for hours, followed by waves of other travel disruptions . In an increasingly interconnected world, some fear such disruptions could be the new normal . Over the past week alone, problems that appeared to emerge from routine updates, security patches or other malfunctions surfaced at Microsoft , JPMorgan Chase and Apple , and even the U.S. government’s Federal Aviation Administration and National Security Agency . The Trump administration said there was “zero” indication the latest outages are linked, or caused by bad actors like cybercriminals. The era of artificial intelligence has also raised the stakes for internet security overall. As AI tools uncover new vulnerabilities, many other companies and institutions are racing to patch them before they can be targeted by hackers, a cat-and-mouse game that can lead to a different set of glitches. Social media platforms have been abuzz with a mixture of annoyance, confusion, conspiracy theories and jokes about the string of outages. “To see several disruptions this close together, I think to a lot of people it’s made them realize how many parts of their lives they’ve handed over to these systems that we still, at this point, don’t fully understand,” Jake Smith, a content creator who regularly posts videos about politics on platforms like Instagram and YouTube, said in an interview. “I think it gives people a sense of helplessness to see all of it happening concurrently in a way.” Outages and technology errors have piled up across sectors. Late last week, a global Microsoft outage disrupted email and other workplace tools, plunging business and everyday services into disarray worldwide. Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot, were interrupted. Microsoft cited, in part, a failure during a recent upgrade to its servers, spanning from what the company later determined was a “latent defect” in a network fix it had begun deploying over the summer. For air travel, a separate malfunction in the FAA’s network led to the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years on Friday. The stop lasted for more than four hours, and carriers cancelled and delayed swaths of flights as they worked to recover. Just days later, United Airlines saw its own system outage — forcing it to delay departing flights on Monday. Online banking troubles also piled up on Monday. JPMorgan Chase said a software…

1f82ba88e7.title: 'Explosions around me': Endurance swimmer Lewis Pugh's risky journey through Strait of Hormuz
1f82ba88e7.summary: British endurance swimmer Lewis Pugh has completed a three-day swim through the Strait of Hormuz to draw attention to the environmental consequences of the Iran war. Pugh, 56, set out on November 15 from the Musandam peninsula on the southern tip of the Strait of Hormuz. He completed his swim by rounding the Cape of Hormuz, covering about 15 kilometres in total by November 18. "Just 30 minutes after I began swimming, an oil tanker was struck a few kilometres away," Pugh, who is a UN Patron of the Oceans, said in a post on social media platform X. "The explosions rocked the sea around me. Over the following days, I witnessed further attacks on commercial shipping and saw vessels engulfed in flames," he added. Wearing only swimming trunks, goggles and a cap bearing the UN logo, Pugh swam through the 'pungent smell of chemicals', making some stops on the way. "Stop the fighting. Open the Strait. Clean up the pollution," Pugh said in his message. Iran has in recent weeks claimed to have carried out a series of attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz and off the coast of Oman and the UAE, often blaming operators for hitting sea mines. More than 130 attacks on commercial vessels have been reported in the region since the conflict began on February 28.

2eab1cec44.title: Trials in Iraq under way for thousands of ISIS suspects transferred from Syria
2eab1cec44.summary: Iraq on Sunday opened the trials of thousands of ISIS suspects transferred from Syria, starting with six Syrians accused of joining the group and fighting against the former Assad regime and Kurdish forces. The six men stood before Karkh Criminal Court in Baghdad, the first defendants in a mass trial that will decide the fate of 5,704 suspects transferred this year by the US-led anti- ISIS coalition. The accused were tried in two separate but adjacent courtrooms. In one, Judge Haider Naji read out the charges against three of the men: membership of the terrorist organisation Islamic State in Iraq and the Levant. 'The authorities knew': Basra gas blast victims speak out “The final conclusions: the Directorate of Intelligence and Counter-Terrorism has established that the defendant belongs to terrorist gangs, participated in battles, threatened national security, and constitutes a threat to national and international security,” Judge Naji told each of the three men individually. The judge said the evidence was based on intelligence reports from various agencies, as well as testimony from victims of the group, Iraq residents, people in displacement camps and ISIS's own media publications. All three men had joined ISIS in 2016, the court heard. They were fighters who took part in raids and battles against the former Syrian regime and the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF). None of them had a lawyer. Each accepted representation by a court-appointed defence lawyer. Judge Naji then adjourned their trials until December 7, “in order to give you the opportunity to defend yourself, to absorb what has been read to you from security reports and to have a suitable period to prepare your defence”. Sunday's proceedings mark the start of the trial phase for suspects transferred from prisons in north-eastern Syria to Iraq in February, under a US military-supported operation, following the collapse of Kurdish-led control in the area. The men had been held for years in Syria without charge or access to a judicial system. Iraq agreed to receive them, investigate them from scratch and try them exclusively under Iraqi law, with no extradition to their home countries before proceedings are concluded. In September, the Supreme Judicial Council said investigations had been completed for 5,704 prisoners, including 3,497 Syrians and 474 Iraqis, and citizens of 67 countries in total – 16 Arab states, 19 EU countries and 32 others. b454d5e18c.title: Saudi Arabia's new 15% tax: Who will pay and who is exempt?
b454d5e18c.summary: Saudi Arabia's new 15 per cent minimum tax on large multinational companies, which comes into effect on January 1, will not apply to all businesses operating in the kingdom. The rules target groups that meet specific revenue thresholds. The domestic minimum top-up tax , announced by the Zakat, Tax and Customs Authority (Zatca), is intended to ensure profits generated by qualifying multinational groups in Saudi Arabia are subject to a minimum effective tax rate of 15 per cent. The measure forms part of international tax reforms led by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development and the G20, which seek to establish a global minimum tax on large multinational businesses . The tax will apply to entities in Saudi Arabia that belong to multinational groups with consolidated annual revenue of at least €750 million ($822.58 million) in at least two of the four preceding financial years. It factors in the revenue of the entire multinational group, rather than that generated by its Saudi operations alone. This means that a Saudi subsidiary or branch of a qualifying international group could fall within the scope of the rules even if its own revenue is considerably below €750 million. Purely domestic companies that do not have operations overseas or belong to a qualifying multinational group will not be covered, according to Zatca. The new tax is intended to ensure that qualifying multinational companies pay at least 15 per cent tax on their profits in Saudi Arabia. Companies already paying an effective tax rate of 15 per cent or more would generally not face an additional charge. For example, if a multinational group makes 100 million riyals ($26.6 million) in profit in Saudi Arabia and pays tax at an effective rate of 10 per cent, it could face an additional tax to bring the rate up to 15 per cent. However, the new tax will not necessarily apply to all of those profits, as the rules allow companies to exclude certain amounts linked to employee salaries and the value of physical assets, such as buildings and equipment. The final amount a company pays will therefore depend on its profits, the taxes it already pays and any exclusions or relief it qualifies for under the new rules. Saudi Arabia currently imposes a standard corporate income tax rate of 20 per cent on the taxable share of foreign investors in resident companies and on qualifying non-resident businesses. 9804de97d5.title: OpenAI calls for industry-wide AI brake tied to perplexity
9804de97d5.summary: OpenAI OPENAI is calling for frontier AI developers to adopt common limits on model development tied partly to perplexity, arguing that improvements in the metric can foreshadow the emergence of powerful and unpredictable new capabilities. In a post Sunday, OpenAI Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki proposed an industry standard that would establish measurable thresholds developers agree not to cross until corresponding advances are made in understanding and monitoring AI behavior AIQ ARTY THNQ BOTZ CHAT . Perplexity measures how well a model predicts the next token, with lower readings representing better performance. OpenAI generally tracks its logarithm, also known as cross-entropy loss, and Pachocki argued that the measure has remained unusually useful for tracking the underlying intelligence created during pretraining even as downstream AI benchmarks rapidly become obsolete. OpenAI said GPT-3.5 registered log-perplexity of about 0.99 on its main internal evaluation dataset, while GPT-4 reached about 0.91. As losses moved below 0.8, the company began seeing transformative capabilities in areas including cybersecurity and mathematics. A model at roughly 0.76 began producing what Pachocki described as groundbreaking mathematical results. Looking ahead, Pachocki said OpenAI expects further transformative capabilities as models move into roughly the 0.68-0.70 range, although the company does not know what those capabilities will be. That uncertainty underpins the proposed development limits. Pachocki said frontier labs should agree on shared evaluation and red-teaming standards and establish a first threshold they would not cross until monitoring technology reached a defined milestone, such as a successor to current chain-of-thought monitoring systems. The proposal comes as OpenAI sees AI beginning to contribute to its own development. Pachocki said an acceleration in pretraining research could emerge as soon as 2027 if AI systems begin generating fundamental algorithmic advances, potentially speeding progress faster than alignment and monitoring techniques can keep pace. OpenAI acknowledged that perplexity is an imperfect common standard. Results can be difficult to compare between laboratories because developers use different datasets and training mixtures, and perplexity does not capture all capability gains, including those produced by chain-of-thought reasoning. Still, Pachocki argued that greater transparency around the measure could provide the industry…

c30c5e3b0e.title: OpenAI Proposes Shared AI Development Limits Tied to Safety Milestones
c30c5e3b0e.summary: OpenAI Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki on November 22, 2026 released internal perplexity measurements and proposed shared limits on frontier AI development, warning that alignment and monitoring research may not keep pace if pretraining advances accelerate as soon as 2027. The disclosure concerns log-perplexity, the logarithm of perplexity, also called cross-entropy loss. Perplexity measures how well a model predicts the next token on average; lower values indicate better predictions. OpenAI’s figures use a fixed snapshot of held-out data from its internal codebase, the main evaluation dataset it has tracked since GPT-3.5. Pachocki reports that GPT-3.5 measured about 0.99 and supported fluent conversation, forming the basis for the original ChatGPT, while GPT-4 measured about 0.91 and could productively use chain-of-thought reasoning. New cybersecurity and mathematics capabilities emerged at losses below 0.8. At about 0.76, a model began producing notable results on open mathematics problems after OpenAI had spent more than a year posing such problems to its models. Pachocki expects further significant capabilities around the 0.68–0.70 log-perplexity window, extrapolating from recent progress, while acknowledging that he does not know what they will be and that current evaluations may not test for them. The proposal asks frontier developers not to cross limits based on perplexity and other measurements until researchers’ ability to understand and monitor AI behavior reaches a concrete milestone. One example is a successor to chain-of-thought monitors, which inspect a model’s written reasoning for signs of misalignment. Developers would also jointly establish evaluation norms, red-team safety cases before such models are first used, and shared transparency standards. The initial limit is intended to lead toward a common framework for successive limits. Pachocki says OpenAI disclosed the figures despite giving competitors a clearer picture of its position because he considers shared safety measures urgent. The acceleration scenario is conditional: Pachocki says a rapid series of fundamental pretraining advances could conceivably occur if AI begins contributing substantially to algorithmic research, while alignment and monitoring progress is unlikely to keep pace with the full potential acceleration. 7dae378395.summary: Anthropic's ( ANT ) IPO did little to stem the AI trade's meltdown this week, as the Nasdaq erased its year-to-date gains, leaving it roughly 18% off its October all-time high. The biggest winners of the artificial intelligence boom are down double-digit percentages for the week, and even more so over the past month, as seen on Yahoo Finance's AlphaSpace chart. Nvidia ( NVDA ) shares are down 42% over the past four weeks, as Jensen Huang's departure as CEO intensified pressure on an already shaky chip sector. Peer AMD ( AMD ) is down roughly 20%. Meanwhile, memory maker Micron ( MU ) has fallen more than 33% over the past month and is down 50% from its June all-time high. Concerns over tighter data center regulations, restrictions on chip exports to China, and broader financing worries have weighed across the sector. Although Anthropic's IPO wasn't the clearing event markets had hoped for, some strategists see the debut as a net positive for the AI trade. "We're finally getting details with respect to what's underneath the curtain" when it comes to the AI developers, Raymond James Investment Management chief market strategist Matt Orton said on Yahoo Finance's Market Hang. "Hopefully the market will kind of start to calm down and realize that there's a lot of really high-quality companies that are on fire sale right now," he added. Orton wouldn't compare the meltdown seen in the AI trade to the 2000 dot-com bubble, noting that startups are now staying private longer as they receive the financing they need and that some of the selling may be year-end positioning to protect gains. "The market is really healthy," Orton said. Nomura's Charlie McElligott points out that in recent sessions investors have been broadly selling rather than just rotating into defensive sectors. Instead of "buying the dip," money is moving out of equities and into cash and US Treasurys, where prices move inversely with yields. On Friday, the 10-year Treasury ( ^TNX ) yield sank by 14 basis points to 4.91%. McElligott will be watching this upcoming week, when computer-driven, volatility-targeted funds could step in and buy, testing whether the recent sell-off is just a dip or a sign that investors are heading for the exits. Called MAI Code 2 and MAI Code 2 Flash, the models are designed for everything from complex software development to everyday coding tasks. Microsoft claims the model delivers 98% of GPT-6.1 Sol 's performance at just 40% of its cost, averaged across four coding benchmarks. The company also added that developers preferred MAI Code 2's frontend designs over those generated by GPT-6 Sol in 64% of blind comparisons, covering interfaces, visualizations, and other graphical projects. Meanwhile, MAI Code 2 Flash prioritizes speed and efficiency. It's built for everyday tasks such as explaining code, fixing minor bugs, and making targeted edits. Microsoft states that it delivers comparable performance to GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 at 65% and 20% of their respective costs. It is worth noting, though, that these comparisons come from Microsoft's evaluations of specific coding tasks and use promotional pricing for its models. The company also acknowledges that the models aren't yet optimized for particularly complex scientific research or extremely long-running agentic tasks. 3e22e70eba.title: Microsoft President Warns of More Tech Outages in Coming Months
3e22e70eba.summary: The risk of widespread technology outages could remain elevated in the coming months as organizations race to patch software vulnerabilities and upgrade aging infrastructure, Microsoft President and Vice Chair Brad Smith warned Sunday. "I think we have to be prepared, frankly, for the coming months because this isn't the type of thing that just gets done in a couple of weeks," Smith said on CBS News' Face the Nation . "The whole information infrastructure of the world is in effect being upgraded right now." The warning follows a turbulent stretch of unrelated technical failures that disrupted major banks, airlines, air traffic control and Microsoft's own global cloud services. While officials have ruled out coordinated cyberattacks, the back-to-back disruptions underscored how heavily businesses, government agencies and travelers rely on interconnected digital systems. Smith said artificial intelligence has accelerated the discovery of weaknesses in computer code. While that helps defenders fix flaws, malicious actors can use the same tools to target systems — forcing organizations to deploy updates at a breakneck pace that leaves less time for testing. "What AI did earlier this year was basically make it much easier for people to find vulnerabilities in code, and then you can either use that knowledge to patch the code, or if you're a bad actor, you can use that knowledge to try to hack into systems," he said. Because organizations are patching vulnerabilities "at a pace we have never seen before," the rush itself creates instability, particularly on legacy systems, Smith said. "Especially when you have older infrastructure, especially when you're trying to patch at such a pace, especially when you have to go so fast that you can't take as much time to test what you're changing in the code, you do increase the risk of something going wrong," he added. Smith urged consumers to install security updates promptly and called on companies to modernize older infrastructure and improve coordination with the government. "If you get an update on your phone or your laptop with a patch, apply it because I think that's going to keep your technology far safer," he said. 74b3c446b8.summary: Climate talks in Turkey collapsed without a deal as the countries of the world failed to unite on reducing fossil fuel use or putting up money for a greener planet. The Cop31 summit ran two days beyond its original deadline as negotiators made a last-ditch push for a deal. But the final text unveiled on Sunday afternoon proved too feeble for a host of nations, including European countries and the Pacific islands threatened by climate change. What delegates said after Cop31 ended with no deal The result is the first UN climate summit to end without a headline deal since an infamous occasion in Copenhagen in 2009. UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres said he was "deeply disappointed". "Temperatures keep shattering records," he said. "Climate extremes keep intensifying. Emissions remain far too high. And every delay makes our task harder and more costly." The mood was bitter as delegates made clear their objections. Cop31 President Murat Kurum was accused of disrespect by African negotiators and at one point shooed away UN climate chief Simon Stiell as Stiell tried to take the floor. Mr Kurum said some countries had "got hung up on a single word or phrase" and raised irrelevant issues. "There is nothing more to be done. We did everything in our power. The decision belongs to 196 countries. Therefore, we will respect their decision," he said. Disappointed negotiators said the deal lacked ambition at a time when many fear an “overshoot” – temperatures rising by more than the 1.5°C limit that has been the key global target for a decade. The draft text did not mention fossil fuel use or offer any specifics about money. Tuvalu, a small Pacific island nation, said the two weeks of meetings at Cop31 had been “challenging due to the lack of engagement and transparency” in trying to reach a decision. “Listening to parties who diminish the credibility of signs of climate change is disappointing,” said Maina Vakafua Talia, Tuvalu’s Minister for Home Affairs, Climate Change and Environment. Egyptian negotiator Wael Aboulmagd was one of many to say his country could not accept the text. “We will carry the lessons of this session forward and, as always, will work constructively … to rebuild momentum and deliver what the most vulnerable are owed,” he said. It is normal for Cop summits to extend into overtime and Mr Kurum had said earlier on Sunday he was still hopeful, with “minor requests” to change the text. 716c53fa8f.title: OpenAI’s chief scientist has thoughts on how to limit AI development
716c53fa8f.summary: A new blog post from OpenAI’s chief scientist Jakub Pachocki discusses potential limits on AI development, with a focus on a measurement called perplexity. Slowing AI development became a particularly hot topic after a former OpenAI and Anthropic researcher said the companies were “gambling with our lives,” and even Anthropic’s IPO filing suggested that the technology could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to society.” Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei then published a plan to “pace the frontier,” seemingly endorsed by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk. Among other things, Amodei called for companies to agree to “common safety standards as well as limits on the rate of unchecked AI progress.” But to establish a speed limit on AI development, you need to agree on how you measure speed. Pachocki’s post — described by Altman as “the most important thing OpenAI has published in a while” — suggests perplexity (not to be confused with the company of the same name ) could be that measurement. In Pachochki’s argument, benchmarks that focus on AI’s “downstream capabilities” have quickly become outdated as the technology advances. But perplexity — which “measures how well a model predicts the next token on average; lower perplexity means better predictions” — has remained “informative.” Pachochki’s post includes a chart of how the perplexity of OpenAI’s models has fallen since GPT 3.5. “GPT‑4, at ~0.91, was proficient at utilizing chain-of-thought reasoning productively, which motivated the subsequent targeted elicitation of this capability and the creation of modern reasoning models,” he wrote. “Now, as we have reached losses below 0.8, we have seen the emergence of transformative capabilities in fields like cybersecurity and mathematics.” So in his view, perplexity could provide the basis for “a shared benchmark for general intelligence,” which AI companies could then use to establish “common limits.” With perplexity serving as a standard measurement for AI progress, the companies would commit not to go past a certain threshold “until our ability to understand and monitor AI behavior achieves a certain concrete milestone.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . e72749412f.summary: Neuroscientist Anil Seth argues that conscious AI is more mythology than engineering roadmap — and that treating chatbots as minds distorts ethics, product design, and our understanding of human experience. His essay "The Mythology Of Conscious AI" won the 2025 Berggruen Prize and resurfaced on Hacker News in November 2026 as frontier labs keep shipping more fluent models. This post distills Seth's argument for builders , links it to Henry Shevlin's DeepMind interview , and records what developers said in the HN thread. Seth published on Noema with a January 2026 timestamp on the page. The ideas are not tied to one model release, but November 2026 readers encounter them beside: Seth's core warning: if we grant consciousness to systems that persuade , we change law, marketing, and mental health obligations — even when science has not demonstrated inner experience. Brain outline with a pulse line, illustrating Seth''s split between doing and being Seth defines intelligence roughly as achieving complex goals by flexible means . Consciousness , following Thomas Nagel, concerns what it is like to be a subject. LLMs score on benchmarks and chat . That satisfies many intelligence tests without settling phenomenology . Seth lists three biases that push us to merge the two: Language models hit bias (3) hardest. Seth notes few claim AlphaFold is conscious despite similar underlying stacks — chat is the difference. Seth criticizes calling false outputs "hallucinations," which are conscious-perception terms in humans. He prefers confabulation — making things up without knowing — which describes behavior not felt experience . Product teams should hear that as a copy audit task: Aligns with Hungry Butler sycophancy research : commercial incentives plus human-like tone change user behavior even without consciousness. Heart shape with circuit lines, illustrating moral stakes when products sound conscious Seth's deepest technical challenge targets the assumption that the right computation on silicon could guarantee consciousness. He outlines four arguments (summarized from Noema): He does not claim mathematics forbids all future conscious machines. He argues today's dominant stack and today's hype cycle are poor guides . Seth stresses stakes beyond automation : That pairs with Shevlin's FT message: building deliberate conscious AI without public care plans is reckless . Seth supplies why the premise may be wrong ; Shevlin supplies governance if the premise is pursued…

d198a9d536.title: America’s Outages Expose A Crisis Of Trust – OpEd
d198a9d536.summary: At a camping and survival store in Los Angeles, customers bought emergency kits and water while talking about Microsoft and grounded flights. It is a long way from being unable to open an email to wondering whether there will be water in the tap tomorrow. This month, some Americans covered that distance in a matter of days. It felt like the opening of the film “Leave the World Behind.” The lights are still on and the kitchen is stocked but, without a reliable link to the outside world, the people in the house have no idea how far the trouble has spread. As false warnings of a nationwide blackout circulated on social media, some Americans started asking the kind of questions a survival video game puts to its players. How much food do you have? How long will your batteries last? Should you fill the bathtub while the water still runs? The first major disruption came on Nov. 12, when a Microsoft outage affected Outlook and other services. The next day, a technical failure prompted the Federal Aviation Administration to halt departures nationwide. On Nov. 16, some bank customers struggled to access their accounts and a separate failure delayed United Airlines flights. The day after, a software patch disrupted the National Security Agency’s classified internal communications network. The agency staggered employee arrivals and restricted campus access to essential personnel that evening. The NSA said its critical operations continued. A scheduled federal emergency alert test went ahead that week. The blackout predicted online never came. At a congressional hearing on Nov. 18, officials including FBI Deputy Director Christopher Raia said they had found no evidence that the outages were connected or caused by a coordinated cyberattack. Lawmakers separately asked about reports of possible Iranian-linked plots in the US. Then news broke that White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross had been fired. For Americans already skeptical of Washington, the timing made it easy to wonder whether officials knew more than they were saying. On Saturday, reports indicated that the FBI was investigating an apparent breach of the National Crime Information Center, a database law enforcement agencies use to share records on fugitives, missing people and stolen property. The scope of the suspected breach was unclear and there was no immediate indication it was linked to the earlier outages. By then, the earlier disruptions had already raised a question. How did a few days…

5d6177b7de.title: Birbal AI offers 14-day pilots of Mustashar, a private AI assistant that runs on an organisation's own servers
5d6177b7de.summary: Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates: Birbal AI, an Emirati national AI company based in Abu Dhabi, is offering government entities and companies a 14-day pilot of Mustashar (مستشار, "adviser"), a private AI assistant that runs on an organisation's own servers, on a fully air-gapped network or in a UAE data centre. Mustashar answers staff from the organisation's own documents, policies and systems in Arabic and English, and the documents and conversations are never used to train public models. Staff in many organisations already paste contracts and customer data into public AI chatbots, outside their organisation's policies. Mustashar gives each team a ChatGPT-style assistant that stays inside the organisation's own environment instead. Every answer shows the document and page it came from, so people can check it before they act on it. Staff only get answers from documents they are allowed to open, and the assistant works with the organisation's identity provider and user groups for single sign-on. IT and compliance teams see usage, connected sources, where the model runs and where the data is stored, with a log of every question, answer and source, and controls for how long conversations are kept. Mustashar connects to file stores such as SharePoint and Google Drive, and to systems such as SAP, Oracle and CRMs through connectors that Birbal AI builds. Its agents draft letters, summarise cases, fill forms and update systems, with approval steps. Search, chat and summaries work in Arabic and English, including documents that mix the two languages. Organisations can run open models on their own servers or cloud models they approve, and change models later without rebuilding. For the most sensitive work, Mustashar can run fully air-gapped, on servers inside an isolated network with no connection to the internet. The 14-day pilot starts with one department and its key documents, on infrastructure the organisation chooses. Birbal AI connects the file stores and systems with the organisation's access rules, staff ask real questions for 14 days, and the organisation receives a report on answer quality and time saved, with clear pricing before any rollout. After the pilot, Mustashar is licensed by number of users, either as an annual licence on the organisation's own servers or as a subscription hosted in a UAE data centre. 12f3753176.summary: By William Collins, consultant in stock markets – Eurasia Business News, November 22, 2026. Article no 3280 The question dominating Wall Street is no longer whether artificial intelligence will transform the economy. It is whether investors paid too much, too soon, for the profits that transformation might deliver. Friday’s technology selloff sharpened that distinction: the Nasdaq Composite plunged 5.28%, wiping out its 2026 gains, while the S&P 500 dropped 3.7%. Nvidia fell approximately 14%, and newly listed Anthropic surrendered most of its initial public offering gains. The declines intensified fears that the AI investment boom is unwinding. But falling share prices do not establish that the technology has failed. They demonstrate that investors are demanding a different price for its promise. Friday, November 20, turned a technology correction into a broader confidence shock. Axios reported the Nasdaq down 17.9% and the S&P 500 down 11.6% in its performance comparison. Bloomberg separately reported that the S&P 500 had fallen more than 10% from its October record, putting it in correction territory. The Nasdaq-100, which is distinct from the broader Nasdaq Composite, fell 5.6% Friday and approached a bear market after losing nearly 20% from its recent high. These distinctions matter. Different indexes track different groups of companies, and figures measured at different times should not be treated as interchangeable. The consistent message, however, was unmistakable: investors were rapidly retreating from the trade that had powered much of the market’s earlier advance. Nvidia’s 14% decline marked its worst session in almost two years. The chipmaker lost 22.9% over the week, its weakest weekly performance since October 2008. The longer decline was even more striking. Nvidia had fallen 47.5% from its October 6 peak, erasing approximately $2.7 trillion in market capitalisation. That loss represents a reduction in the market value of outstanding shares, not an equivalent amount of cash leaving Nvidia’s accounts. Investors also faced overlapping concerns. Axios described declining confidence in AI, tightening credit and a scandal involving Nvidia’s leadership as pressures on the stock. Nvidia’s performance therefore cannot be read as a pure verdict on semiconductor demand: company-specific uncertainty was interacting with broader market anxiety. 04504f1c47.summary: When Notable Capital poured roughly 10% of the U.S. portion of its $1 billion-plus fund into Anthropic’s Series E, many limited partners were perplexed by the massive bet. Claude’s maker was still trailing its biggest rival, OpenAI, and DeepSeek had released its R1 model just weeks earlier, threatening to overtake closed-source competitors. Moreover, at $61.5 billion, Anthropic’s valuation was by far the highest that the predominantly early-stage venture firm had invested at in its 25-year history. But investors at Notable, formerly known as GGV Capital before its 2024 split from its China operations, were confident in Anthropic’s future. A team that included managing partners Hans Tung and Glenn Solomon and principal Dan Cahana crunched the numbers and found that developers were increasingly favoring Claude over ChatGPT, using Claude 70% of the time, a reversal from the previous year. “We just knew that for AI, the developer is at the center because they’re the early adopters,” Tung, a co-founder of the firm, told TechCrunch. Having navigated the complexities of U.S.-China relations firsthand, Notable was also convinced that “mission-critical” work would always require U.S.-based, closed-source models, Tung said. Less than two years later, Notable’s LPs are no longer questioning the outsized investment. On Wednesday, Anthropic raised $81.3 billion in the largest IPO in history, reaching a fully diluted valuation of about $1.5 trillion before its shares began trading the next day, a paper return of roughly 15 times. Notable is, of course, not the only firm sitting on a massive paper windfall from Anthropic. Even traditional late-stage investors, who rarely see venture-scale multiples, are set for a big win. Singaporean sovereign wealth fund GIC had been researching Anthropic throughout 2024, but it didn’t make its first investment until after Chris Emanuel, head of the fund’s tech investments, met with Anthropic CFO Krishna Rao at Che Fico, an Italian restaurant in San Francisco, in early 2025. 76701fb2ae.title: OpenAI top scientist sounds alarm over AI, calls for global limits on powerful models
76701fb2ae.summary: AI developers should adopt common limits on increasingly powerful models and use "perplexity" as a common metric for measuring AI progress across the industry, OpenAI's chief scientist has said. The proposal, detailed by OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki, was unveiled amid growing concern inside and outside the industry about the potential risks of AI's rapidly growing capabilities. "I further propose common limits, based on perplexity and other measurements, that developers are committed to not crossing until our ability to understand and monitor AI behaviour achieves a certain concrete milestone," Pachocki wrote. Pachocki described perplexity as a model intelligence metric that measures how well a model predicts the next token — the basic unit of data — on average, and wrote that lower perplexity means better predictions. Pachocki said AI could help drive fundamental advances in AI training methods as soon as 2027, potentially accelerating progress faster than advances in monitoring and safety. Developers should commit to not cross agreed capability thresholds until new monitoring and safety mechanisms are in place, Pachocki added, in a proposal backed by CEO Sam Altman. Pachocki advocated an industry standard that sets a first limit on development and defines which milestones must be met before that limit is exceeded. Altman backed the proposal, saying in a post on X that the industry should seek agreement on common limits for AI development. Altman described Pachocki's essay as "the most important thing OpenAI has published in a while," and said such limits would help ensure safety and control.

c51f57c082.summary: A bruising sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks on Friday knocked the S&P 500 down 3.7%, dragging the index to its worst weekly loss in more than 18 months, and knocked the Nasdaq composite into the red for the year. The benchmark index is now in what professional investors call a “correction,” having fallen more than 10% from its Oct. 6 all-time high. The last time the S&P 500 had a correction was March 2025, as the Trump administration’s trade war rattled the market. Its weekly loss, marking its worst such decline since April 2025, as the trade war escalated, capped a seven-day losing streak, the longest such string of losses since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. The Nasdaq composite, which is more greatly influenced by tech stocks, slumped 5.3%, pulling it into negative territory for the year. Its weekly loss was also just shy of its worst week since March 2020, when the pandemic ground the global economy to a halt. The Dow Jones Industrial Average, with less exposure to technology stocks, fell 1.9%. RELATED STORY | Anthropic begins trading as a $1.5 trillion company in the biggest IPO on record The technology sell-off spread around the globe: Japan’s Nikkei and South Korea’s Kospi each fell more than 5% overnight. European indexes fell sharply as well. AI stocks have hefty market values and have a much bigger impact on the market’s direction. They were responsible for Wall Street’s big gains this year and are now behind the big slide for the market. AI stocks have been losing ground partly over worries that their big market values and heavy spending are unjustified. Fears of a bubble within the sector have also been exacerbated by the results of the recent midterm elections, with candidates advocating for a slowdown in data center construction winning at both the federal and state level. “The whole notion that AI can continue to spend unlimited amounts of money and support the stock market, I think the notion of that is ending as we speak, that’s what’s being priced right now,” said Michael Antonelli, market strategist at Baird. "But I don’t think that means that the overall bull market that started in October 2022 is over.” Chip stocks, big beneficiaries of the build out of AI data centers, led the way lower. Advanced Micro Devices dropped 12.6% and Broadcom fell 12.1%. The PHLX Semiconductor Index sank 9.2%. 45e1bf6a01.title: AI 'kill switch' no solution to growing cybersecurity risks: Former OpenAI board member
45e1bf6a01.summary: A former OpenAI board member cautioned Sunday that an emergency shutdown mechanism for artificial intelligence would provide limited protection against rising cybersecurity risks, as US lawmakers seek to introduce federal regulations for the rapidly developing technology. Helen Toner, executive director of Georgetown University's Center for Security and Emerging Technology, told Fox News on Sunday that a single "kill switch" would not be sufficient to address the challenges posed by AI. "There's not gonna be a single kill switch that can fix all our problems, unfortunately," Toner warned Toner said emergency shutdown systems could mitigate certain risks but emphasized that autonomous AI systems and those operating outside US jurisdiction would be harder to regulate. She also questioned whether technology companies were fully disclosing the causes of recent widespread outages, suggesting that some disruptions could stem from urgent efforts to address security flaws before cybercriminals exploit them. Addressing reported discussions between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping on AI safety, Toner said Washington and Beijing share an interest in avoiding potentially disastrous incidents involving the technology, despite their mutual distrust. news_share_description subscription_contact

cc8aa072ff.title: OpenAI’s chief scientist calls for industry-wide limits on AI models
cc8aa072ff.summary: OpenAI’s chief scientist Jakub Pachocki has asked rival AI labs to agree on limits they won’t cross with their most powerful models. He made the case in an essay published on Sunday, and CEO Sam Altman was quick to back him. The idea is built around perplexity, a score for how well a model guesses the next piece of text. The better the guesses, the lower the score, and Pachocki wants every lab to use the same number to show how far along its models are. We decided to provide more transparency into pretraining progress at OpenAI for the sake of moving toward shared safety bars. In “Perplexity and Intelligence” I argue for common limits based on perplexity and other measurements, with progress beyond them gated on our ability to understand AI behavior. — Jakub Pachocki (@merettm) November 22, 2026 From there, he calls for “common limits, based on perplexity and other measurements” that developers would promise not to cross. The promise would stand until labs truly understand what their models are doing and have better tools to watch them, such as a successor to today’s chain-of-thought monitors. Labs would also agree on common ways to test models and to check each other’s safety claims. Jakub Pachocki doesn’t say where the first limit should sit or when it should kick in. But he does show OpenAI’s hand a little, as the company has published the perplexity scores of its own models for the first time. The numbers fall from about 0.99 for GPT-3.5 to under 0.8 for its newest models. Each drop bought new skills: first fluent conversation, later expert-level cybersecurity, and most recently results on open maths problems. Announcing the essay, titled “Perplexity and Intelligence,” Pachocki said OpenAI is sharing the data “for the sake of moving toward shared safety bars.” All of this comes at a nervous moment for the industry, with worry about the pace of AI progress spreading well beyond the labs. Sam Altman, for his part, wrote on X that shared limits would help keep AI safe and under control. He also called Pachocki’s essay “the most important thing OpenAI has published in a while.” But Sam Altman has sounded this note before. At Salesforce’s Dreamforce conference, he said no company should let its safety depend on what its rivals do, and so has Pachocki. In a September essay , he warned that no one is ready for machines that keep getting smarter this fast. Lawmakers are moving as well, with U.S. Senator Bernie Sanders tabling a bill to ban superintelligence…

Levent Alpöge, a member of the company's technical staff, made the announcement Friday by way of a four-page explanation posted on his website. He said that he believes by working with Claude, he has found a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis. "Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line," Alpöge wrote. "No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line." Formulated in 1859, the Riemann Hypothesis centers on the distribution of prime numbers — those that are only divisible by one and themselves — as they grow towards infinity. Alpöge said his discovery came late Sunday night. He messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei to ask about "my ability to announce," as the San Francisco-based company was about to make major news with its stock market debut. A day after the company's initial public offering — the most valuable in history — Alpöge revealed he'd solved the problem that has proved elusive for more than 150 years. Anthropic did not respond to an email from The Associated Press requesting comment on Alpöge's claim. Alpöge released his and Claude's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis within 17 million lines of Lean code, a programing language that allows people to program proofs of mathematical theorems. Traditionally the findings buried in that code would be published in a formal paper, said Alex Kontorovich, distinguished professor and department chair of mathematics at Rutgers University. "Usually when somebody gives you a paper, that's also kind of code for a proof and you have to actually read the paper, follow it yourself, figure out if you believe every single line in that paper. d633a2eaea.title: Microsoft is making Copilot more useful by helping you manage files and PC problems
d633a2eaea.summary: While Copilot may not be everyone's first choice of AI platform, Microsoft is leaving no stones unturned to make it better. Announced at Microsoft Ignite 2026, their annual developer conference, the Hybrid Intelligence Initiative will bring the best of both worlds together: on-device AI models making use of your device's NPU and the raw power of cloud processing via data centers. The prospect of having an AI agent taking over your whole system can seem daunting at first, but Microsoft has made sure to keep it in check by introducing containment, identity and manageability in Windows . These will make sure that the agent is limited to what it can access on the system while distinguishing an agent's activity from a real human's. On top of that, govern access given to agents and monitor what they're up to. This will allow users to give commands in natural language instead of manually locating and editing files on the PC. Troubleshooting is just about to get easier with Copilot, all thanks to local PC diagnostics by allowing the agent to identify the issues. Copilot will be able to scan the PC and help the user understand the issues it discovers. While Microsoft hasn't confirmed whether Copilot will gain the ability to fix the discovered issues on its own, for now it is purely for identifying the issues. Privacy and control remain front and center. Copilot operates locally in a read-only mode to scan system data, and it will always prompt you for explicit permission before accessing your files or personal data. Once granted, it doesn't just point out errors, but also breaks down the root cause and provides step-by-step guidance on how to fix them. Microsoft has slowly, but surely, realized that trying to force AI into every single corner of the operating system can backfir e. Hence, they've started to scale back and remove superficial Copilot integrations from specific Windows utilities where user adoption was low or where it felt intrusive, such as Snipping Tool, Photos, Widgets, and Notepad. It's refreshing to see them make an effort to set things right and bring features that might be useful and not just to hit the "AI checkbox". Microsoft has a new Copilot app (again), and this one wants to do everything for you Microsoft wants you to know Copilot AI is not just for entertainment Microsoft wants Copilot to be your new workspace, with Word, Excel, and Powerpoint built in

af10e891c5.title: OpenAI'ın baş bilim insanından yapay zeka gelişimine sınır getirilmesi çağrısı
af10e891c5.summary: OpenAI'ın baş bilim insanı Jakub Pachocki , yapay zeka modellerinin giderek artan yeteneklerinin beraberinde getirdiği riskleri kontrol altına almak için teknoloji şirketlerinin ortak gelişim sınırları belirlemesini önerdi. Pachocki, 22 Kasım'da yayımladığı blog yazısında , yapay zeka geliştiricilerinin modellerin davranışlarını daha iyi anlayıp denetleyebilecekleri güvenlik mekanizmaları oluşturulana kadar belirli sınırları aşmamaları gerektiğini savundu. Pachocki'nin önerisi, yapay zekanın gelişimini tamamen durdurmayı değil, teknolojik ilerlemeyi güvenlik çalışmalarının hızına göre düzenlemeyi amaçlıyor. OpenAI CEO'su Sam Altman da Pachocki'nin gönderisinin OpenAI'ın bir süredir yayınladığı en önemli şeylerden biri olduğunu ifade ederek yazılan öneriye destek verdi . Yapay zekanın gelişimi nasıl ölçülecek? Pachocki'nin önerisinin merkezinde, yapay zeka modellerinin performansını ölçmek için kullanılan perplexity adlı ölçüt yer alıyor. Bu ölçüt, bir modelin metindeki bir sonraki kelimeyi veya veri parçasını ne kadar doğru tahmin edebildiğini gösteriyor. Daha düşük perplexity değeri, modelin tahmin yeteneğinin daha iyi olduğu anlamına geliyor. Pachocki'ye göre yapay zeka modellerinin belirli görevlerdeki başarısını ölçen testler, teknolojinin hızlı gelişimi nedeniyle zamanla geçerliliğini kaybedebiliyor. Perplexity ise modellerin temel eğitim sürecindeki ilerlemeyi takip etmek için daha tutarlı bir ölçüm sunabiliyor. OpenAI, bu yaklaşımı desteklemek amacıyla modellerinin eğitim süreçlerine ilişkin daha önce kamuoyuyla paylaşmadığı bazı verileri de yayımladı. Şirketin kendi değerlendirme verilerine göre GPT-3.5'in log-perplexity değeri yaklaşık 0,99 , GPT-4' ün ise 0,91 seviyesindeydi . Değerin 0,8'in altına düşmesiyle birlikte matematik ve siber güvenlik gibi alanlarda önemli yeni yetenekler ortaya çıktı. Pachocki, log-perplexity değerinin 0,68 ile 0,70 aralığına gerilemesiyle yeni ve önemli yeteneklerin ortaya çıkabileceğini öngörüyor. Ancak bu değerlerin henüz şirketler için belirlenmiş resmi gelişim sınırları olmadığını belirtelim. Yapay zeka gelişimi 2027'de daha da hızlanabilir Pachocki'nin dikkat çektiği bir diğer konu da yapay zekanın kendi gelişim sürecine katkıda bulunması oldu. Yapay zeka sistemlerinin yeni modellerin eğitim yöntemlerini geliştirmek için kullanılması, teknolojik ilerlemeyi önemli ölçüde hızlandırabilir. f8b881f88a.title: When Microsoft, Apple, and the FAA can't keep it up, it's a system of a down
f8b881f88a.summary: Outage after outage after outage is a syndrome that needs radical treatment No Access November is going well this year. Among the many organizations to adopt Outage As A Service (OAAS) were Microsoft , Apple , the FAA , and any number of European supermarkets . Even the NSA has succumbed. For us, at least, outage is word of the year. It's certainly deeply embedded in the public mind, with schoolchildren reportedly referring to the 19th century Irish famine as "the potato outage." There's no danger of an outrage outage. OAAS is synonymous with infrastructure failure, a more useful term that begins to hint at cause and cure as well as effect. In all of the latest crop, what we know is depressingly familiar. Microsoft's O365 meltdown was a cascading failure caused by a botched upgrade that took stuff offline and melted down as it tried to come back. The FAA was a migration from Jurassic hardware that wasn't end of life so much as living fossil. The Eurofridge-cum-fondue-maker was a control system so badly written it fell apart if you raised an eyebrow at it. Clearly, nobody had. Until now. These are all different classes of OAAS that have been around for decades. Security-based outages are still outages, and a packet flood is still a packet flood whether it's a botnet DDoS or finger trouble in the config dashboard. Each of them has a root cause with obvious fixes – a faulty mental model of network/server interaction, chronic underfunding, a complete supply chain with little cyber-security expertise. All these, like the poor, will be with us always. They won't fix themselves. Infrastructure that works is invisible, and invisible things are forgotten until they break. What's needed is an infrastructure that watches itself, that is designed to be adaptive and resilient, one that refuses to connect to danger and nulls out any that gets through. There have been attempts to create a ground-up architecture that is inherently risk resistant. One such is SCION (Scalability, Control, and Isolation On Next-generation networks). It redesigns routing between domains around explicit path selection, separate control and data planes, and mechanisms for trust and failure isolation. The result is a very resilient, very reliable, and very secure infrastructure that reflects the designers' tenet that you can't patch the internet into any of these things. Start from scratch or GTFO. SCION started about 15 years ago, and it works well enough to be adopted by entities like the…

a610666769.title: Trump calls on Nvidia board to rehire Jensen Huang after scandal
a610666769.summary: US President Donald Trump has called on the Nvidia board to rehire Jensen Huang, repeating earlier claims that the company's former chief executive remains the best man for one of Silicon Valley's biggest jobs. "I hope the board of Nvidia rehires Jensen Huang. It would be the best thing for the company, and also, for the USA," Mr Trump said in a post on Truth Social on Monday. The statement is the latest intervention by the White House, after Mr Huang stepped down as chief executive this month over his affair with a tech executive linked to China 's intelligence service. On Friday, Mr Trump said he wanted to see Mr Huang given a "second chance" at the major chip company. Jensen Huang won't make Steve Jobs-style comeback, Apple chief's biographer says On Sunday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent refused to rule out the possibility that Mr Huang could return. But Mr Bessent said an investigation had to determine whether chips had been sold to banned states. "We've been in touch with the temporary management, with the lead directors, with their lawyers, ⁠and we do need answers. It behoves Nvidia to move quickly ​on ⁠this because we want ‌to know what the culture was," Bessent told CBS. Mr Huang also admitted to a second affair with a colleague at Nvidia. He resigned two weeks ago , plunging the chip maker into record losses. US regulators, Congress and the FBI want to know whether Singapore-based Megaspeed, led by the woman Mr Huang had an affair with, Alice Huang, bought Nvidia's most advanced chips and funnelled them to China, breaching US government rules. "We do ​need to see who was in charge of ​compliance there," Mr Bessent ‌said. "We will see which level of the business knew about this. Was it ⁠at the lower levels? Was it at the middle level? Did ⁠it go all the way to the top?" Mr Trump said on Friday that he would like Mr Huang to apologise and return to Nvidia. Asked whether he agreed with such an outcome, Mr Bessent said more information ​was needed. "I think we have to see where the buck stops," he added. Nvidia board chairman Harvey Jones has said the company will not rehire Mr Huang . Director of US National Intelligence Jay Clayton told CNN on Sunday that “there are chips that have ended up in places that they should not”, referring to China.

10898fa08f.title: Anthropic Is Worth $1.2 Trillion. Is It a Better Buy Than Nvidia?
10898fa08f.summary: By Adam Spatacco – Nov 23, 2026 at 5:15AM EST 10 stocks we like better than Anthropic › Anthropic ( ANT -8.50% ) made stock market history on Nov. 19, completing the largest initial public offering (IPO) ever. The artificial intelligence (AI) developer behind Claude raised $81 billion , surpassing the roughly $75 billion raised by Elon Musk's Space Exploration Technologies earlier this year. The blockbuster debut illustrates Wall Street's appetite for premier AI stocks . However, Anthropic's valuation raises an important question: Is the frontier lab a better investment than Nvidia ( NVDA -14.01% ) , the semiconductor giant powering much of the AI revolution? Although Anthropic's growth is impressive, Nvidia offers a more attractive combination of profitability, valuation, and shareholder returns. Let's dig into why. Anthropic is experiencing unprecedented commercial momentum as enterprises integrate Claude models into their operations. The company's revenue increased from $386 million in 2024 to $4.6 billion in 2025, representing growth of roughly 1,090%. During the first nine months of 2026, revenue reached $33.2 billion, demonstrating the rapid acceleration in demand for its AI products. Perhaps even more impressive, Anthropic's annualized revenue run rate reached $81 billion as of the end of October. Moreover, the number of customers generating at least $100,000 in trailing annual revenue increased from more than 950 in September 2025 to more than 11,900 in September 2026. With that said, Anthropic's valuation already reflects enormous expectations. As of this writing (Nov. 20), Anthropic boasts a market capitalization of roughly $1.2 trillion. This implies the company trades at roughly 14.8 times its $81 billion annualized revenue run rate. To be clear, this is different from a conventional price-to-sales (P/S) ratio since the run rate annualizes recent activity rather than measuring revenue actually generated over 12 months. More importantly, Anthropic is unprofitable. The company reported an operating loss of roughly $1.3 billion during the first nine months of 2026. In addition, its underlying operations incur significant expenses for training and operating AI models. Anthropic disclosed nearly $900 billion in infrastructure commitments extending through 2045 , including obligations to Microsoft Azure, Amazon Web Services, Alphabet ’s Google Cloud, and SpaceX. 9bb950da8b.title: Google'dan yapay zeka ajanları için simüle edilmiş internet ortamı: Mirror Dimension
9bb950da8b.summary: Google , Chrome ’un web sitelerinde kullanıcı adına çok adımlı görevler gerçekleştirebilen yapay zeka ajanlarının güvenliğini değerlendirmek için “ Mirror Dimension ” adlı yapay bir internet ortamı oluşturdu. Chrome AI Security ekibinin geliştirdiği sistem, gerçek web sitelerini taklit eden binlerce simüle edilmiş sayfada ajanları test ediyor. Böylece denemeler sırasında gerçek sitelerde işlem yapılmasının veya kullanıcıların etkilenmesinin önüne geçiliyor. Google’a göre ajanları doğrudan internet üzerinde test etmek hem güvenlik riski taşıyor hem de sonuçların tekrarlanmasını zorlaştırıyor. Web siteleri sürekli değiştiği için aynı testi aynı koşullarda yeniden çalıştırmak mümkün olmayabiliyor. Ayrıca modelin test edildiğini fark ederek davranışını değiştirmesi, yani eval awareness olarak tanımlanan durum, değerlendirmelerin gerçekçiliğini azaltıyor. Mirror Dimension’da ajan, YouTube gibi gerçek adreslere gittiğini düşünüyor. Ancak Chrome, gVisor adlı yalıtılmış bir ortamda çalışıyor ve ağ trafiği yerel bir proxy üzerinden simüle edilmiş sitelere yönlendiriliyor. Proxy, tarayıcının bağlantıyı güvenli kabul etmesi için test ortamına özel TLS sertifikaları oluşturuyor. Ortamda e-ticaret, sosyal medya, tarif ve yerel hizmet siteleri gibi farklı kullanım senaryoları bulunuyor. Bu siteler elle hazırlanmıyor. Bir araştırma ajanı ihtiyaçları ve site özelliklerini belirliyor, oluşturucu ajan HTML, CSS ve JavaScript kodlarını yazıyor, eleştiri ajanları ise erişilebilirlik, form doğrulama, hatalar ve farklı ekran boyutlarını kontrol ediyor. Sistem aynı zamanda dolaylı prompt injection saldırılarını da test ediyor. Zararlı talimatlar sayfalardaki metin ve görsellere, ARIA etiketlerine veya WebMCP yanıtlarına gizlenebiliyor. Google’ın otomatik test hattı, her güvenlik mühendisi başına günde 1.000’den fazla saldırı test adayı üretebiliyor. Bu sayı başarılı saldırıları değil, test adaylarını ifade ediyor. Google, Mirror Dimension’ı Chrome’un iç güvenlik testlerinde kullanacağını belirtiyor ve kamuya açılacağına dair bir duyuru henüz yapmadı. Görsel kaynak: ChatGPT

507e30a830.title: Recap: Anthropic IPO, tech rout, Nvidia, and outage aftermath
507e30a830.summary: Happy almost-Thanksgiving, after what frankly has been a helluva few weeks in tech. Personally, I’ve found the last couple news cycles to be surreal, strange, and consequential. As we’re barreling towards the holiday (and the very end of 2026), I reckoned it might be useful to distill down a few key thoughts about what the news of recent weeks might mean moving forward. Anthropic out, tech rout… Anthropic last week went public in a day-one 17% stock pop that mutated pretty quickly into a widespread tech rout. The Claude maker, still valued over $1 trillion even after its stock dropped 8% on Friday , instantaneously became an AI bellwether—and the broader market news was simply bad. The Nasdaq finished the week down 2.66% year-to-date, and both the Dow and the S&P 500 closed in correction territory. Expect volatility through the end of the year. I don’t know if the AI bubble will “officially” pop before Dec. 31, but we may well remember this moment as the instability before everything changed. Most of Anthropic’s employees may be paper millionaires, but it’s a rough road ahead. Life after Jensen has commenced… After Jensen Huang’s shocking ouster, Nvidia reported earnings last week, revealing beats across the board. This muted some of the deepest fears about Nvidia’s near-term future, but that earnings win doesn’t change much, as questions about the company’s future abound: Can Nvidia be relied upon to carry on as AI’s central bank, for both startups and data center financing deals? What will happen to neoclouds like CoreWeave and Lambda Labs without Huang as guarantor? And who will be Nvidia’s next CEO? Arm’s Rene Haas keeps coming up, but nothing’s over until it’s over. And Nvidia’s future, in short, will remain uncertain for months (and maybe years) to come. Outages, hacks, and midterm reverberations… It was only on Oct. 29 that news of the astonishing $6.3 billion Binance hack made headlines, and since then, there’s been a frightening wave of outages, from the FAA ground stoppage on Nov. 13 to the Microsoft outage that took down email (on the same day Huang was ousted no less). There have also been outages at Chase, Bank of America , Apple , and even internal systems at the NSA. Look for cybersecurity conversations to ramp up even more over the coming weeks and months—and cross over with the new crop entering Congress, who will likely have many questions for tech giants and key figures over the coming months about cyber safety, data centers, and the AI…

5103ccfb12.title: OpenAI publishes a progress chart and asks every AI lab to agree on shared limits
5103ccfb12.summary: Nobody has agreed to anything yet, but the company that set the pace for the industry is now asking it to brake together. If you build on frontier models or hold AI stocks, watch what a shared limit would do to release dates and compute bills. Jakub Pachocki, OpenAI's chief scientist, published a post on Sunday, November 22, titled 'Perplexity and Intelligence,' that proposes a common yardstick for how far AI labs should push their models. According to TechCrunch, the idea is that companies would commit not to go past a set threshold of perplexity, which measures how well a model predicts the next word, 'until our ability to understand and monitor AI behavior achieves a certain concrete milestone.' It's a voluntary pledge. No lab has signed anything, and no binding cap exists. The post comes with a chart, and the chart is the argument. TechCrunch reports that Pachocki's chart tracks OpenAI's models on this score, where lower is better. GPT-4 sat at roughly 0.91, when it became good at step-by-step reasoning. Pachocki writes that once losses fell below 0.8, 'we have seen the emergence of transformative capabilities in fields like cybersecurity and mathematics.' ShiftDelete.Net adds that he expects further jumps in a 0.68 to 0.7 window and says he doesn't know what they will be. Pachocki's answer, as ShiftDelete.Net relays it, is that handing competitors a clearer picture of where OpenAI stands is a cost 'outweighed by the urgency of establishing shared safety measures across the industry.' Frankly, the choice of metric is smart and also convenient. Perplexity is hard to game with a benchmark-tuned model, and it needs no outside grader. But Pachocki himself lists the weak spots: labs use different datasets, perplexity doesn't map neatly onto tasks people care about, and chain-of-thought can raise capability without moving the number. A limit built on a number every lab measures differently is a limit each lab can argue its way around. OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki published an essay saying no AI lab, including OpenAI, has solved alignment well enough to keep scaling at full speed, just three days after OpenAI shipped GPT-6 Astra, its first model to cross a Critical cybersecurity threshold. beca9fe66d.title: OpenAI Chief Scientist Proposes Perplexity Thresholds for Shared AI Safety Limits
beca9fe66d.summary: On November 22, 2026, OpenAI Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki proposed that frontier artificial intelligence laboratories adopt shared pretraining perplexity thresholds as binding development speed limits, urging developers to halt capability scaling past defined mathematical loss boundaries until verified behavioral monitoring and alignment safeguards are established across the industry. In a technical policy publication released on November 22, 2026, OpenAI Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki published an essay titled “Perplexity and Intelligence” arguing that the global AI community must move beyond downstream benchmarks to govern frontier safety. Pachocki stated that while specialized evaluation leaderboards saturate and become obsolete across model generations, pretraining log-perplexity—measured as cross-entropy loss on held-out text and code—provides a consistent, durable indicator of emergent intelligence across foundation model architectures. To establish a shared scientific baseline among frontier developers, Pachocki disclosed historical pretraining figures evaluated on a fixed snapshot of OpenAI’s internal codebase. He argued that unpredictable capabilities originate directly from pretraining compression rather than fine-tuning alone. Pachocki proposed that leading labs agree on common development limits, committing not to train past designated perplexity thresholds until researchers achieve concrete milestones in behavioral monitoring and alignment verification. The disclosed metrics demonstrate how incremental reductions in base model loss produce qualitative leaps in latent competence. According to Pachocki, GPT-2 established paragraph coherence, while GPT-3 introduced in-context learning. GPT-3.5 reached a log-perplexity of approximately 0.99 on the evaluated corpus, enabling fluent conversational dialogue for ChatGPT. When GPT-4 reached roughly 0.91, the architecture began utilizing chain-of-thought reasoning productively, prompting targeted post-training elicitation that led to dedicated reasoning models. The progression below 0.80 loss marked a larger transformation. OpenAI observed that models reaching a log-perplexity of approximately 0.76 began resolving open problems in mathematics and conducting autonomous cybersecurity vulnerability analysis. 261097f540.summary: The company’s co-founders are now wildly rich, while countless Americans face AI-driven threats to their jobs and fears of a stock bubble T he sultans of Silicon Valley and the wizards of Wall Street rejoiced this week when Anthropic raised an eye-popping $81bn in the largest initial public offering in history. They saw the AI company’s IPO as a gung-ho affirmation of Silicon Valley’s and Wall Street’s marriage of technology and capitalism. For many employees at the company that developed Claude, the public offering must have been a thing of dreams. With the IPO valuing Anthropic at $1.5tn, the company’s seven co-founders each came away with stakes worth about $20bn , while, by one estimate , 600 of Anthropic’s more than 5,000 employees will have holdings topping $100m and 2,800 others will have shares worth more than $10m. But while the IPO fueled jubilation in Silicon Valley and Wall Street, I’m sure that many Americans resented the fact that Anthropic’s employees and early investors became immensely rich even as millions of Americans distrust and dread AI, fearing that it could have disastrous results for workers, the overall economy and humankind. And let’s not forget that millions of Americans are furious about the many datacenters that have been foisted on their communities; many of those centers have pushed up electricity prices, disrupted communities, received big tax breaks and created annoying, round-the-clock noise. Anthropic’s successful IPO and the huge media attention it received have in ways shined a spotlight on the country’s immense wealth and income inequality. A small elite did marvelously, while the masses have nothing to celebrate. They feel left out and left behind in the IPO’s financial frenzy at the same time that many Americans are deeply worried that AI is a high-tech grim reaper that will someday come for their – and their children’s – jobs. What’s more, many workers and retirees have only recently discovered that their 401k’s and index funds have investments in AI companies that they didn’t know about or choose. Notwithstanding Anthropic’s big day, there are growing fears among workers and retirees that an AI bust or burst bubble could take a hugely painful bite out of their retirement funds. According to a recent JP Morgan analysis , corporations with ties to AI make up 49% of the S&P 500’s market value, and if those companies’ shares drop 20% or 30% in value, that’s going to pummel the finances of millions of Americans. Anthropic PBC, the U.S. company behind the Claude chatbot, saw its shares fall 8.5% on their second trading day, according to the report. The timing hurts. Chinese AI labs had been weighing or preparing share sales while a high-profile American rival tested public investors. Instead of a clean read-across, they got a wobble. Bloomberg also put the rout in China’s technology shares at roughly US$1.7 trillion, a figure that dwarfs any single listing. This analysis separates what Bloomberg confirmed from what remains open. Anthropic’s valuation and first-week trading are on the record, and our earlier look at how the Anthropic offering closed covers the mechanics. The Chinese side is murkier. No listing dates, offer prices or deal sizes have been confirmed for any of the three AI labs, and nobody has shown that Anthropic’s stock drove their timing. Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. Bloomberg’s central point is simple. Several Chinese AI developers wanted to tap public markets, and the window narrowed just as they prepared to move. The outlet identified DeepSeek, Moonshot AI and StepFun as Anthropic competitors that were weighing or preparing share sales. It also pointed to Z.AI Co and CXMT Corp, two Chinese companies whose shares had struggled. That framing matters for a reason. Investors rarely judge a first-time issuer in isolation. They compare it with peers that already trade, and they price in how those peers behaved. When struggling Chinese listings sit next to a freshly listed American AI company that slipped on day two, the bar for the next issuer rises. Bloomberg did not claim that Anthropic’s slide caused any Chinese company to delay. The report describes a clouded backdrop, not a chain of cause and effect. We treat it the same way here. The launch addresses a familiar problem. Some jobs need more judgment than a quick chatbot reply, yet come up too often to hand to a flagship model every time. Summarizing a short meeting transcript is a different assignment from tying its decisions back to a budget and a stack of project notes. A model that can finish the second job with fewer corrections could save meaningful time across a team. Neon gives Google a distinct tier for users who face that kind of work regularly. Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers can find Gemini 4 Neon under Deeper analysis in the model picker. Google says Gemini Tasks can also run on Neon, and the app can draw on relevant material from connected Google apps such as Gmail and Docs. While flights and Microsoft applications have since returned to normal, readers across the US have shared their frustrations with the Guardian. Many have directed their anger at the Trump administration, questioning its competence and calling for greater accountability and transparency about the systems millions of people rely on. Mona Berrier, a 69-year-old retiree in California, questioned the lack of backup systems after a router installation involving the replacement of copper wires with fiber-optic cables by contractor L3Harris in Arkansas caused a data overload in the FAA’s telecommunications infrastructure. “I find it impossible to believe a single router brought the nation to its knees. There would have to be no redundancy or no contingency for backup plans. Is it possible for any government to run that way?” she said. Berrier, who said the incident was making her “more reticent” about travelling, also expressed a broader distrust of the administration. “I don’t believe anything this administration says. Not a day goes by without a lie, a grift exposed or some attempt to hide information from the public. What we get is propaganda that is intended to mislead and manipulate,” she added. Jeffrey Stark, a resident of Ashland, Oregon, also pointed to L3Harris and questioned the government’s relationship with the contractor. “The scapegoat for the FAA shutdown is L3Harris,” Stark said. “What [transportation] secretary [Sean] Duffy fails to mention is that the US government has a $1bn investment in L3Harris. This is a case of the tail wagging the dog. And it is a textbook example of what fascism looks like when a government invests in and directs private corporations.” For Timothy Paulson, a freelance writer based in New York City, the groundstop was “jarring”. “Having lived through 9/11, I felt the weight of it then, so the contrast with the triviality provided by TV wrestler [and homeland security secretary] Markwayne Mullin and reality show Duffy’s pathetic dog-and-pony show wasn’t just disheartening, it was Kafkaesque,” he said. 6a89f22c07.title: Are recent tech outages the new normal? The Director of National Intelligence weighs in:
6a89f22c07.summary: The FBI is investigating a hack of its national law enforcement database as recent tech outages disrupt services across major companies and government agencies The FBI is investigating a hack of its national law enforcement database as recent tech outages disrupt services across major companies and government agencies Recent technology outages causing banking delays, transportation issues, and email disruptions are raising concerns for many Americans. On Saturday, the FBI reportedly began investigating the hack of its National Crime Information Center database, which contains records on fugitives, missing persons, criminal history, and stolen property. The FBI has historically been a target for hackers. President Donald Trump commented on the apparent hack, saying it isn't good. Over the past week, outages have impacted services at Microsoft, JPMorgan Chase, Apple, and government agencies such as the Federal Aviation Administration and the National Security Agency. The Trump administration stated that these outages were caused by routine efforts to upgrade computer systems and address vulnerabilities, rather than a cyberattack. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton addressed the situation, warning Americans to expect more disruptions as systems undergo upgrades. "Our systems are going to need to be upgraded, and as part of that ongoing upgrade, we are going to have glitches, gaps, interruptions in service. That is going to happen," Clayton said. On Sunday, more than half of Delta flights were delayed. The airline said this was due to a problem with an automation system. It's a program that ensures an aircraft isn't too heavy to fly. We reached out to Delta for a comment on the situation, and the airline said the system is now working. Lawmakers from both parties are demanding answers following the recent outages, especially as millions of Americans prepare to travel during the holiday season.
