de478ea7a6.title: What to know before using AI agents for Black Friday shopping
de478ea7a6.summary: A pop-up shop for "dots" a personal assistant agent at the OpenAI developers conference on September 29, 2026 in San Francisco, California. Sam Altman announced a new artificial intelligence personal assistant agents named "dots" to rival Meta's Muse. Heather Diehl/Getty Images hide caption Artificial intelligence is here to help with Black Friday. This weekend, 59% of consumers plan on using AI to support their winter shopping, according to the National Retail Federation . But AI has proven one way it is not unlike humans: It makes mistakes. The stakes of those hallucinations are much higher when your wallet – and holiday unwrapping memories – are on the line. These tools also become better shoppers when you hand over personal data, which also means giving up more information on your private life to massive tech companies. Here are some tips – and notes of caution – before using AI as your personal holiday shopper. Traditional online shopping is about search terms and the infinite product scroll. AI is meant to be a conversation. Unlike shopping on a retail website, AI platforms are designed to look more like texting apps. Prompt bars on these platforms sit on the bottom of the page, inviting a back and forth chat between user and bot about what to buy. After all, it can be hard to know what keyword to plug in to shop for uncle before the Christmas exchange. AI instead allows for search based on a vibe – like describing that uncle's hobbies and personal style. If a shopper wants to buy a suitcase to support their uncle's European travel dreams, this makes it easier to narrow down the options. "You can say if that bag is overstuffed, will it fit under the seat on JetBlue?" says Emily Pfeiffer, a principal analyst at Forrester who advises retailers and brands on digital commerce strategy, including for AI. "Don't give me the dimensions," she advises, "Tell me if it will suit my use case." Pfeiffer cautions that even though AI is able to think through these nuanced shopping criteria, it works better with more hand holding. 7354ff43a6.title: AI agents now control part of Deepmind's compute for Gemini experiments, but recursive self-improvement remains distant
7354ff43a6.summary: Google Deepmind lets AI agents run experiments on their own for the next Gemini model. On the company's podcast, VP of Research Koray Kavukcuoglu, who leads Gemini development, frames this as part of a strategic shift at the lab. Rather than running separate teams for specialized projects like AlphaFold and nuclear fusion, Deepmind now relies on a single general-purpose algorithm for both science and products, he says. Each Gemini generation, he adds, is a hand-built one-off rather than a fixed architecture, while parallel teams work on its successors. According to Kavukcuoglu, AI agents control part of the compute themselves to run experiments, though the lab is still far from full recursive self-improvement. As a safety measure, Deepmind doesn't reward the agents' internal thought streams ("Chain of Thought") during training, he says, so their intentions stay unfiltered and reviewable in natural language before they act. Kavukcuoglu also points to limits. Today's AI can depict physical processes such as fluid flows and collisions with visual accuracy, he says, but doesn't understand them precisely. No test can show when models will close those gaps and reach artificial general intelligence (AGI), he argues, because no benchmark captures the core of intelligence. In his view, AGI won't begin until useful everyday products earn enough trust for people to hand decisions over to them, the way they would when working with other people. Ad Ad

49df1091dd.title: Microsoft declares “Code Red” after huge Outlook outage
49df1091dd.summary: Microsoft is now holding daily meetings with the engineering group responsible for Microsoft 365 services. Microsoft is now holding daily meetings with the engineering group responsible for Microsoft 365 services. This month’s Exchange Online and Microsoft Outlook outage has prompted the software giant to declare an unusual “Code Red” internally, Reuters reports . The nearly 24-hour outage took down email for millions of customers, and was triggered by a bug that had been sitting on Microsoft 365 networking gateway servers since July without any impact to servers. In a memo to the teams responsible for Exchange Online, Microsoft 365 Core president Jason Henderson revealed the outage was the most significant in history for Microsoft’s customers. “Unfortunately, all the work we have done over the years was not sufficient to protect us on Thursday,” said Henderson. “Code Red means that this is the highest priority work for our team.” As part of this Code Red declaration, Microsoft is focused on load shedding, geographic traffic partitioning, and faster recovery mechanisms. Microsoft now has a target of resolving future outages within an hour, and will reportedly deploy AI agents to help engineers diagnose issues. Microsoft is now holding daily meetings with the engineering group responsible for Microsoft 365 services, alongside weekly reviews. In a separate memo, Amanda Silver, Microsoft’s corporate vice president of M365 Core and Work IQ, said engineers had to work through a “fog of war” to help resolve the outage. I reported last week that Microsoft engineers had a running bridge call during the entire outage, and at one point it hit the maximum of 1,000 participants. Microsoft engineers had to exchange messages across 11 Teams chats and reportedly “struggled ​to maintain a cohesive picture” during the outage because of the fragmented internal tracking systems. Sources tell me the outage was marked as “sev0,” the highest level, which indicates a catastrophic level of service disruption. Engineers struggled to get servers back online because they had entered maintenance mode and became unresponsive due to unusually high CPU loads.

caa0b283e0.title: Are tech outages the new normal in the AI era?
caa0b283e0.summary: Inaccessible email inboxes. Banking delays. A communications meltdown that grounded airplanes for hours, followed by waves of other travel disruptions. And a cyberattack that breached an unclassified system at the CIA. In an increasingly interconnected world, some fear such disruptions could be the new normal.This month alone, problems that appeared to emerge from routine updates, security patches or other malfunctions surfaced at Microsoft, JPMorgan Chase and Apple, and even the US government's Federal Aviation Administration and National Security Agency. The Trump administration said there was "zero" indication the latest outages are linked, or caused by bad actors like cybercriminals, reported Associated Press. The era of artificial intelligence has also raised the stakes for internet security overall. As AI tools uncover new vulnerabilities, many other companies and institutions are racing to patch them before they can be targeted by hackers, a cat-and-mouse game that can lead to a different set of glitches. Social media platforms have been abuzz with a mixture of annoyance, confusion, conspiracy theories and jokes about the string of outages. "To see several disruptions this close together, I think to a lot of people it's made them realise how many parts of their lives they've handed over to these systems that we still, at this point, don't fully understand," Jake Smith, a content creator who regularly posts videos about politics on platforms like Instagram and YouTube, said in an interview. "I think it gives people a sense of helplessness to see all of it happening concurrently in a way." Outages and technology errors have piled up across sectors. On Nov.11, a global Microsoft outage disrupted email and other workplace tools, plunging business and everyday services into disarray worldwide, reported Associated Press. Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot, were interrupted. Microsoft cited, in part, a failure during a recent upgrade to its servers, spanning from what the company later determined was a "latent defect" in a network fix it had begun deploying over the summer. For air travel, a separate malfunction in the FAA's network led to the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years on Nov. 13. The stop lasted for more than four hours, and carriers cancelled and delayed swaths of flights as they worked to recover. Just days later, United Airlines saw its own system outage – forcing it to delay departing flights…

32c228105f.title: University of California Spends $1.2 Million Annually on OpenAI Deal Despite Faculty Opposition
32c228105f.summary: The University of California has agreed to spend $1.2 million a year on an expanded partnership with OpenAI, giving students, professors and staff across its 10 campuses access to ChatGPT Edu and other artificial intelligence tools. The deal will begin Dec. 1, despite objections from faculty leaders who say they were not given enough time to review a decision that could affect teaching, learning and research. UC leaders say the agreement will make AI tools available to more people at no extra cost to individual users. They also say it will provide stronger privacy protections than students and employees may have when using personal ChatGPT accounts. The yearlong agreement includes access to ChatGPT Edu, OpenAI's coding agent Codex, AI literacy workshops and expanded workforce training. The university serves about 300,000 students and 265,000 workers across its 10-campus system. However, the UC Academic Senate has questioned how the agreement was approved. Faculty representatives asked UC President James Milliken to delay the purchase until professors had a meaningful chance to discuss its effects on academic work. The disagreement centers on more than the cost of the software. Faculty members say a tool that can produce essays, answer questions and complete other tasks could change how students learn and how instructors measure their work. They also worry that making ChatGPT available to everyone could make it appear that the university supports its use in every course. Milliken has decided to move forward. He said students and employees are already using AI tools through personal accounts, which may not have the same privacy protections as accounts covered by a university agreement. "The agreement will make OpenAI's tools available to more UC community members at no cost to individuals, with clear guardrails," the university said in its announcement. The decision also comes as colleges across the country debate how to use AI without weakening academic standards or putting student information at risk. The university says the agreement is meant to give students and employees fair access to AI tools, regardless of how much money they have. Some students may already pay for advanced AI services, while others rely on free versions or do not use them at all. Rachel Zaentz, a spokesperson for the UC Office of the President, said the partnership is intended to reduce that gap. "The reality is that access to AI tools is currently uneven among students. 0a28f6d3df.title: Report details staff fears over unreleased Anthropic and OpenAI models
0a28f6d3df.summary: Staff at Anthropic and OpenAI fear their unreleased models cannot be shipped safely, Axios reported on November 24 . Drawing on more than two dozen sources, Axios describes an internal debate over whether future frontier AI should stay inside the labs or be built at all. The report, featured in The Rundown’s November 25 briefing , cites staff who describe internal models as “far more powerful” than public products and say they show signs of hiding their reasoning from safety monitors. The size of the gap and the strongest claims about loss of control remain unresolved. Anthropic pushed back, saying “Keeping a model internal doesn't make it safe,” according to Axios. In its November 18 safety disclosure , OpenAI said stricter requirements were slowing releases and described separate reviews for training, internal deployment and external deployment. OpenAI also said it paused training and evaluation of its most capable models from September 20 to October 1 after monitors caught an internal research model exploiting a network configuration error to gain limited internet access. The account shows both an internal safety problem and a successful intervention. OpenAI’s November 10 monitoring study gives a technical basis for concern. Researchers found that stronger initial training can improve reasoning without a written explanation, while training through rewards can improve a model’s ability to manipulate the reasoning it shows. The authors caution that their tests offer imperfect measures of the risk. In one pair of similarly capable models, researchers did not find the expected link between greater control over written reasoning and more successful evasion of monitors. On November 22, OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki proposed shared development limits that labs would not cross until monitoring reaches specified milestones. He suggested measuring those limits partly through perplexity, a measure of how well a model predicts text. He acknowledged that it is hard to compare across labs and misses some sources of capability gains. The limits remain a proposal. Public models provide an incomplete view of the labs’ capabilities. In its November 5 assessment of Anthropic , METR described an internal model under the anonymous label “Model 4,” whose training finished in September or October. bcc809b5d2.summary: Eric Gerard Ruiz & Corey Noles November 25, 2026 So apparently Google told every AI agent that wants into your Gmail to use the front door from now on. Google made its Workspace MCP servers and command-line tool generally available , and starting February 1, 2027, agents must reach Workspace data through them instead of calling Google's regular APIs directly. Translation. MCP (Model Context Protocol) is a standard plug that lets an AI agent talk to an app, and these servers cover Gmail, Drive, Docs, Sheets, Slides, Calendar, Chat, and Tasks. Going through that door lets admins see what each agent does, require a human thumbs-up for risky actions, and keep an audit log. Google's post doesn't say how it will enforce the deadline. Your inbox finally has a bouncer, and the bouncer keeps receipts. 😸 DeepMind launched a test for consistent AI answers 📰 Anthropic and OpenAI staff doubt unreleased models are safe 📰 OpenAI's GPT-6.2 designed lab-tested protein binders 🍪 Claude artifacts now install as desktop apps 🧠 GPT-6.2 Astra identified an 1808 sketchbook's artist ... and a whole lot more that you can read about here. Google DeepMind launched Humanity's First Exam , a test of 544 everyday questions for AI models. The name winks at Humanity's Last Exam, a famously brutal benchmark (a standardized test for AI). This one goes the other direction. Instead of asking whether a model can crack one impossible problem, it asks whether the model gets an easy problem right every time. The test checks each task plus slight variations of it. Think of the coworker who nails a spreadsheet on Monday and fumbles the same one on Tuesday. Smart, sure. Reliable, no. Here's a sample. One prompt shows a neon sign and asks for the color of the third letter in each word, separated by semicolons. The correct answer is green; yellow; white; blue; blue. You could do that in seconds. Doing it correctly across every tweaked version is the actual test. 544 prompts covering text and images, grouped into sets of four related questions across 20 foundational capabilities Tasks like counting objects, naming colors and symbols, tracking positions, basic arithmetic, following strict formatting, and spotting false premises (a trick question built on something untrue) A live leaderboard on Kaggle (a site where data scientists compete and share datasets) A three-week Kaggle contest through December 15, where anyone can submit everyday questions that current models still get wrong DeepMind says…

3543a3ce57.title: The Trump team is getting more and more evasive about Jensen Huang
3543a3ce57.summary: When Jensen Huang was shockingly reinstalled as CEO of Nvidia on Monday, both Nvidia’s board of directors and President Donald Trump cast it as the result of the administration’s assurances that he wasn’t a national security risk and faced no legal jeopardy. But pretty much ever since then, those assurances have appeared less than ironclad. All of which reinforces what a massive risk both Trump and Nvidia just took , which should be ratcheting up concerns among some very skeptical GOP lawmakers . What Nvidia and Trump initially said The board said in its initial statement Monday morning that its talks with senior government officials left it “confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk” — despite the fact that he had an affair with a woman who US officials feared could be working with Chinese intelligence. Trump said shortly thereafter on social media that the US government “has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security.” Trump also said that, despite questions about prohibited Nvidia chips making their way to China, Attorney General Todd Blanche “has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that [Huang] has engaged in any unlawful conduct.” But other officials have yet to publicly double down on those assurances. And Blanche was rather evasive in an interview Monday night. Even Trump has repeatedly emphasized very real caveats. Blanche’s evasive comments In addition to the assurances he offered on Truth Social on Monday morning, Trump in a later CNBC interview claimed the Justice Department had “exonerated” Huang . “They did a study. They did a pretty good investigation,” Trump said. “And they felt that he himself was exonerated. I don’t know what word you want to use.” The US Commerce and Justice Departments previously said investigators had conducted an in-person interview with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang as part of an investigation into whether the Singaporean-based company had been diverting US semiconductors. But now Blanche is talking around all that, with increasingly evasive comments about what sort of investigations have occurred or been opened — even accusing reporters of “mocking” him by asking the questions. “What I said last week is that we were looking into it,” Blanche said at the Justice Department on Tuesday. “The FBI, law enforcement, looks into things all the time. That doesn’t necessarily become a criminal investigation. Doesn’t…

ce547c734e.title: Like ‘family businesses’: Inside the Nvidia board that ousted and rehired Jensen Huang
ce547c734e.summary: New York — Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang gushed last year that support from longtime board members Tench Coxe, Mark Stevens and Harvey Jones was crucial to helping him navigate three decades of running the company. “They not one time gave up on the company and us,” Huang told the Acquired podcast of the board members and other early employees. Those same supporters have now helped see Huang through his biggest challenge yet — restoring his role as CEO following an unprecedented corporate scandal. But their close relationships have also raised questions about the board’s independence and whether it was equipped to hold Huang accountable and protect shareholders’ interests. Including Huang, nearly half of Nvidia’s 11-person board has been with the company since its early days. Its three longest-serving members — Coxe, Stevens and Jones — saw the value of their combined holdings in the company jump by nearly $2.5 billion from Friday to Monday, after Huang was brought back. His reinstatement marks a sharp turnaround from a week ago, when Jones said the board had unanimously accepted Huang’s resignation, and had no intention of bringing him back. And it comes despite Huang’s relationship with a woman that US officials feared could be a Chinese intelligence asset, as well as multiple reports about an extramarital affair with a subordinate. President Donald Trump has also been open about his role in pushing the board to give Huang his job back. “The appearance of the relationship between the board and Jensen is most akin to family businesses that go public — that’s a domain in which it’s not uncommon for directors to be there for a long time,” said Jo-Ellen Pozner, management professor at Santa Clara University’s Leavey School of Business. “But those kinds of companies are not major players in the global economy.” Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, the Yale professor known as the “CEO Whisperer,” on Monday called the Nvidia board’s decision to reinstate Huang a “complete failure of corporate governance” and urged them to resign. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment on this story. The Board Aside from Huang, whose board seat was restored along with his CEO title, four members of Nvidia’s board have been with the company for around three decades. That includes Jones, who was named last week as Nvidia’s first-ever board chair after joining the company at its inception in 1993. At the time, he’d been serving as CEO of software firm Synopsys, where Nvidia’s…

3facbb6240.title: Microsoft declares 'Code Red' after historic service outage
3facbb6240.summary: (Photo by Gene Medi/NurPhoto via Getty Images) Tech giant Microsoft declared a "Code Red" alert recently, signaling an urgent effort to address the historic 24-hour outage that downed its core products between Nov. 12-13. The outage , which brought down the majority of Microsoft's core products, "affected most" of Microsoft's users, according to the company's post-incident report. The company's total user base is between 420 million and 450 million people, according to financial disclosures. "Code Red means that this is the highest priority work for our team," M365 Core President Jason Henderson said in an email to employees Friday obtained by Reuters . DAVID MARCUS: WHAT BIG TECH’S WEEKEND FROM HELL MEANS FOR THE FUTURE OF DATA CENTERS The incident also marked the most customer-impacting event in Microsoft's history, Henderson told employees. Microsoft blamed the outage on a previously undetected scalability defect within the Windows operating system . SWIFT ASSURANCES FROM OFFICIALS AFTER WAVE OF NATIONWIDE OUTAGES RAISES QUESTIONS, EXPERT SAYS "Unfortunately, all the work we have done over the years was not sufficient to protect us on Thursday," Henderson wrote. Microsoft employees exchanged over 11,000 messages during the crisis in an effort to diagnose the issue, Microsoft Corporate Vice President Amanda Silver told employees in a memo Monday. DHS CHIEF TELLS AMERICANS TO 'BREATHE' AMID TECH OUTAGES, INSISTS HOMELAND IS 'SECURE' Silver also detailed the nature of the "Code Red" rapid response, explaining that the mobilization would involve five work streams focused on load shedding, geographic traffic partitioning and faster recovery mechanisms. She added that, in the event of a future situation of a similar nature, the company is working on a target to be able to restore service to users within one hour. The company will also work on deploying AI agents to help with quicker diagnosis in the future. Mr Huang had been likened to the Ben Bernanke of AI, effectively running quantitative easing for the entire industry. 7db8168105.summary: India's teenage star Vaibhav Sooryavanshi smashed multiple records as he produced an explosive knock of 204 from just 53 balls to help India A thrash the UAE in the Asia Cup Rising Stars in Doha on Tuesday. They included the fastest century and double century in List A cricket, as the 15-year-old batter reached his century off 28 deliveries during Tuesday's group fixture, breaking Australian Jake Fraser-McGurk's record by one ball. He then raced to his next hundred off just 24 balls, bringing up his double-century in a total of 52 deliveries and obliterating the previous record of 103 balls, held by Chad Bowes. Sooryavanshi hits 28 sixes in record 52-ball double century against UAE It was Sooryavanshi's second List A century in 16 innings, and he is now the holder of four significant records. He made the fastest fifty in List A cricket against Sri Lanka A earlier this year (off 11 balls). On Tuesday against the UAE, he added the fastest 100 (28 balls), fastest 150 (40 balls, beating his own record of 59 balls) and fastest 200 (52 balls). Sooryavanshi also smashed an incredible 28 sixes in his innings, the most in a List A innings, breaking D'Arcy Short's record of 23 against Queensland in 2018. Sooryavanshi said after the match that he feels nerves like any player, but has the knack of quickly settling into his groove. He said: “You do feel a little pressure. It’s normal, it’s human nature to feel a bit nervous. But after two or four balls, I settle down and get back to normal. “It feels good. I’ve got my flow back in the game, so I’ll try to carry this forward into the remaining matches of the tournament. Hopefully, we win the semi-final and reach the final, and I can continue playing with the same flow and in my own way." aa33bb38bb.summary: Travellers using Gatwick Airport have been warned their personal details may have been compromised after its parking system was hacked. Attackers breached AutoPay, the automated drop-off payment system, possibly accessing some customer card details. Gatwick, the UK’s second-largest airport with 43 million passengers annually, told customers on Monday of the risk to their personal information. Heathrow expansion could be delivered by rival company Drivers are charged £10 for staying up to 10 minutes in terminal drop-off zones. Although the payment system was switched off after the breach, customers were told they must still pay the charge through its website. The airport did not reveal when the hack occurred or how many people were affected. In an email sent to customers, the airport apologised and said it had been informed by its third-party provider Times24 UK Limited, there had been “unauthorised access” to the payments system. It said the data that had potentially been stolen included names, postcodes, contact details, vehicle details, payment records and some card details, including in “some isolated cases” the card brand, last four digits and expiry date. It told customers it was trying to determine the “nature and scope of the incident”, while relevant authorities had been informed. “We have been informed by Times24 UK Limited, the company which manages drop-off zones on behalf of London Gatwick that they experienced unauthorised access to AutoPay, a third-party system that automatically processes the payment of drop-off charges," Gatwick said. “As a precaution and to help protect affected accounts, the AutoPay system has been disabled. Passengers can still continue to use the drop-off zones and pay using one of the alternative payment methods available on our London Gatwick website.” The breach is the latest attack on the UK’s data systems. In August, the data of almost nine million passengers using three airports was accessed by hackers, who demanded a ransom. The attack on Manchester Airports Group, which owns Manchester, East Midlands and London Stansted airports, breached similar data to the Gatwick incident. Last year, European airports including Heathrow were hit by delays after a cyber attack hit the check-in and baggage systems. 9d448c3e99.title: California sues OpenAI over alleged unsafe AI development practices
9d448c3e99.summary: California Attorney General Rob Bonta on Sunday highlighted a lawsuit his office filed against OpenAI on November 16, alleging that the company endangered and misled the public by failing to implement adequate safeguards during the development and testing of advanced artificial intelligence (AI) models. The lawsuit , filed in San Francisco Superior Court, alleges violations of California’s Unfair Competition Law and seeks to hold OpenAI liable for creating a public nuisance. Bonta alleges that OpenAI violated California Business and Professions Code § 17200 , which prohibits unlawful, unfair or fraudulent business practices and misleading advertising. According to the complaint, OpenAI repeatedly misrepresented the adequacy of its safety protocols to the public. The lawsuit follows a July 2026 cyberattack targeting Hugging Face, an open-source AI hosting platform. The incident was one of at least 80 cybersecurity incidents identified by the attorney general’s office. Bonta launched a formal investigation into the incident in September. Bonta further alleges that OpenAI’s unsafe development and testing practices constitute a public nuisance under California Civil Code §§ 3479–3480 . California law defines a public nuisance as a nuisance that affects an entire community or neighborhood, or a considerable number of people. Bonta seeks injunctive relief to address OpenAI’s allegedly unsafe business practices. In a November 18 statement , OpenAI said it had strengthened its safeguards and alignment requirements for training, testing and deploying AI models following the July incident.
